questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: True about the definition of Postural Hypotension:
options: Decrease in Systolic blood pressure 20 mmHg after 6 mins of standing
Decrease in Systolic blood pressure 20 mmHg after 3 min of standing
Decrease in Diastolic blood pressure 20 mmHg after 6 mins of standing
Decrease in diastolic blood pressure 20 mmHg after 3 mins of standing
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Decrease in Systolic blood pressure 20 mmHg after 3 min of standing

Orthostatic hypotension or postural hypotension is defined as a sustained drop in systolic BP of ≥20 mmHg or diastolic BP of ≥10 mmHg after 3 min of standing.

It can manifest as lightheadedness/dizziness, weakness or tiredness, difficulty thinking/concentrating, blurred vision, and anxiety.

In non-neurogenic causes of orthostatic hypotension such as hypovolemia, the drop in the blood pressure is accompanied by a compensatory increase in heart rate of >15 beats/min. In neurogenic causes, there is aggravation or precipitation of orthostatic hypotension by autonomic stressors like a meal, hot bath, or exercise.

Non-neurogenic causes of orthostatic hypotension include

• Cardiac pump failure - myocardial infarction, myocarditis, aortic stenosis
• Hypovolemia - dehydration, diarrhea, hemorrhage
• Metabolic - adrenocortical insufficiency, pheochromocytoma
• Venous pooling - sepsis, prolonged standing, or recumbency
• Medications - alpha-blockers, diuretics, phenothiazines, tricyclic antidepressants

Treatment includes removing reversible causes like drugs causing hypotension. Non-pharmacological interventions include patient education regarding staged moves from supine to upright, raising the head of the bed, and increasing dietary fluid and salt. If these fail, drugs like fludrocortisone and midodrine can be given.
questions.learning: Decrease in Systolic blood pressure 20 mmHg after 3 min of standing Orthostatic hypotension or postural hypotension is defined as a sustained drop in systolic BP of ≥20 mmHg or diastolic BP of ≥10 mmHg after 3 min of standing.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 32-year-old married woman who came for the evaluation of infertility was found to have a septum in her uterine cavity. What would be the appropriate management of this case?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Hysteroscopy and septoplasty

The appropriate management for a 32-year-old woman with a septate uterus is hysteroscopy and septoplasty.

Hysteroscopic septoplasty refers to the resection of the uterine septum under hysteroscopic guidance. The septum can be resected either with a resectoscope or a laser. It does not scar the uterus and avoids the necessity of cesarean sections for future pregnancies. There is a reduced risk of pelvic adhesions, compared with transabdominal approaches.

A septate uterus is characterized by a septum in the endometrial cavity. It is caused by the failure of the medial segments of the Müllerian ducts to regress. This creates a permanent septum within the uterine cavity.

The septum can project partially from the fundus or extend completely to the cervical os. It is the most common congenital uterine malformation in women with infertility.

Other options:

Option A: Hysterectomy is not advisable since the patient has come for infertility evaluation and desires pregnancy.

Options B & D: Laparoscopy/laparotomy and metroplasty are not preferred for the treatment of a septate uterus due to the following:

• Requirement of cesarean section for subsequent pregnancies to prevent uterine rupture.
• Postoperative pelvic adhesions leading to infertility.

Note: Jone's and Tompkin's metroplasties are surgeries for the septate uterus that involve a transabdominal approach. They cause uterine scarring and are hence not preferred.
questions.learning: Hysteroscopy and septoplasty — The appropriate management for a 32-year-old woman with a septate uterus is hysteroscopy and septoplasty. Hysteroscopic septoplasty refers to the resection of the uterine septum under hysteroscopic guidance.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: After a normal delivery of a healthy baby, how soon should a primigravida initiate breastfeeding?
questions.explanation: According to WHO and national health guidelines, the initiation of breastfeeding for a healthy baby delivered via a normal vaginal delivery should occur within 1 hour of birth. This "golden hour" is critical for establishing successful long-term lactation and promoting maternal-infant bonding through skin-to-skin contact. Waiting for 1 hour or more (Option B) or several hours (Option C and D) is unnecessary and detrimental, as it delays the baby's intake of colostrum—the first milk rich in antibodies and essential nutrients. Early suckling also stimulates the release of oxytocin in the mother, which helps in uterine contraction and reduces the risk of postpartum hemorrhage. Options C and D reflect outdated practices. For a primigravida (a first-time mother), early initiation is especially important for building confidence and ensuring a proper latch under the guidance of healthcare staff. Universal adherence to the "within 1 hour" rule is a foundational component of the Baby-Friendly Hospital Initiative (BFHI)
questions.learning: According to WHO and national health guidelines, the initiation of breastfeeding for a healthy baby delivered via a normal vaginal delivery should occur within 1 hour of birth.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following methods is used to test the blood taken from a neonate for metabolic disease screening?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Tandem Mass Spectrometry

Tandem mass spectrometry is used to screen a blood sample for metabolic diseases.

Mass spectrometry is a very sensitive quantitative analytical technique used to measure a wide range of clinically relevant analytes. It identifies molecules based on their mass or molecular size. A sample is vaporized such that a positive charge is produced on the molecule. An electric field is applied so that particles move. At the same time, a magnetic field is applied, so the cations are deflected and hit on the detector. For molecules of identical charge, the time required for the molecule to reach the detector is inversely proportional to the mass of the molecule.

In tandem mass spectrometry, two mass spectrometers (MS) are arranged sequentially. The first MS separates big peptides, based on their mass. From this observation, the parent ion can be directed into the second MS. Here the ions collide with argon gas molecules and are broken into smaller ions. These daughter ions are detected and quantified by their mass spectrum in the second instrument.

Tandem MS is used to screen blood samples from newborns for the presence and concentrations of amino acids, fatty acids and other metabolites. Abnormalities in metabolite levels can serve as diagnostic indicators for a variety of genetic disorders like phenylketonuria.
questions.learning: Tandem Mass Spectrometry Tandem mass spectrometry is used to screen a blood sample for metabolic diseases. Mass spectrometry is a very sensitive quantitative analytical technique used to measure a wide range of clinically relevant analytes.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: The mechanism of action of tissue plasminogen activator is _____
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Enhance fibrin degradation

The mechanism of action of the tissue plasminogen activator is to enhance fibrin degradation.

Tissue plasminogen activators activate plasminogen bound to fibrin, and catalyze the conversion of plasminogen to plasmin, resulting in increased formation of plasmin. This results in fibrinolysis of formed thrombus (thrombolysis).

It is indicated in pulmonary embolism with hemodynamic instability, acute ischemic stroke, and acute myocardial infarction. Recombinant variants of t-PA like reteplase and tenecteplase have a longer half-life.

All thrombolytics can cause bleeding, which may be counteracted by the administration of antifibrinolytics, such as aminocaproic acid and tranexamic acid.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which ocular condition is treated as shown in the image?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Keratoconus

Intracorneal ring segments (Intacs) are used in the management of keratoconus, a progressive corneal ectasia.

• Intacs are placed in the corneal stroma
• They flatten and regularize the corneal curvature
• Improve irregular astigmatism and visual acuity

Indications:

• Mild to moderate keratoconus
• Contact lens intolerance
• Alternative to delay or avoid keratoplasty

Often combined with corneal collagen cross-linking (CXL) for stabilization

Why not others:

• Cataract: Treated with lens extraction
• Corneal ulcer: Treated medically (antibiotics/antifungals)
• Glaucoma: Managed with medications/surgery affecting aqueous outflow

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: An 18-year-old girl presented with seizures and her radiological image is as given below. Knowing that the MR spectroscopy of the lesion showed elevated choline, alanine, and lactate, what is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Neurocysticercosis

The given radiological image and history of seizures suggests a diagnosis of neurocysticercosis.

Neurocysticercosis presents with seizures, hydrocephalus, raised ICP, and may even cause signs of chronic meningitis. The given image shows multilobulated cystic lesions (with scolex) in the subarachnoid space, typical parenchymal brain calcifications are suggestive of neurocysticercosis caused by T. solium (Cysticercosis cellulose).

• Cyst with a dot sign: seen in both MRI and CT and the dot represents the eccentrically placed scolex of the parasite.

MR Spectroscopy features of neurocysticercosis include elevated lactate, alanine, succinate, and choline levels and reduced levels of N -acetyl aspartate and creatine. Escobar's pathological stages describe 4 stages - vesicular, colloidal vesicular, granular nodular, and nodular calcified.

Other options

• Solid or ring enhancement is typical in the post-contrast images of tuberculoma. A central focus of calcification with a ring of peripheral enhancement (the "target sign") is also described in tuberculosis but is not specific to it.
• Cerebral toxoplasmosis appears as multiple hypodense regions predominantly in the basal ganglia and at the corticomedullary junction. It can be associated with ring enhancing lesions as well.
• Cryptococcosis is usually associated with normal scans but may show cerebral atrophy, hydrocephalus or mass lesions as well.
questions.learning: Neurocysticercosis — The given radiological image and history of seizures suggests a diagnosis of neurocysticercosis. Neurocysticercosis presents with seizures, hydrocephalus, raised ICP, and may even cause signs of chronic meningitis.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 40-year-old diabetic patient presented with the squint. On examination, the secondary deviation was found to be more than the primary deviation. Forced duction test is negative. Which of the following types of squint is most likely to be present in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Paralytic squint

The above clinical scenario is suggestive of paralytic squint. It is characterized by the presence of secondary deviation more than the primary deviation and a negative forced duction test.

The squint may be either comitant or incomitant.

• Comitant squint: The angle of squint measured is same in all gazes.
• Incomitant squint: The angle of squint measured is different in different gazes.

The differences between comitant and incomitant squint are shown in the table below:

Features
Comitant squint
Incomitant squint

Magnitude of squint
Same in all gazes
Varies with the gaze

Diplopia
Absent
Present

Ocular movements
Full
Restricted

False projection
Absent
Present

Abnormal head posture
Absent
Present

Secondary deviation
Equal to primary deviation
More than primary deviation

The incomitant squint is further divided into two main types: Paralytic and restrictive.

Paralytic squint occurs due to the paralysis of extraocular muscle while restrictive squint is due to the mechanical restriction caused by tight or fibrosed muscle.

Forced duction test(FDT) differentiates between these two types. In this test, the eye is moved mechanically with the help of a forceps.

• The test is negative if there is no resistance to the movement. It is seen in a paralytic squint.
• The test is positive if there is resistance to the movement. It is seen in a restrictive squint.
questions.learning: Paralytic squint — The above clinical scenario is suggestive of paralytic squint. It is characterized by the presence of secondary deviation more than the primary deviation and a negative forced duction test.

questions.text: Upon reactivation of VZV, the virus is transported through the nerve axon to the skin. Which of the following proteins is most likely involved in the transport process leading to disease recurrence?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Kinesin

During reactivation of varicella-zoster virus (VZV), the virus travels from the dorsal root ganglion along the axon to the skin.

Axonal transport mechanisms:

●  Anterograde transport (cell body → axon terminal/skin): mediated by kinesin along microtubules.

●  Retrograde transport (axon terminal → cell body): mediated by dynein.

During VZV reactivation, the virus moves anterogradely toward the skin, causing herpes zoster (shingles).

Other proteins:

C. Lamin: structural protein of the nuclear lamina.

D. Selectin: adhesion molecule involved in leukocyte rolling during inflammation.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 50-year-old woman presents with a breast lump that was surgically excised, and the histopathological examination findings are provided. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The microscopic examination reveals clusters of malignant cells "floating" within abundant pools of extracellular mucin, which is the hallmark of mucinous (colloid) carcinoma of the breast. This rare subtype of invasive ductal carcinoma typically affects postmenopausal women and generally carries a more favorable prognosis. Lobular carcinoma (Option A) characteristically shows a "single-file" infiltration pattern due to the loss of E-cadherin. Medullary carcinoma (Option B) presents with lymphoplasmacytic infiltration and a syncytial growth pattern but lacks mucin pools. Phyllodes tumor (Option D) is a fibroepithelial lesion characterized by leaf-like stromal projections and hypercellularity rather than extracellular mucin. Therefore, the distinct appearance of mucin-filled spaces confirms the diagnosis of mucinous carcinoma
questions.learning: The microscopic examination reveals clusters of malignant cells "floating" within abundant pools of extracellular mucin, which is the hallmark of mucinous (colloid) carcinoma of the breast.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Which of the following radioactive isotopes is not used for brachytherapy?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Iodine-131

I-131 is a beta-emitter that is taken up by thyroid tissue as well as differentiated thyroid cancers and is used for systemic radiotherapy.

Brachytherapy is a form of radiation therapy in which a radioactive source is placed directly into or near the target tissue to deliver localized radiation treatment. It is commonly used for treating various types of cancer.

Other options:

A) Iodine-125: This radioactive isotope is commonly used in brachytherapy for treating prostate cancer. It emits low-energy gamma rays that can effectively target and treat the cancerous tissue.

C) Cobalt-60: This isotope is not typically used in brachytherapy but rather in external beam radiation therapy. Cobalt-60 emits high-energy gamma rays and is commonly used in radiation therapy machines called cobalt units or teletherapy units. These units deliver radiation from outside the body, targeting the tumor.

D) Iridium-192: This is a commonly used radioactive isotope in brachytherapy. It emits high-energy gamma rays and is used for treating various types of cancer, such as cervical, prostate, and breast cancer. Iridium-192 is often used in temporary brachytherapy, where the radioactive source is temporarily placed in the body and then removed after a specific period of treatment.

In summary, while Iodine-125 and Iridium-192 are commonly used in brachytherapy, Cobalt-60 is primarily used in external beam radiation therapy. Iodine-131 is not typically used in brachytherapy but has other medical applications, such as thyroid cancer treatment and diagnostic imaging.
questions.learning: Iodine-131 I-131 is a beta-emitter that is taken up by thyroid tissue as well as differentiated thyroid cancers and is used for systemic radiotherapy.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A patient receives succinylcholine during surgery for muscle relaxation and soon develops hyperthermia, muscle rigidity, tremors, and tachycardia. What is the most appropriate treatment for this condition?
questions.explanation: The clinical features of hyperthermia, muscle rigidity, tremors, and tachycardia following succinylcholine administration indicate Malignant Hyperthermia. This life-threatening genetic condition is triggered by certain volatile anesthetics and depolarizing relaxants like succinylcholine. The specific treatment and antidote is Dantrolene sodium. It works by inhibiting calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum in skeletal muscle, thereby reversing the hypermetabolic state. Neostigmine (Option A) is an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor used to reverse non-depolarizing blocks; it is contraindicated here as it can exacerbate the metabolic crisis by increasing acetylcholine. Atropine (Option C) is an anticholinergic that could worsen the condition by inhibiting sweating and increasing heart rate. Midazolam (Option D), a benzodiazepine, provides sedation but does not address the underlying calcium-mediated pathophysiology. Immediate management also involves stopping the trigger, hyperventilation with 100% oxygen, and active cooling. Immediate administration of Dantrolene is crucial to prevent severe complications and mortality
questions.learning: The clinical features of hyperthermia, muscle rigidity, tremors, and tachycardia following succinylcholine administration indicate Malignant Hyperthermia.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following are components of SOFA scoring system? I. PaO₂/FiO₂ ratio II. Mean arterial pressure III. Glasgow Coma Scale IV. Prothrombin Time with INR Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. I, II and III

The Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA) score is used to assess the severity of organ dysfunction in critically ill patients, particularly those with sepsis. It evaluates six organ systems, assigning a score from 0 to 4 for each system. A higher SOFA score is associated with an increased risk of mortality.

• I. PaO₂/FiO₂ ratio ✔

• Assesses respiratory function and is a component of the SOFA score.

• II. Mean arterial pressure (MAP) ✔

• Assesses cardiovascular function.
• SOFA uses MAP and the need for vasopressors to grade cardiovascular dysfunction.

• III. Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) ✔

• Assesses neurological function.
• Lower GCS scores indicate more severe neurological dysfunction.

• IV. Prothrombin Time with INR ✘

• Incorrect.
• SOFA assesses coagulation using platelet count, not PT/INR.
questions.learning: I, II and III — The Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA) score is used to assess the severity of organ dysfunction in critically ill patients, particularly those with sepsis.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following agents inhibits Complex IV of the electron transport chain?
questions.explanation: The electron transport chain (ETC) can be inhibited at different sites by specific poisons. Complex IV (cytochrome c oxidase) is the terminal enzyme of the ETC responsible for transferring electrons to molecular oxygen. Cyanide is a potent inhibitor of Complex IV. It binds to the ferric iron (Fe³⁺) in cytochrome a3, preventing the reduction of oxygen to water. This abruptly halts oxidative phosphorylation, leading to cellular hypoxia despite adequate oxygen levels—often termed histotoxic hypoxia. Other options act at different complexes : 1. Rotenone inhibits Complex I 2. Carboxin inhibits Complex II (succinate dehydrogenase) 3. Antimycin A inhibits Complex III 4. Thus, cyanide specifically inhibits Complex IV of the electron transport chain
questions.learning: The electron transport chain (ETC) can be inhibited at different sites by specific poisons. Complex IV (cytochrome c oxidase) is the terminal enzyme of the ETC responsible for transferring electrons to molecular oxygen.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Renal Electrolytes · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 62-year-old man is brought to the emergency department with sudden-onset severe headache and progressive drowsiness for 1 hour. He has a history of long-standing hypertension. On examination, he responds only to painful stimuli and has left-sided weakness. The right pupil is dilated and sluggishly reactive to light. CT scan of the head reveals a right basal ganglia hemorrhage with midline shift. The patient is intubated, and intravenous mannitol is administered to reduce intracranial pressure. Which of the following acute renal effects is most likely to occur following administration of this medication?
options: Decreased serum sodium, increased tubular flow, increased tubular fluid osmolality
No change in serum sodium, decreased tubular flow, increased tubular fluid osmolality
Increased serum sodium, no change in tubular flow, increased tubular fluid osmolality
Decreased serum sodium, no change in tubular flow, decreased tubular fluid osmolality
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Decreased serum sodium, increased tubular flow, increased tubular fluid osmolality

Mannitol is an osmotic diuretic that is freely filtered at the glomerulus but not reabsorbed, leading to an increase in tubular fluid osmolality. This prevents water reabsorption in the proximal tubule and descending limb of the loop of Henle, resulting in osmotic diuresis with increased tubular flow.

In the acute setting, mannitol increases plasma osmolality, drawing water from intracellular to extracellular compartments, including from brain parenchyma—thereby reducing intracranial pressure. This initial water shift into the intravascular space causes dilutional hyponatremia, even before diuresis becomes prominent.

Thus, the key acute renal effects are:

• Increased tubular flow due to osmotic diuresis
• Increased tubular fluid osmolality
• Decreased serum sodium (dilutional hyponatremia initially)
questions.learning: Decreased serum sodium, increased tubular flow, increased tubular fluid osmolality Mannitol is an osmotic diuretic that is freely filtered at the glomerulus but not reabsorbed, leading to an increase in tubular fluid osmolality.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which among the following instruments is not used in the Sahli's method of hemoglobin estimation?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. D

Option D is RBC pipette, it is not used in Sahli's method of hemoglobin estimation. The instruments used are comparator with brown glass standard(Option A), graduated hemoglobin tube(Option B), Sahli's pipette (Option C)and stirrer.

Sahli's method of estimation of hemoglobin is based on colorimetric measurement of the intensity of color developed on the addition of dilute hydrochloric acid (N/10 HCl) reagent to the blood.

In Sahli's method, hemoglobin is converted to acid hematin with the action of dilute hydrochloric acid (N/10 HCl). The brown color of the acid hematin is matched to its intensity with a standard brown glass comparator in a visual colorimeter called Sahli’s colorimeter. It can be used to estimate oxyHb and reduced Hb.

Sahli's method is a simple bedside test and is cost-effective. However, it has some disadvantages, which include visual errors, the inability to measure other forms of hemoglobin like carboxyhemoglobin, methemoglobin, and sulfhemoglobin, fading of the comparator over time, and the color of acid hematin fading quickly.

The visual error can be reduced by taking the average of three readings; first, when the color is slightly darker than the standard; second, when the color exactly matches the standard; and third, when the color is slightly lighter than the standard.
questions.learning: D Option D is RBC pipette, it is not used in Sahli's method of hemoglobin estimation. The instruments used are comparator with brown glass standard(Option A), graduated hemoglobin tube(Option B), Sahli's pipette (Option C)and stirrer.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: Identify the postmortem change given in the image.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Marbling

The postmortem change shown above is marbling, which is an external sign of putrefaction.

In marbling, the superficial veins of roots of the limb, thighs, sides of the abdomen, and shoulders are stained greenish-brown or purplish-red, in a linear branching pattern. It is usually prominent 36–48 hours after death occurs due to the formation of sulfhemoglobin subsequent to hemolysis of red blood cells.

In putrefaction, bacteria from the gut enter into and multiply in the surrounding tissues, eventually spreading through the blood vessels to other parts of the body. The bacterium Clostridium welchii is largely responsible for the putrefactive changes spreading through the body, due to its production of the enzyme lecithinase. The first external sign of putrefaction in a body lying outside in the air is a greenish discoloration of the skin over the region of the cecum.

Other options:

Option B: Tattooing around the entry wound of a bullet is due to the deposition of unburnt powder particles. These are difficult to remove. They are also called stippling or peppering. This is seen up to 50 cm of firing

Option C: Postmortem hypostasis/Postmortem staining/Postmortem lividity/Livor mortis/Suggilation refers to bluish-purple or reddish-purple discoloration of the superficial layers of the dermis. It is an early postmortem change that occurs due to the stagnation of blood in the vessels of the dependent parts due to the effect of gravity.

Option D: Filigree burns also known as Lichtenberg's flowers are superficial, thin, irregular, and tortuous markings on the skin indicative of a lightning strike. They resemble the branches of a tree and are usually found over the skin of the shoulders or the flanks.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: The following image of a FAST scan in a trauma patient suggests:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Positive fast

The image of FAST in a trauma patient suggests Positive FAST as there is a fluid collection in the abdominal cavity. The thin anechoic area located between the liver(on the left) and the Kidney(on the right) is a collection of fluid visualized in this RUQ Sonogram image.

FAST stands for Focused assessment with sonography for trauma. It is a rapid diagnostic examination to assess patients with potential thoracoabdominal injuries. It is performed within 2-4 minutes.

Technique:

• Patient in the supine position
• 3.5-5.0 MHz convex transducer
• Following regions are scanned :

• Subxiphoid: assess for pericardial effusion and left lobe liver injuries
• Right upper quadrant: assess for right liver injuries, right kidney injury, and Morison pouch
• Left upper quadrant: assess for splenic injury and left kidney injury
• Suprapubic region: assess the bladder and pouch of Douglas

An "extended FAST or eFAST" scan may be performed: left and right thoracic views to assess for pneumothorax and haemothorax.

Sequentially order of FAST is:- pericardial sac, the Right Upper Quadrant (RUQ), Left Upper Quadrant (LUQ), and pelvis.

4 ‘Ps’ are evaluated in sequence: Pericardial sac → Perihepatic region → Perisplenic region → Pelvis.

Note:-

In Pneumoperitoneum, air is collected in the peritoneal cavity which is usually hyperechoic not anechoic and would appear white in the ultrasound image.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Consider the following statements: Statement-1: In fetal growth restriction, there is always oligohydramnios. Statement-2: In fetal growth restriction, there is placental insufficiency leading to redistribution of blood flow to fetal brain shunting it from fetal kidney. Which one of the following is correct?
options: Both Statement-1 and Statement-2 are true and Statement-2 is the correct explanation for Statement-1.
Both Statement-1 and Statement-2 are true and Statement-2 is not the correct explanation for Statement-1.
Statement-1 is true but Statement-2 is false.
Statement-2 is true but Statement-1 is false.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Statement-2 is true but Statement-1 is false.

Fetal Growth Restriction (FGR) is commonly caused by uteroplacental insufficiency, resulting in chronic fetal hypoxia. The fetus adapts by redistributing blood flow (“brain-sparing effect”) to vital organs such as the brain, heart, and adrenal glands, at the expense of the kidneys, gastrointestinal tract, and peripheral tissues.

Why are the statements correct/incorrect?

• Statement-1. In fetal growth restriction there is always oligohydramnios: False. Oligohydramnios is common but not universal. It is mainly seen in placental insufficiency-related (late-onset/asymmetric) FGR, whereas some cases (e.g., constitutionally small fetus or certain early-onset FGR) may have normal amniotic fluid volume.
• Statement-2. In fetal growth restriction there is placental insufficiency leading to redistribution of blood flow to the fetal brain, shunting it from the fetal kidney: True. Reduced renal perfusion decreases fetal urine production, which can result in oligohydramnios.
questions.learning: Statement-2 is true but Statement-1 is false. Fetal Growth Restriction (FGR) is commonly caused by uteroplacental insufficiency, resulting in chronic fetal hypoxia.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Identify the most common location of Nasopharyngeal carcinoma:
questions.explanation: Nasopharyngeal carcinoma (NPC) most commonly arises from the Fossa of Rosenmüller (recessus pharyngeus). In endoscopic or anatomical diagrams of the nasopharynx, this is a deep, slit-like space located posterior to the torus tubarius (the opening of the Eustachian tube). In the provided image, label 2 corresponds to this characteristic anatomical site. NPC has a strong association with the Epstein-Barr Virus (EBV) and is highly prevalent in certain regions like Southern China. Early symptoms are often subtle and include unilateral middle ear effusion (glue ear) due to Eustachian tube blockage or painless neck lymphadenopathy (Trottier’s triad). Other locations in the nasopharynx (Options A, C, and D) such as the roof or the posterior wall are less common primary sites. Because the tumor is often hidden in this recess, NPC is frequently diagnosed at a locally advanced stage, requiring a high index of clinical suspicion

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: A patient under general anesthesia is identified to be in a “cannot intubate, cannot ventilate” (CICV) situation. What is the most appropriate immediate next step in management?
questions.explanation: A "cannot intubate, cannot ventilate" (CICV) scenario is a critical anesthesia emergency that requires an immediate surgical airway to prevent hypoxic brain injury. An emergency cricothyroidotomy is the fastest and most reliable method because the cricothyroid membrane is superficial and easy to access quickly. Nasopharyngeal airways (Option A) and laryngeal mask airways (Option C) are non-invasive measures that by definition have already failed in a CICV state. A tracheostomy (Option D) is a complex surgical procedure that takes significantly more time to perform than a cricothyroidotomy and is not suitable for a rapid hypoxic emergency. Therefore, cricothyroidotomy is the mandated life-saving intervention
questions.learning: A "cannot intubate, cannot ventilate" (CICV) scenario is a critical anesthesia emergency that requires an immediate surgical airway to prevent hypoxic brain injury.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Identify the CTG pattern shown in the given image.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Early deceleration

The given CTG shows early decelerations. It is seen in fetal head compression.

In early decelerations, the onset, nadir, and recovery of deceleration coincide with the beginning, peak, and ending of uterine contraction respectively.

This finding in CTG is suggestive of fetal head compression causing vagal nerve activation.

Other options:

Option A: The CTG given below shows late decelerations, Here the fetal heart rate begins to drop after the end of uterine contraction. It is mostly associated with uteroplacental insufficiency and fetal hypoxia.

Other causes of late decelerations include:

* Placental pathologies like- postmaturity, hypertension, diabetes, placental abruption

* Excessive uterine contractions

* Excessive use of oxytocin

* Epidural anesthesia

Option B: The CTG given below shows variable decelerations as seen in umbilical cord compression.

Option D: The CTG given below shows a sinusoidal pattern. It resembles a sine wave. It is often associated with fetal anemia, fetomaternal hemorrhage, and fetal acidosis.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Please analyze the image provided and determine the specific abnormality or injury present.
questions.explanation: The provided image displays a classic dendritic ulcer, characterized by its linear, branching, tree-like appearance with terminal bulbs. This finding is pathognomonic for Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV) keratitis, a form of viral keratitis. These ulcers are highlighted when stained with fluorescein or rose bengal. Fungal keratitis (Option B) typically presents with feathery margins and satellite lesions. Bacterial keratitis (Option C) usually shows a well-defined, round, or oval suppurative infiltrate with an overlying epithelial defect. Interstitial keratitis (Option D) involves inflammation within the stroma without primary epithelial ulceration. Patients with HSV dendritic ulcers often report pain, photophobia, and blurred vision, along with decreased corneal sensation. Management includes topical antiviral agents like acyclovir. Therefore, based on the unique branching pattern visible in the image, viral keratitis is the definitive diagnosis

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Mayo’s repair is done for:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Umbilical hernia

Mayo’s repair (also called the vest-over-pants repair) is a tissue repair technique used for umbilical hernia, in which the fascial edges are overlapped to reinforce the defect.

Why not the other options?

• A. Inguinal hernia: Common repairs include Lichtenstein, Shouldice, Bassini.
• B. Femoral hernia: Common repairs include McVay (Cooper’s ligament), Lockwood, Lotheissen, McEvedy.
• D. Incisional hernia: Usually treated with mesh repair.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: Which method of measurement of scoliosis has been depicted in the image given below?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Cobb's angle

The given image depicts the measurement of the curvature of scoliosis using the Cobb's angle.

Scoliosis is characterized by the lateral curvature of the spine in the coronal plane when the patient is upright. Confirmation of the diagnosis is achieved through full-length lateral and posteroanterior X-rays of the spine. A Cobb's angle greater than 10% on the radiograph is diagnostic of scoliosis.

The measurement of Cobb's angle consists of three steps:

• Locating the superior-end vertebra of the curve.
• Locating the inferior-end vertebra of the curve.
• Drawing perpendicular lines from the superior surface of the superior-end vertebra and from the inferior surface of the inferior-end vertebra and making them intersect.

The angle formed by these perpendiculars represents the degree of spinal curvature, referred to as Cobb's angle.

Nash and Moe's method and Perdriolle and Vidal method are tools for assessing the vertebral rotation in scoliosis.

Other options:

Option B: Baumann's angle is the angle formed between a line drawn through the lateral epiphysis and the long axis of the humerus. Normally, it measures less than 80 degrees but increases in cases of supracondylar fractures.

Option C: Ferguson's angle is measured between the upper endplate of the S1 vertebra and a horizontal line. A normal Ferguson angle is typically around 34 degrees. A decreased Ferguson angle can be observed in advanced spondylolisthesis.

Option D: Bohler's angle is the angle formed by two lines tangent to the highest points of the anterior and posterior facets of the calcaneus. This angle is decreased in calcaneal fractures.
questions.learning: Cobb's angle — The given image depicts the measurement of the curvature of scoliosis using the Cobb's angle. Scoliosis is characterized by the lateral curvature of the spine in the coronal plane when the patient is upright.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient presents with pedal edema, elevated jugular venous pressure (up to the mandible), and ascites. What is the most likely diagnosis in this case?
questions.explanation: The clinical combination of pedal edema, ascites, and markedly elevated JVP is classic for right-sided Cardiac failure (congestive heart failure). The elevated JVP is a direct reflection of increased central venous pressure and the heart's inability to handle venous return. While Renal failure (Option B) and Liver failure (Option C) characteristically cause pedal edema and ascites due to fluid overload or hypoalbuminemia, they do not typically cause an elevation in the JVP waveform; in those conditions, JVP is usually normal or low. Brain injury (Option D) is unrelated to systemic edema patterns. In right-sided heart failure, the back-pressure from the heart leads to systemic venous congestion, which manifests as hepatomegaly, ascites, and lower limb swelling. Management focuses on diuretics to reduce volume and treating the underlying cause, such as left-sided failure or pulmonary hypertension. Bedside assessment of the JVP is the most critical physical exam finding for localizing the source of systemic edema to the heart

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: In malignant hyperthermia, a mutation affecting the ryanodine receptor (RYR) triggers a severe reaction to certain anesthetic agents. What is the primary ionic imbalance resulting from this receptor defect?
options: Increased sodium influx into the muscle cell
Increased potassium uptake into the sarcoplasmic reticulum
Increased chloride efflux from the muscle cell
Increased calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum
questions.explanation: Malignant hyperthermia is a pharmacogenetic disorder of skeletal muscle. It is triggered by volatile anesthetics (like halothane) or succinylcholine in individuals with a mutation in the RYR1 gene. This mutation results in a hypersensitive ryanodine receptor, which causes a massive, uncontrolled release of calcium ions from the sarcoplasmic reticulum into the sarcoplasm. This excess calcium drives sustained muscle contraction and a state of hypermetabolism, leading to muscle rigidity, extreme tachycardia, and a rapid rise in body temperature. Sodium influx (Option A) and chloride efflux (Option C) are not the primary defects in this condition. Potassium uptake (Option B) is not actively regulated by the sarcoplasmic reticulum in this pathway; in fact, potassium is typically released out of cells during rhabdomyolysis. Therefore, aberrant calcium signaling is the central physiological mechanism
questions.learning: Malignant hyperthermia is a pharmacogenetic disorder of skeletal muscle. It is triggered by volatile anesthetics (like halothane) or succinylcholine in individuals with a mutation in the RYR1 gene.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A diabetic patient presents to you with visual acuity of 6/9 in one eye. Further investigations revealed pre-retinal hemorrhages with neovascularization at the optic disc. What is the next step in management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Pan-retinal photocoagulation

The clinical vignette is suggestive of proliferative diabetic retinopathy with high-risk characteristics and the next step in management is pan-retinal photocoagulation.

Diabetic retinopathy is used to describe retinal changes seen in diabetic patients. It is classified into the following types:

• Non-proliferative diabetic retinopathy (NPDR)
• Proliferative diabetic retinopathy (PDR)
• Diabetic maculopathy
• Advanced diabetic eye disease

Fundoscopy in NPDR reveals hard exudates, cotton-wool spots, and microaneurysms. Hard exudates are small, discrete yellowish, waxy areas with crenated margins.

Proliferative diabetic retinopathy is marked by NVD or NVE which is the hallmark of the condition. Condensation of connective tissue surrounding the newly formed vessels results in the formation of a fibrovascular epiretinal membrane. Vitreous detachment and hemorrhage may also occur. Preretinal hemorrhages are considered a high-risk characteristic. In addition, changes seen in NPDR may also be present.

The condition usually develops 25 years after the onset of the disease. Hence, it is more commonly seen in patients with type I diabetes.

The image below shows NVD.

PDR with high-risk characteristics is managed with pan-retinal photocoagulation. Laser treatment helps by inhibiting the release of vascular endothelial growth factors (VEGF). Anti-VEGFs are recommended before pan-retinal photocoagulation in patients with PDR.

Diabetic maculopathy can be classified as:

• Focal exudative maculopathy: Microaneursysms, hard exudates, and hemorrhages can be seen.
• Diffuse exudative maculopathy: Diffuse retinal edema with few hard exudates.
• Ischemic maculopathy: Microaneursysms, hemorrhages, few hard exudates. Fluorescein angiography reveals areas of non-perfusion.
• Mixed maculopathy: Features of both exudative and ischemic maculopathy.

An FFA image showing features of macular ischemia is given below.

Other options:

Option A: Focal laser photocoagulation is the treatment of choice for focal diabetic macular edema (DME) that does not involve the fovea.

Option C: Grid laser photocoagulation can be used in diffuse DME not responding to anti-VEGFs and intravitreal steroids.

Option D: Scleral buckling can be used in cases of advanced PDR with tractional retinal detachment.
questions.learning: Pan-retinal photocoagulation — The clinical vignette is suggestive of proliferative diabetic retinopathy with high-risk characteristics and the next step in management is pan-retinal photocoagulation.

• Embryology: Epidermis is derived from ectoderm
• Incorrect concepts:
• Stratum corneum = outermost layer but consists of dead (anucleate) cells, so not a true “cellular” layer
• Dermis and hypodermis arise from mesoderm, not endoderm

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 45-year-old alcoholic obese male patient presented to the emergency department with severe pain abdomen radiating to the back. Blood investigations revealed increased serum amylase and lipase levels. Which of the following should be avoided in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 5% dextrose

The clinical presentation of the patient is suggestive of acute pancreatitis. 5% dextrose should be avoided in this condition.

Acute pancreatitis is a condition characterized by inflammatory damage to the pancreas. Various causes of acute pancreatitis are:

* Gallstone-induced (most common cause)

* Alcohol (2nd most common cause)

* Trauma (most common cause in children)

* Iatrogenic- Post-endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP)

* Drug-induced pancreatitis (Thiazides, Azathioprine, Anti-cancer drugs, etc)

* Hypertriglyceridemia

* Hypercalcemia

* Scorpion bite

* Idiopathic

Clinical presentation of acute pancreatitis is characterized by epigastric pain radiating to the back which is relieved by bending forward, nausea, and vomiting. Acute hemorrhagic pancreatitis can present with certain named signs like:

* Cullen’s sign: Discoloration around the umbilicus

* Grey Turner’s sign: Discoloration in the flanks

* Fox sign: Discoloration in the inguinal region

* Bryant’s sign: Discoloration on the scrotum

Blood investigations show increased serum amylase and lipase levels. Serum lipase is more sensitive and specific than serum amylase but it rises late. USG cannot help establish the diagnosis of pancreatitis. Plain erect chest x-ray and abdominal radiographs are not diagnostic of acute pancreatitis and can only be used to rule out certain differentials. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CECT) is the imaging investigation of choice, but may not always be needed. Various scoring systems are used to grade the severity of acute pancreatitis based on blood investigations and radiographic findings.

Management:

In the management of acute pancreatitis, it's crucial to avoid stimulating the pancreas further, as it can exacerbate inflammation and worsen symptoms. Therefore, solutions containing glucose, such as 5% dextrose, should be avoided because they can trigger pancreatic enzyme secretion.

5% Dextrose is also a hypotonic solution and cannot maintain plasma oncotic pressure and will exaggerate the underlying third space loss.

Instead, fluids should be administered intravenously as necessary, but they should be non-stimulating to the pancreas, such as normal saline or lactated Ringer's solution.

Early initiation of oral feeds is encouraged as soon as vomiting and abdominal pain is controlled. In severe acute pancreatitis, if the patient cannot stop vomiting or cannot tolerate enteral feeds, total parenteral nutrition is then given. TPN is based on clinical status, nutritional needs, and response to other management strategies. However, enteral feeds are the mainstay of nutritional therapy in acute pancreatitis.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: In a patient who has sustained electrical burns and has stable vital signs, the urine appears red in color. Which abnormal finding is most likely to be detected on serological (blood) investigation?
questions.explanation: In patients with electrical burns, deep tissue injury commonly leads to rhabdomyolysis, a condition characterized by extensive skeletal muscle breakdown. Damaged muscle cells release large amounts of intracellular contents into the bloodstream, most notably myoglobin and potassium (K⁺). The presence of red-colored urine in this setting is due to myoglobinuria, not hematuria. Therefore, RBCs in urine (Option A) are typically absent or minimal, as the discoloration is pigment-related rather than due to bleeding. A critical and early serological abnormality in rhabdomyolysis is hyperkalemia, caused by the massive release of potassium from injured muscle cells. Hyperkalemia is potentially life-threatening, as it can precipitate fatal cardiac arrhythmias, making it the most important immediate laboratory finding to monitor. Creatinine levels (Option B) may rise later due to acute kidney injury from myoglobin-induced nephrotoxicity, but this is not the earliest or most characteristic finding. Hemoglobin levels (Option C) are usually unaffected unless there is significant associated blood loss. Thus, in a stable patient with electrical burns and red urine, increased serum potassium is the most likely and clinically urgent serological finding
questions.learning: In patients with electrical burns, deep tissue injury commonly leads to rhabdomyolysis, a condition characterized by extensive skeletal muscle breakdown.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A male patient sustained a fall after which he developed swelling of the knee. Laboratory investigations show increased APTT, with normal bleeding time and normal PT. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

Solution- Key clues:

• Male patient → think X-linked disorder
• Knee swelling after trauma → hemarthrosis (deep bleeding) ⭐

• ↑ aPTT

Diagnosis: Hemophilia A

Correct answer is B because isolated prolonged aPTT with normal PT and normal bleeding time indicates intrinsic pathway factor deficiency, most commonly factor VIII deficiency (Hemophilia A).

Clinical presentation with hemarthrosis after minor trauma is typical of hemophilia.

| PT | Normal | Extrinsic pathway OK

| aPTT | ↑ | Intrinsic pathway defect

Von Willebrand disease causes mucocutaneous bleeding with prolonged bleeding time. ITP causes thrombocytopenia. DIC prolongs PT, aPTT, and reduces platelets.

| Bleeding type | Deep | Mucosal | Mucosal

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which of the following cell organelles is associated with killing bacteria and viruses?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Lysosomes

Lysosomes contain hydrolytic enzymes and are associated with killing bacteria and viruses.

Lysosomes  are membrane-bound organelles broken off from the Golgi apparatus, containing roughly 40 different acid hydrolases (enzymes that function best in acidic pH ≤5). These hydrolases include proteases, nucleases, lipases, glycosidases, phosphatases, and sulfatases.

Lysosomal enzymes provide an intracellular digestive system that digests damaged cellular structures, food particles ingested by the cells, and foreign particles like bacteria and viruses. The membrane around the lysosomes prevents the hydrolytic enzymes from being in contact with the other substances in the cell and prevents them from being digested.

When an enzyme is congenitally absent, the cell becomes engorged with the material the enzyme normally degrades. This leads to lysosomal diseases e.g Gaucher disease is caused due to a deficiency of glucocerebrosidase.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 48-year-old man with HIV presents to the outpatient department with a 3-month history of cough, fever, night sweats, and weight loss. He is on antiretroviral therapy with Tenofovir 150 mg, Lamivudine 300 mg, and Dolutegravir 50 mg once daily at night. He has been diagnosed with tuberculosis and started on antitubercular therapy. What dose adjustments, if any, are required in this patient?
options: Add Dolutegravir 50 mg in the morning
Add Lamivudine 300 mg in the morning
questions.explanation: As established in Question 61, this case focuses on the significant drug interaction between Rifampicin (part of TB therapy) and Dolutegravir (DTG). Rifampicin induces the metabolism of DTG, dramatically reducing its effectiveness. To maintain an adequate therapeutic level for HIV control, the Dolutegravir dose must be doubled. Since the patient is taking 50 mg at night, the adjustment is to add another 50 mg in the morning. Tenofovir (Option B) and Lamivudine (Option D) do not require modification. Saying "No adjustment" (Option A) would lead to HIV treatment failure and potential viral resistance. Managing TB/HIV co-infection is clinically complex due to these metabolic interactions. The "double-dose DTG" strategy is the standard global protocol to ensure that neither the TB nor the HIV treatment is compromised. Clinicians must meticulously review the ART regimen whenever anti-tubercular therapy is initiated in an HIV patient

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: In a female patient who has been recently diagnosed with mild depression, what is the recommended initial treatment approach?
questions.explanation: According to international clinical guidelines (such as NICE or APA), the "first-line treatment" for "mild depression" is psychological therapy, specifically "Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT)" (Option A). CBT helps patients identify and change negative thought patterns and behaviors contributing to their low mood. Antidepressants (Options B and C) are generally "not recommended" as the primary treatment for mild depression, as their efficacy relative to placebo is much lower in mild cases than in moderate-to-severe depression. Combined therapy (Option B) is the gold standard for moderate-to-severe depression. Vagus nerve stimulation (Option D) is an invasive neuromodulation technique reserved only for treatment-resistant, severe chronic depression. For a recently diagnosed mild case, starting with non-pharmacological interventions like CBT, exercise, and sleep hygiene is the safest and most effective approach. If the patient’s condition fails to improve after an adequate trial of psychotherapy, the treatment plan should be reassessed for the potential addition of medication
questions.learning: According to international clinical guidelines (such as NICE or APA), the "first-line treatment" for "mild depression" is psychological therapy, specifically "Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT)" (Option A).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: The structure shown originates from which pharyngeal arch during embryological development?
questions.explanation: The image displays the malleus and incus, which are two of the three middle ear ossicles. Embryologically, the malleus and incus are derived from the cartilage of the first pharyngeal arch, known as Meckel's cartilage. Specifically, the dorsal end of Meckel's cartilage ossifies to form these structures. In contrast, the stapes (except for its footplate) is derived from the cartilage of the second pharyngeal arch, known as Reichert's cartilage (Option B). The third arch (Option C) gives rise to the greater horn of the hyoid and the stylopharyngeus muscle. The fourth arch (Option D) contributes to laryngeal cartilages like the thyroid and epiglottis. Understanding ossicular development is vital for diagnosing congenital hearing loss syndromes, such as Treacher Collins, where first arch derivatives are malformed. The malleus remains attached to the tympanic membrane, while the incus acts as a bridge to the stapes, facilitating sound conduction to the inner ear
questions.learning: The image displays the malleus and incus, which are two of the three middle ear ossicles. Embryologically, the malleus and incus are derived from the cartilage of the first pharyngeal arch, known as Meckel's cartilage.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which of the following uses CRISPR-Cas9 technology?
questions.explanation: CRISPR-Cas9 is a revolutionary and highly precise technology used for DNA Editing. It is derived from a natural defense mechanism used by bacteria to fight off viral infections. The system consists of two primary components: the Cas9 enzyme, which acts like a pair of "molecular scissors" to cut DNA at a specific location, and a guide RNA (gRNA), which ensures the scissors cut in the exact right place. Once the DNA is cut, the cell's natural repair mechanisms can be harnessed to delete, add, or replace genetic material. This technology has immense potential in treating genetic disorders, improving crop yields, and advancing basic biological research. It is distinct from post-transcriptional modifications, which occur to RNA after it has been synthesized. While "DNA Editing Solution" might sound similar, the core scientific application is the act of editing the genome itself
questions.learning: CRISPR-Cas9 is a revolutionary and highly precise technology used for DNA Editing. It is derived from a natural defense mechanism used by bacteria to fight off viral infections.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: A smoker who was given an interscalene block for an arthroscopic acromioclavicular joint reconstruction 2 days ago was followed up by a Chest x-ray which showed as below. He is asymptomatic at present and is comfortably resting on the bed. What is the next step in management?
options: Insert chest drain as soon as possible
Wait and watch and give supplementary oxygen if needed
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Wait and watch and give supplementary oxygen if needed

The next step of management is to wait and watch and give oxygen if needed. This is a case of postoperative asymptomatic pneumothorax.

As the patient is asymptomatic with no symptoms of dyspnoea or respiratory distress the best way to manage is to wait and watch.

Postoperative pneumothorax is seen mostly in patients with pre existing lung conditions like asthma or in chronic smokers. The pre-existing blebs or bullae in the individuals rupture due to pressure gradients created by the positive pressure from ventilation or the arthroscopic pump and shaver system used during surgery.

The pressure gradient from the positive pressure of anesthesia and the ipsilateral lung is highest in the lateral decubitus position.

The other complications that can occur are subcutaneous emphysema, pneumomediastinum.
questions.learning: Wait and watch and give supplementary oxygen if needed The next step of management is to wait and watch and give oxygen if needed. This is a case of postoperative asymptomatic pneumothorax.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: At what cut-off respiratory rate will you consider “fast breathing” in a 2-year-old child?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. ≥40 per minute

Fast breathing (tachypnea) is an important clinical sign used in the Integrated Management of Neonatal and Childhood Illness (IMNCI/IMCI) to identify possible pneumonia. The respiratory rate cut-off varies with age. In a 2-year-old child (12–59 months), a respiratory rate of ≥40 breaths/minute is considered fast breathing.

Why are the other options incorrect?

• A. ≥60 per minute: Cut-off for young infants <2 months.
• B. ≥50 per minute: Cut-off for infants 2–12 months.
• D. ≥30 per minute: Below the diagnostic threshold for fast breathing in a 2-year-old.
questions.learning: ≥40 per minute Fast breathing (tachypnea) is an important clinical sign used in the Integrated Management of Neonatal and Childhood Illness (IMNCI/IMCI) to identify possible pneumonia.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Gene involved in juvenile myoclonic epilepsy:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. GABRA-1

Mutation in GABRA-1 is associated with juvenile myoclonic epilepsy.

Juvenile myoclonic epilepsy (JME), also known as Janz syndrome or impulsive petit mal, is the most common generalized epilepsy in young adults. It may be caused due to mutation in many genes including CACNB4, CLNC2, GABRD, GABRA1, and Myoclonin1/ EFHC1

It typically begins between the ages of 12 and 18 (adolescence). The defining seizure type in JME is generalized myoclonic seizures, which occur in all patients. These seizures are typically mild and primarily affect the upper extremities in the morning causing the patient to drop things. However, they often go unnoticed and are only brought to medical attention after a generalized tonic-clonic seizure, which tends to occur after sleep deprivation or alcohol consumption. Some cases of childhood absence epilepsy may evolve into JME.

Diagnosis of JME relies on the patient's clinical history and electroencephalogram (EEG) findings. EEG typically shows bursts of generalized irregular 4- to 6-Hz spike-and-wave activity, particularly after awakening. JME is generally a lifelong condition.

Valproate is considered the most effective medication. Lamotrigine, levetiracetam, and topiramate are also approved for JME.

The characteristic EEG pattern is shown in the image below:
questions.learning: GABRA-1 Mutation in GABRA-1 is associated with juvenile myoclonic epilepsy. Juvenile myoclonic epilepsy (JME), also known as Janz syndrome or impulsive petit mal, is the most common generalized epilepsy in young adults.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: What is the type of cartilage present in the histology section given below?
questions.explanation: The histology section shows a homogeneous, glassy (translucent) basophilic matrix with chondrocytes housed in lacunae, often arranged in small isogenous groups. This appearance is characteristic of hyaline cartilage, the most common cartilage type in the body, found in costal cartilages and tracheal rings. Elastic cartilage (Option B) would show a dense network of dark-staining elastic fibers within the matrix, providing flexibility to structures like the auricle. Fibrocartilage (Option D) contains heavy bundles of Type I collagen and fewer chondrocytes, often arranged in rows, and lacks a perichondrium; it is found in intervertebral discs. While articular cartilage (Option C) is a form of hyaline cartilage, it is a specific anatomical designation for cartilage covering joint surfaces; the general tissue type shown is hyaline. Therefore, based on the classic "glassy" matrix and cellular arrangement, hyaline cartilage is the correct histological diagnosis
questions.learning: The histology section shows a homogeneous, glassy (translucent) basophilic matrix with chondrocytes housed in lacunae, often arranged in small isogenous groups.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: SPIKES protocol is for:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Breaking bad news

SPIKES protocol is for breaking bad news.

Each letter represents a phase in the six-step sequence.

• S - setting
• P - perception
• I - invitation or information
• K - knowledge
• E - empathy
• S - summarizing or strategizing

Key components of the SPIKES strategy include:

• Demonstrating empathy
• Acknowledging and validating the patient's feelings
• Exploring the patient's understanding and acceptance of the bad news
• Providing information about possible interventions
questions.learning: Breaking bad news SPIKES protocol is for breaking bad news. Each letter represents a phase in the six-step sequence. • S - setting • P - perception • I - invitation or information • K - knowledge • E - empathy • S - summarizing or strategizing Key…

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 32-year-old lady comes with complaints of erythematous scaly rash, loose stools, and cognitive dysfunction. The rash involved her forearm, neck, and face. She seems to have difficulty remembering things from the recent past. Her electrolytes are within normal range. She admits to having shifted to a corn-based diet due to economic reasons. Which of the following would improve her symptoms?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Oral Nicotinamide supplementation

The given clinical features suggests the diagnosis of pellagra, due to her corn-based diet. Oral nicotinamide supplements can improve her symtpoms.

Niacin can be synthesized in the body from tryptophan. Two compounds, nicotinic acid and nicotinamide, have the biological activity of niacin. The nicotinamide ring of the coenzymes nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD) and nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide phosphate (NADP) participate in oxidation/reduction reactions.

The initial symptoms of pellagra include loss of appetite, generalized weakness, irritability, abdominal pain, and vomiting. This is followed by bright red glossitis and a characteristic pigmented, scaly skin rash in sun-exposed areas. This rash is known as Casal’s necklace when it forms a ring around the neck.

The 4Ds of pellagra:

• Diarrhea
• Dermatitis
• Dementia, leading to
• Death

It is diagnosed by measuring urinary levels of 2-methyl nicotinamide and 2-pyridone.

Other options:

Option B: Thiamine (Vitamin B1) deficiency leads to conditions like beriberi and Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome, which are characterized by symptoms such as muscle weakness, peripheral neuropathy, cardiovascular issues, and confusion. While cognitive dysfunction can result from thiamine deficiency, rash and loose stools do not fit with thiamine deficiency. Therefore, thiamine would not address the full spectrum of this patient’s symptoms.

Option C: Vitamin C deficiency causes scurvy, which is associated with symptoms like bleeding gums, bruising, joint pain, and fatigue. Scurvy is not associated with a rash like the one described, nor does it typically cause cognitive dysfunction or diarrhea. Hence, high-dose vitamin C would not improve this patient’s symptoms.

Option D: Corn-based diets are low in niacin and tryptophan, leading to pellagra over time, especially if the diet is not balanced with other niacin-rich foods. While stopping the corn-based diet could prevent further niacin deficiency, it will not immediately address the existing deficiency and symptoms like rash, diarrhea, and cognitive dysfunction. The patient would still need niacin supplementation to resolve the current symptoms.
questions.learning: Oral Nicotinamide supplementation — The given clinical features suggests the diagnosis of pellagra, due to her corn-based diet. Oral nicotinamide supplements can improve her symtpoms.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A young male patient presents with a history of high-grade fever for the last 5 days. When his hands were examined, the following lesions were seen which were painless and a new regurgitant murmur is heard. Echocardiogram shows the presence of a mass on the mitral valve. Which of the following abdomen finding will be present here?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Splenomegaly

In the above clinical scenario of a patient presenting with high-grade fever, new-onset murmur, and faint, red, painless macules on palms and soles (called as Janeway lesions), the most probable diagnosis for this patient would be infective endocarditis (IE). The most common abdominal finding is splenomegaly..

Infective endocarditis is characterized by the presence of large, friable, irregular vegetations on heart valves. Patients with infective endocarditis can have cardiac or non-cardiac manifestations.

Cardiac manifestations of IE:

* Presence of new regurgitant murmurs

* Congestive heart failure due to valve dysfunction

* Perivalvular abscesses and intracardiac fistulae- This is caused due to the extension of infection beyond the valves and into the adjacent myocardial tissue

* Conduction system defects- due to the damage of the interventricular septum by the abscess.

* Embolization of coronary arteries

Noncardiac manifestations of IE are:

* Arterial emboli- causing pain of ischemia of the organs

* Roth's spots- retinal hemorrhages with a pale center

* Janeway lesions- In contrast to Osler's nodes, these are faint, red, painless macules on palms and soles. They occur as a result of septic embolization and are commonly associated with staphylococcal IE.

* Glomerulonephritis

* Positivity for rheumatoid factor

* Petechiae on the oral and conjunctival mucosa

* Splinter subungual hemorrhages-painless, dark red lines in the nailbed.

* Mycotic aneurysms

* Splenomegaly

* Osler’s nodes (shown in the image below) are tender, red nodules that typically appear on the pads of the fingers and toes. Occurs due to immune complex deposition and vasculitis.

Image given below shows Roth spots.

Pearl PF0379: Modified Duke's criteria for diagnosis of infective endocarditis

Diagnosis of Infective endocarditis is by Duke's Criteria, which requires either:

* Clinical criteria

* Pathologic criteria

If clinical criteria are used, definitive endocarditis is defined by the presence of 2 major or 1 major + 3 minor or 5 minor criteria.

Presence of single pathological criteria is definitive of infective endocarditis.

Clinical Criteria

Major Criteria

1. Positive blood culture

Typical microorganism for IE from 2 separate blood cultures.

(or)

Persistently positive blood culture of an organism consistent with IE from:

• Blood cultures drawn >12 h apart.
• All of 3 or a majority of ≥4 separate blood cultures, with first and last drawn at least 1 h apart.

(or)

Single positive blood culture for Coxiella burnetti or phase I IgG antibody titer of >1:800.

2. Evidence of endocardial involvement

Echocardiographic identification of oscillating intracardiac mass on valve or implant or in the path of regurgitant jets

(or)

New Valvular regurgitation

Minor Criteria

1. Predisposing heart lesion or intravenous drug use

2. Fever ≥38.0°C (≥100.4°F)

3. Vascular lesions: Major arterial emboli, septic pulmonary infarcts, mycotic aneurysm, intracranial hemorrhage, conjunctival hemorrhages, Janeway lesions.

4. Immunological evidence: Glomerulonephritis, Osler nodes, Roth spots, rheumatoid factor.

5. Microbiologic evidence: Positive blood culture but not meeting the major criterion, or serologic evidence of active infection with an organism consistent with infective endocarditis.

Pathological Criteria

1. Microorganisms demonstrated by culture or histologic examination, in vegetation, embolus from vegetation, or intracardiac abscess

(or)

2. Histologic confirmation of active endocarditis in vegetation or intracardiac abscess

Note: The diagnosis of endocarditis is rejected if an alternative diagnosis is established, if symptoms resolve and do not recur with ≤4 days of antibiotic therapy, or if surgery or autopsy after ≤4 days of antimicrobial therapy yields no histologic evidence of endocarditis.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 30-year-old lady presents to the OPD with complaints of fatigue. On examination, there is pallor. Blood investigations showed a hemoglobin of 10g/dl, RBC count of 3 million cells/mm cube, MCV = 70 fL, MCH = 22 pg. What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Iron deficiency anemia

The above clinical findings are consistent iron deficiency anemia

This patient has microcytic (N: 82-96 fL) and hypochromic (N: 27-33 pg) anemia. The differential diagnoses of microcytic hypochromic anemia include iron deficiency, thalassemia, sideroblastic anemia, and anemia of chronic disease. Since there is reduced RBC count (normal 4.5 to 6.5 milllion/cubic mm), the best answer is Iron deficiency anemia.

The single best test to differentiate between various diagnosis of microcytic hypochromic anemia is iron profile.  Low Ferritin and high TIBC( total iron binding capacity) is seen in Iron deficiency anaemia, while Thalassemia major has normal/high ferritin and low/normal TIBC.
