questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A patient presents with sciatica and tenderness in the hamstring muscles. Which nerve supplies the hybrid muscle that is likely to be spared in this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Obturator nerve

The adductor magnus is the hybrid muscle that is likely to be spared in this condition.

In sciatica, the sciatic nerve is typically affected, which branches into the tibial nerve and the common peroneal nerve. The adductor magnus muscle is an example of a hybrid muscle with dual innervation:

• The adductor part of the adductor magnus is innervated by the obturator nerve.
• The hamstring part of the adductor magnus is innervated by the tibial nerve.

During sciatica, the tibial nerve is often affected, which would impact the hamstring part of the adductor magnus. However, because the adductor part of the adductor magnus is innervated by the obturator nerve, it remains functional and is likely to be spared.

The obturator nerve arises from the anterior division of the ventral rami of L2-L4. Near the obturator foramen, it divides into anterior and posterior branches.

• Anterior division supplies pectineus, adductor longus, adductor brevis, and gracilis
• Posterior division supplies adductor magnus, obturator externus. It also supplies adductor brevis if the muscle is not supplied by the anterior division

The image given below shows the course of the obturator nerve.

Other options:

Option A: The common peroneal nerve is a branch of the sciatic nerve and can also be affected in sciatica. It is responsible for innervating muscles in the anterior and lateral compartments of the leg.

Option B: The tibial nerve is a branch of the sciatic nerve and is often affected in sciatica. It supplies the hamstring part of the adductor magnus, which would be impacted during sciatica.

Option C: The femoral nerve is not involved in sciatica. It supplies the quadriceps and other muscles in the anterior compartment of the thigh, and does not innervate the adductor magnus.
questions.learning: Obturator nerve — The adductor magnus is the hybrid muscle that is likely to be spared in this condition. In sciatica, the sciatic nerve is typically affected, which branches into the tibial nerve and the common peroneal nerve.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: During the inflammatory response, which molecule is responsible for promoting the adhesion of leukocytes to the vascular endothelium?
questions.explanation: During inflammation, leukocyte recruitment to the site of injury occurs in steps: rolling → adhesion → transmigration. The initial interaction (rolling) of leukocytes along the vascular endothelium is mediated by selectins, especially P-selectin. P-selectin is expressed on activated endothelial cells and platelets. It binds to carbohydrate ligands (like sialyl Lewis X) on leukocytes, causing them to slow down and roll along the vessel wall. This rolling is crucial because it allows leukocytes to come into close contact with the endothelium, preparing them for firm adhesion. Why other options are incorrect: (B) Platelet-activating factor (PAF) : Involved in leukocyte activation and chemotaxis, not primary adhesion (C) VCAM-1 : Mediates firm adhesion (via integrins), not the initial adhesion/rolling (D) Complement : Plays a role in opsonization and chemotaxis, not adhesion
questions.learning: During inflammation, leukocyte recruitment to the site of injury occurs in steps: rolling → adhesion → transmigration. The initial interaction (rolling) of leukocytes along the vascular endothelium is mediated by selectins, especially P-selectin.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A woman with an obstetric score of G2P1 comes to the clinic at 14 weeks of gestation for her antenatal checkup. A uterine artery doppler was suggested by the doctor. What would it detect?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Early-onset preeclampsia

A uterine artery doppler would detect early-onset preeclampsia.

The development of a diastolic notch and resistance to flow in the uterine artery doppler suggests the development of gestational hypertension, pre-eclampsia, and fetal growth restriction later in the pregnancy. A high resistance index in the second trimester is associated with a sixfold increase in the incidence of preeclampsia. The trophoblastic invasion of maternal uterine vessels in the first half of pregnancy results in a decrease in vascular resistance. This can be detected by Doppler studies.

Other screening tests which can be used for the prediction of pre-eclampsia include:

• Mean arterial pressure ≥90 mm Hg in the second trimester
• Absence of end-diastolic frequencies in umbilical artery doppler
• Roll over test

Preeclampsia is a multi-system disorder marked by blood pressure ≥140/90 mm Hg with proteinuria after the 20th week of gestation in a previously normotensive and non-proteinuric woman. Usually, there is an invasion of the extravillous trophoblasts (specifically, endovascular trophoblasts) into the walls of the spiral arteries. In the first trimester, the trophoblastic invasion up to the decidual segments occurs. The myometrial segments are invaded in the second trimester. This second wave of endovascular trophoblast migration fails to happen in preeclampsia.

The pathogenesis can be explained by an imbalance in the prostaglandins - a deficiency of PGI2 (vasodilator) and increased thromboxane (vasoconstrictor). The deficiency of nitric oxide and elevated antiangiogenic factors are other mechanisms responsible.

Features include headache, visual disturbances, epigastric pain, and thrombocytopenia. Risk factors include young maternal age, nulliparity, metabolic syndrome, and hyperhomocysteinemia.

Other options:

Option B: Late-onset preeclampsia occurs > 34 weeks. It often has a favorable outcome.

Option C: Fetal growth restriction can be detected by abnormal uterine artery Doppler notching at 20-24 weeks of gestation.

Option D: Placenta accreta or morbidly adherent placenta arises due to partial or total absence of decidua basalis. Sonography is recommended for diagnosis. Better results can be obtained with power doppler.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: What is the correct order of using eye drops and eye ointment?
options: Eye drops first, ointment 15 min later
Ointment first, eye drops 15 min later
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Eye drops first, ointment 15 min later

Eye drops first followed by ointment 15 minutes later is the correct way of usage.

An ointment is thicker in consistency and needs to stay on the eyes for a longer time for absorption of the medication. Hence, it is generally put in the eyes at bedtime.

Eyedrops are watery thin and can be absorbed faster. Hence eyedrops are put first, and after 10-15 minutes, once they are completely absorbed, eye ointment can be applied.

Eye ointments are usually avoided during the daytime as they cause marked blurring of vision.
questions.learning: Eye drops first, ointment 15 min later Eye drops first followed by ointment 15 minutes later is the correct way of usage. An ointment is thicker in consistency and needs to stay on the eyes for a longer time for absorption of the medication.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 24-year-old woman visits the infertility clinic with a complaint of recurrent abortions. Upon investigations, she is found to have a septate uterus. Which of the following corrective procedures has the best obstetric outcome?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Transcervical resection of septum

Transcervical hysteroscopic resection of the septum has the best obstetric outcome.

The procedure involves the resection of the septum under hysteroscopic guidance. Hence, it doesn't scar the uterus and avoids the necessity of cesarean sections for future pregnancies improving obstetric outcomes.

Metroplasty is the surgical resection of the intrauterine septum. This is done by approaching the uterus transabdominally via 3 methods:

• Jones metroplasty
• Strassmann metroplasty
• Tompkins metroplasty

All of these methods are not preferred nowadays as they cause uterine scarring.
questions.learning: Transcervical resection of septum Transcervical hysteroscopic resection of the septum has the best obstetric outcome. The procedure involves the resection of the septum under hysteroscopic guidance.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 45-year-old woman presents with redness and a Peau d’orange appearance involving more than two-thirds of her breast, without a palpable lump. The skin involvement extends to the chest wall, suggestive of inflammatory breast carcinoma. What is the appropriate TNM stage for this patient?
questions.explanation: In the TNM classification for breast cancer, Inflammatory Breast Cancer (IBC) is uniquely and specifically categorized as T4d. IBC is a clinical diagnosis characterized by rapid onset of breast erythema, edema, and a Peau d'orange (orange peel) skin texture, which results from the blockage of dermal lymphatics by tumor emboli. It is distinct from other T4 stages: T4a (Option A) refers to involvement of the chest wall (ribs, serratus, or intercostals); T4b (Option B) refers to skin involvement (ulceration or nodules) that does not meet the clinical criteria for inflammatory cancer. T3 (Option C) refers only to tumor size (>5 cm). IBC is a highly aggressive form of breast cancer with a high risk of early systemic metastasis. Management involves a multimodal approach: neoadjuvant chemotherapy to downstage the disease, followed by modified radical mastectomy and post-operative radiation. The clinical presence of diffuse skin edema (peau d'orange) is the definitive marker that elevates the stage to T4d

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A patient has a cavernous sinus infection affecting the nerve located medially within the sinus. To assess involvement of the abducens nerve, in which direction should you ask the patient to move their eye?
questions.explanation: The cavernous sinus contains several cranial nerves (III, IV, , , and VI). The abducens nerve (CN VI) is unique because it travels through the center of the sinus, medially placed near the internal carotid artery, while the others are in the lateral wall. As established previously, the abducens nerve innervates the lateral rectus muscle, which is responsible for abducting the eye. Therefore, to test its function and confirm involvement, the clinician must ask the patient to look laterally (away from the midline). Looking superiorly (Option A), inferiorly (Option B), and medially (Option C) primarily tests the muscles innervated by the oculomotor nerve (CN III). In cavernous sinus thrombosis, the abducens nerve is often the first nerve affected due to its central location. Patients will present with an inability to move the eye outward and will experience double vision when trying to do so. This clinical correlation is a classic "must-know" for medical examinations
questions.learning: The cavernous sinus contains several cranial nerves (III, IV, , , and VI). The abducens nerve (CN VI) is unique because it travels through the center of the sinus, medially placed near the internal carotid artery, while the others are in the lateral wall.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A 35-year-old man presents with epistaxis, bleeding gums, and multiple ecchymoses. Laboratory investigations show hemoglobin of 8.5 g/dL, a platelet count of 12,000/µL, and a total leukocyte count of 52,000/µL with 83% blasts that are CD33-positive on flow cytometry. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The patient presents with signs of bone marrow failure (anemia, severe thrombocytopenia causing bleeding) and a high white blood cell count (leukocytosis). The presence of 83% blasts is diagnostic of an acute leukemia (threshold is ). The critical differentiating factor is the flow cytometry result showing CD33+. CD33 is a myeloid-specific marker, confirming Acute Myeloid Leukemia (AML). Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia (ALL) (Option B) would typically express B-cell (CD19, CD20) or T-cell markers. Chronic Lymphocytic Leukemia (CLL) (Option C) involves mature-looking lymphocytes and lacks a high blast count. Myelodysplastic Syndrome (MDS) (Option D) features cytopenias and dysplasia but by definition has fewer than 20% blasts. AML is common in adults and requires urgent induction chemotherapy. The clinical picture of bleeding gums and nosebleeds often points toward the M3 subtype (APL) or monocytic subtypes, but CD33 positivity broadly confirms the myeloid lineage
questions.learning: The patient presents with signs of bone marrow failure (anemia, severe thrombocytopenia causing bleeding) and a high white blood cell count (leukocytosis).

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 53-year-old male patient was admitted following a road traffic accident. Paradoxical respiration was seen. His chest X-ray is shown below. He was given analgesics and oxygen was administered via face mask but he developed respiratory failure. What is the best line of management in this case?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Mechanical ventilation

The given clinical scenario and the X-ray showing contiguous rib fractures on the right side suggest flail's chest.

It is characterized by contiguous rib fractures and paradoxical respiration following blunt trauma to the chest wall. Mechanical ventilation (like Intermittent Positive Pressure Ventilation) is the management of flail chest with respiratory failure.

Flail Chest :

* A flail chest occurs when a segment of the chest wall does not have bony continuity with the rest of the thoracic cage.

* This condition results from blunt trauma associated with multiple rib fractures, i.e. 2 adjacent ribs or 3 or more ribs fractured in two or more places.

* The blunt force required to disrupt the integrity of the thoracic cage typically produces an underlying pulmonary contusion as well.

Clinical Features:

On inspiration, the loose segment of the chest wall is displaced inwards and less air, therefore, moves into the lungs. On expiration, the segment moves outwards(paradoxical respiration).

Diagnosis - Made clinically, not by radiography. To confirm the diagnosis the chest wall can be observed for the paradoxical motion of a chest wall segment for several respiratory cycles and during coughing. Voluntary splinting as a result of pain, mechanically impaired chest wall movement, and the associated lung contusion are all causes of hypoxia and respiratory failure.

The patient is also at high risk of developing a pneumothorax or hemothorax.

Treatment

* Chest strapping or splinting should be avoided

* Currently, treatment consists of oxygen administration, adequate analgesia (including opiates) or epidural analgesia and physiotherapy.

* IPPV (Intermittent Positive Pressure Ventilation) is reserved for cases developing respiratory failure despite adequate analgesia and oxygen.

Other options:

Option A: Chest tube drainage can be done in traumatic pulmonary contusion associated with pneumothorax or hemothorax

Option B: Intrapleural local analgesia can be given if the patient has a chest tube inserted. Since the chest tube drainage is only done after stabilising the patient, intrapleural analgesia is not the best line of treatment at this stage.

Option D: Surgical fixation of the fracture is done only in patients with severe chest injury and pulmonary contusion. Also, surgery should be proceeded only after the patient's condition is stabilised.
questions.learning: Mechanical ventilation — The given clinical scenario and the X-ray showing contiguous rib fractures on the right side suggest flail's chest. It is characterized by contiguous rib fractures and paradoxical respiration following blunt trauma to the chest wall.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following are causes of hypocalcemia in a child? I. Hypomagnesemia II. Hypophosphatemia III. Metabolic acidosis IV. Pseudohypoparathyroidism Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. I and IV

Hypocalcemia is defined as a low serum ionized calcium or total serum calcium (after correction for albumin). It commonly presents with neuromuscular irritability, including tetany, seizures, muscle cramps, laryngospasm, and prolonged QT interval on ECG.

Among the important causes in children are hypomagnesemia and pseudohypoparathyroidism.

Why is D correct?

• I. Hypomagnesemia ✔

• Correct.
• Magnesium deficiency impairs parathyroid hormone (PTH) secretion and causes PTH resistance, leading to hypocalcemia.
• Hypocalcemia due to hypomagnesemia will not correct until magnesium is replaced.

• II. Hypophosphatemia ✘

• Incorrect.
• Hypophosphatemia is usually associated with increased calcium levels or normal calcium.
• Hyperphosphatemia, not hypophosphatemia, commonly causes hypocalcemia.

• III. Metabolic acidosis ✘

• Incorrect.
• Acidosis reduces calcium binding to albumin, thereby increasing ionized (physiologically active) calcium.
• Alkalosis, not acidosis, precipitates symptomatic hypocalcemia by decreasing ionized calcium.

• IV. Pseudohypoparathyroidism ✔

• Correct.
• It is caused by end-organ resistance to PTH, resulting in:

• Hypocalcemia
• Hyperphosphatemia
• Elevated PTH levels
questions.learning: I and IV Hypocalcemia is defined as a low serum ionized calcium or total serum calcium (after correction for albumin). It commonly presents with neuromuscular irritability, including tetany, seizures, muscle cramps, laryngospasm, and prolonged QT interval…

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A lactating mother reports breast cramping during breastfeeding. Which hormone is primarily responsible for this sensation?
questions.explanation: The "breast cramps" or tingling sensation reported by a breastfeeding mother during the "let-down" reflex is directly caused by Oxytocin (Option D) . When an infant suckles at the nipple, sensory signals are sent to the posterior pituitary, triggering the release of oxytocin. This hormone travels to the breast, where it causes the contraction of myoepithelial cells surrounding the alveoli, squeezing milk into the ducts. These rhythmic contractions are often perceived as cramping. Prolactin (Option C) is responsible for the actual production of milk (galactopoiesis), while estrogen (Option B) and progesterone (Option A) are involved in breast development during pregnancy but actually inhibit milk production until their levels drop after delivery. Therefore, oxytocin is the hormone definitively responsible for the mechanical ejection of milk and the associated maternal cramping. This same hormone also causes uterine contractions postpartum, helping the uterus return to its pre-pregnancy size

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 1½-year-old child presents to the emergency department with breathlessness, cough, cold, and a temperature below 37 °C. On examination, the respiratory rate is 46 breaths per minute, and there are no signs of chest indrawing or other danger signs. What is the most appropriate management for this child?
options: Administer IV antibiotics and refer to a higher center
Administer oral antibiotics, warn of danger signs, and send home
questions.explanation: According to the IMCI (Integrated Management of Childhood Illness) guidelines, the classification of pneumonia depends on the respiratory rate and presence of "danger signs". For a child aged 12–59 months, fast breathing is defined as a respiratory rate 40 breaths per minute. Since this 18-month-old child has a rate of 46 but NO chest indrawing or other danger signs, they are classified as having "Pneumonia" (not "Severe Pneumonia"). The appropriate management for non-severe pneumonia is treatment with oral antibiotics (typically amoxicillin) for 5 days. The child can be managed at home (Option C) after the mother is taught about danger signs that require immediate return. IV antibiotics (Options A and B) are reserved for "Severe Pneumonia" where there is chest indrawing or inability to drink. Home remedies alone (Option D) are insufficient for bacterial pneumonia
questions.learning: According to the IMCI (Integrated Management of Childhood Illness) guidelines, the classification of pneumonia depends on the respiratory rate and presence of "danger signs".

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: In the adjacent graph, plateau phase represents which one of the following properties?
questions.explanation: The provided graph is a cystometrogram, which plots intravesical pressure against volume during bladder filling. The plateau phase (Phase II) of this curve represents the property of plasticity (also known as accommodation). During this phase, the bladder volume increases significantly with only a minimal rise in pressure. This is due to the inherent ability of the smooth muscle (detrusor) to relax and reorganize its fibers as it stretches, allowing the bladder to store large amounts of urine without reaching the micturition threshold prematurely. Elasticity (Option A) refers to the immediate return to original shape after stretching, but plasticity describes the sustained adaptation to new volumes. Contractility (Option C) is the active phase (Phase III) where the muscle shortens to expel urine, resulting in a sharp pressure rise. Automaticity (Option D) refers to self-initiated contraction, which is generally not a feature of a normal bladder under this filling test. Thus, plasticity is the specific physiological property illustrated by the long plateau

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A 70-year-old patient with a history of schizophrenia, and on treatment for drug-induced Parkinson's presents with complaints of constipation, blurred vision, and dry mouth. Which of the following drugs may be responsible for the above symptoms?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Benzhexol

This patient with schizophrenia and drug-induced parkinson's disease with anti-cholinergic symptoms is taking benzhexol (trihexyphenidyl).

Drug-induced Parkinsonism is a condition that is caused by certain drugs that have D2 antagonistic action like typical antipsychotics. Due to the decrease in dopaminergic activity, they result in an unbalanced cholinergic activity. Benzhexol is a centrally-acting antimuscarinic agent. It acts by restoring the cholinergic balance in the striatal interneurons.

The following drugs are implicated in drug-induced parkinsonism:

Drug class

Examples

Typical antipsychotics

Phenothiazines, haloperidol

Atypical antipsychotics
Risperidone, olanzapine

Dopamine depleters
Reserpine, tetrabenazine

Antiemetics
Metoclopramide, levosulpiride

Calcium channel blockers
Flunarizine, cinnarizine

Other options:

Option A: Lithium is used to treat bipolar disorders and major depressive disorder. The main adverse effects are lithium toxicity, serotonin syndrome, and pseudotumor cerebri. Lithium use is usually avoided in patients with a known cardiovascular disease due to an increased risk of cardiac arrhythmias.

Option B: Pramipexole is used in the treatment of Parkinson's disease and restless leg syndrome. The main adverse effects are dyskinesias and postural deformities.

Option D: Selegiline is used in the treatment of major depressive disorder and Parkinson's disease. The main adverse effects are serotonin syndrome, somnolence, and exacerbation of hypertension. Hence, it is not preferred in Parkinson's patients with hypertension.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 70-year-old man presents with cervical lymphadenopathy, a dull tympanic membrane, hearing loss, and tinnitus in the left ear. Tympanometry shows a type B curve. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: In an elderly patient, the triad of a unilateral serous otitis media (evidenced by the dull tympanic membrane and type B tympanogram), unilateral hearing loss/tinnitus, and neck nodes (cervical lymphadenopathy) is highly suggestive of nasopharyngeal carcinoma (NPC). The tumor originates in the nasopharynx (often the Rosenmüller fossa) and obstructs the eustachian tube opening, leading to fluid accumulation in the middle ear. Chronic suppurative otitis media (Option A) would show a perforated eardrum and discharge. A Glomus tumor (Option B) classically causes pulsatile tinnitus and a "red reflex" behind the drum. Sensorineural hearing loss (Option D) would not explain the fluid-related type B tympanogram curve . Any elderly adult presenting with new-onset unilateral middle ear effusion must undergo a nasopharyngoscopy to rule out NPC. Therefore, given the specific combination of otological symptoms and nodal involvement, nasopharyngeal carcinoma is the prioritized diagnosis

questions.topic: Immunology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: Which of the following is the most potent stimulator of naive T-cells?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Mature dendritic cells

Mature dendritic cells are the most potent antigen-presenting cells (APCs) for activation of naïve T cells.

• Express high levels of MHC class I and II molecules.
• Provide strong co-stimulatory signals (B7/CD80–CD86) required for T-cell activation.
• Secrete cytokines that help differentiate T cells.
• Efficiently capture antigens in peripheral tissues and migrate to lymph nodes to present them to naïve T cells.

Other cells:

B. Follicular dendritic cells: Present antigen to B cells in germinal centers.

C. B lymphocytes: Present antigen mainly to already activated/helper T cells.

D. NK cells: Part of innate immunity, not antigen-presenting cells.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Insulin-independent glucose transporter is present in all of the following except?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Adipose tissue

Insulin-dependent (not independent) glucose transporter is found in the adipose tissue.

Glucose uptake by skeletal muscle, cardiac muscle and adipose tissues is via GLUT-4 which is insulin-dependent.

In the cytoplasm of insulin-sensitive cells, the vesicles contain a pool of GLUT-4 molecules. When the insulin receptors of these cells are activated, the vesicles move rapidly to the cell membrane and fuse with it, inserting the transporters into the cell membrane.

The membrane patches containing transporters are endocytosed when insulin action stops, preparing the vesicles for subsequent insulin exposure. Phosphoinositol 3-kinase is activated by the insulin receptor, which causes the vesicles to migrate to the cell membrane

Most of the other GLUT transporters are not insulin-sensitive and are constitutively expressed in the cell membrane. Ex: GLUT-1 in RBC's and brain, GLUT-2 in the beta cells of the pancreas and GLUT-3 present in the brain and kidneys.
questions.learning: Adipose tissue Insulin-dependent (not independent) glucose transporter is found in the adipose tissue. Glucose uptake by skeletal muscle, cardiac muscle and adipose tissues is via GLUT-4 which is insulin-dependent.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A patient presents with a cyst on the neck anterior to the sternocleidomastoid at the junction of the upper and middle third of the muscle. This cyst is due to the persistence of which of the following embryological clefts?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 2nd cleft

A cyst presenting at the junction of the upper and middle third of the sternomastoid muscle at its anterior border is most likely a branchial cyst. It develops from the vestigial remnants of the second branchial cleft.

Branchial cyst is most commonly seen at the junction of the upper and middle third of the sternomastoid muscle at its anterior border. It is usually lined by squamous epithelium and contains thick, turbid fluid full of cholesterol crystals. It is fluctuant and may transilluminate to a lesser extent when it contains clear fluid.

A branchial fistula may be acquired or congenital. The congenital fistula is seen at the junction of the middle and lower third of the sternomastoid. An acquired fistula is usually seen in cases of incomplete surgery for the branchial cyst or spontaneous rupture, and it is seen at the same site as the cyst.

The below image shows a large right-sided branchial cyst.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Deep inguinal ring is a defect in
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Fascia transversalis

Deep inguinal ring is a defect in fascia transversalis.

* This ring lies midway between the anterior superior iliac spine and the pubic tubercle, approximately 1 cm proximal to the inguinal ligament.

* It lies lateral to inferior epigastric vessels.

Pearl PF1931: Inguinal canal

It is a 4 cm long intermuscular canal directed downwards, forwards, and medially.

It extends from the deep inguinal ring to the superficial ring.

Boundaries:

Boundary

Structures forming

Anterior wall

• Skin, superficial fascia, external oblique aponeurosis (whole extent)
• Muscle fibers of internal oblique (lateral 1/3rd)

Posterior wall

• Parietal peritoneum, extraperitoneal tissues, fascia transversalis (whole extent)
• Medially reinforced by the conjoint tendon and reflected part of the inguinal ligament

Roof

• Arched fibers of internal oblique and transversus abdominis forming the conjoint tendon medially

Floor

• Grooved surface of the inguinal ligament
• Lacunar ligament at the medial end

Deep inguinal ring is an oval opening in the fascia transversalis situated 1.25cm above the mid-inguinal point.

Superficial inguinal ring is a triangular opening in external oblique aponeurosis situated 1cm above and lateral to pubic crest (or medial to the pubic tubercle).

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A patient of rheumatic heart disease presents with superior visual field defect in left eye since 1 week, what is the probable cause?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Branch retinal artery occlusion

A patient with rheumatic heart disease (RHD) presenting with superior visual defects for the past one week is likely due to branch retinal artery occlusion (BRAO).

Retinal artery occlusion usually occurs due to an embolus. Emboli can originate between the vasculature from the heart to the ophthalmic artery. Risk factors include Buerger’s disease, hypertension, elevated lipid levels, cigarette smoking, RHD, and diabetes mellitus.

Retinal emboli can be of 3 types: cholesterol (Hollenhorst plaque), platelet-fibrin, and calcific. The emboli associated with cardiac thrombosis as seen in RHD are platelet-fibrin.

Features of BRAO:

• Sudden painless loss of vision in one eye corresponding to the territory of the obstructed artery. Amaurosis fugax can be seen in patients with preexisting carotid disease.
• Retinal whitening is the most notable finding seen due to ischaemia of the inner layers of the retina. Cotton wool spots can also appear.
• Fluorescein angiography (FA) shows diminution in the dye distal to the site of obstruction. There may be some leaks visible at the site of the embolus.
• OCT (optical coherence tomography) initially shows hyperreflective and thickened inner layers of the retina in the obstructed territory, which start thinning out with time.
• Visual field testing is used to assess the extent of loss of vision.

No effective treatment has been found for BRAO. Ocular massage, lasers, or paracentesis can be used to disrupt the embolus. Vasodilation with inhaled amyl nitrite can be done.

In hypercoagulative states, prophylactic anticoagulation can be started to prevent future episodes.

Other options:

Option A: Central retinal artery occlusion occurs due to obstruction at the level of lamina cribrosa. Patient complains of sudden painless loss of vision occurring over seconds.

Option B: Patients with CRVO usually complain of the acute onset of painless blurred vision in one eye. CRVO is seldom asymptomatic.

Option C: Patients with BRVO typically present with peripheral visual field defects in the defective eye. However, in settings of RHD, arterial occlusion is more likely.
questions.learning: Branch retinal artery occlusion — A patient with rheumatic heart disease (RHD) presenting with superior visual defects for the past one week is likely due to branch retinal artery occlusion (BRAO).

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following statements correctly explains or best represents the dose–response curve shown?
options: Drug B is the most efficacious
Drug B is the most potent
Drug C is more efficacious than drug D
Drug A is more potent than drug B
questions.explanation: A dose–response curve illustrates the relationship between drug dose and the magnitude of response. Two key properties are assessed: potency and efficacy. Potency refers to the amount of drug required to produce a given effect and is indicated by the position of the curve along the x-axis. A drug that achieves its effect at a lower dose appears more left-shifted and is therefore more potent. In the graph, Drug B is the leftmost curve, meaning it requires the smallest dose to produce a response, making it the most potent. Efficacy refers to the maximum effect (Emax) a drug can produce, represented by the height of the curve. Drug B has a lower maximal response compared to Drugs A, C, and D, so it is not the most efficacious. Drug D shows the highest efficacy, not Drug C, ruling out option (C). Drug A lies to the right of Drug B, indicating lower potency. Thus, based on its leftward position, Drug B is the most potent drug
questions.learning: A dose–response curve illustrates the relationship between drug dose and the magnitude of response. Two key properties are assessed: potency and efficacy.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 26-year-old primigravida in active labor is undergoing continuous electronic fetal monitoring. Based on the CTG tracing shown below, which of the following is the most likely interpretation of this fetal heart rate pattern?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Late deceleration

Late decelerations are gradual, symmetrical decreases in fetal heart rate (FHR) that begin after the onset of a uterine contraction, reach their nadir after the peak of the contraction, and recover after the contraction has ended. They are caused by uteroplacental insufficiency, leading to fetal hypoxia, and are considered a non-reassuring CTG pattern.

Why not the other options?

• A. Early decelerations: Mirror the uterine contraction; caused by fetal head compression and are usually benign.
• C. Prolonged decelerations: Decrease in FHR lasting 2–10 minutes, not related to the timing of contractions.
• D. Variable decelerations: Abrupt, V- or U-shaped decelerations with variable timing, caused by umbilical cord compression.
questions.learning: Late deceleration Late decelerations are gradual, symmetrical decreases in fetal heart rate (FHR) that begin after the onset of a uterine contraction, reach their nadir after the peak of the contraction, and recover after the contraction has ended.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A male patient comes to the outpatient clinic with dilated tortuous veins in his lower limb. Varicose veins is suspected. Which of the following is the investigation of choice for this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Duplex scan

Duplex ultrasound is the investigation of choice for varicose veins.

Varicose veins refer to subcutaneous dilated veins of more than 3 mm in diameter.

Investigations :

* Clinical examination

* Venous duplex ultrasound which tells about:

* The site of reflux

* Size of vein

* Location of perforators

* Presence of obstruction in the deep venous system

* Indication of pelvic source of reflux or obstruction

* MR venography

* Invasive procedures such as contrast venography or intravenous ultrasound.

Management of varicose veins

Incompetence
Management

Great saphenous vein (GSV) and saphenofemoral (SFJ)

• Endothermal ablation (gold standard treatment for varicose veins). It includes:

• Endovenous laser ablation (EVLA)
• Radiofrequency ablation (RFA)

• Trendelenburg procedure (Flush Ligation of Saphenofemoral Junction (SFJ) after ligation of 6 tributaries) ± stripping (retrogradely up to the knee, to prevent saphenous nerve injury.)

Short saphenous vein (SSJ) and saphenopopliteal (SPJ)

• Flush ligation of SPJ (Stripping is not done to prevent sural nerve injury)
• Endothermal ablation:

• Endovenous laser ablation (EVLA)
• Radiofrequency ablation (RFA)

Perforator

• Dodd and Crockett surgery - Multiple subfascial ligations
• Subfascial endoscopic perforator surgery (SEPS) - smaller incision, so cosmetically better
• Endothermal ablation:

• Endovenous laser ablation (EVLA)
• Radiofrequency ablation (RFA)

New treatment modalities:

* Foam sclerotherapy - The Tessari method is a widely used method to prepare foam for sclerotherapy. Sclerosant: air ratio taken is 1:3 or 1:4.

* Endovenous glue therapy - endoluminal application of cyanoacrylate adhesive

* TriVex - Transilluminated powered phlebectomy
questions.learning: Duplex scan Duplex ultrasound is the investigation of choice for varicose veins. Varicose veins refer to subcutaneous dilated veins of more than 3 mm in diameter.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: Upto 10% of cases of Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) may be caused by genetic conditions. Which of the following are known to be associated with ASD? I. Tuberous sclerosis II. Fragile X syndrome III. Prader-Willi syndrome IV. Patau syndrome Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. I and II

Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) is a neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by persistent deficits in social communication and interaction, along with restricted, repetitive patterns of behavior, interests, or activities. Approximately 5–10% of ASD cases are associated with identifiable genetic syndromes, the most common being Fragile X syndrome and Tuberous sclerosis complex (TSC).

Why is A correct?

• I. Tuberous sclerosis ✔

• TSC is caused by mutations in the TSC1 or TSC2 genes.
• 40–60% of children with TSC have ASD.
• Other features include:

• Hypomelanotic (ash-leaf) macules
• Facial angiofibromas
• Cortical tubers
• Renal angiomyolipomas
• Cardiac rhabdomyomas

• II. Fragile X syndrome ✔

• Most common inherited cause of intellectual disability and the most common single-gene disorder associated with ASD.
• Caused by CGG repeat expansion in the FMR1 gene on the X chromosome.
• Features include:

• Intellectual disability
• Autism
• Long face
• Large ears
• Macroorchidism (post-pubertal)

• III. Prader-Willi syndrome ✘

• Although behavioral abnormalities may occur, it is not a classic genetic syndrome associated with ASD for examination purposes.

• IV. Patau syndrome ✘

• Trisomy 13 causes severe congenital malformations and profound developmental delay but is not typically associated with ASD.
questions.learning: I and II Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) is a neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by persistent deficits in social communication and interaction, along with restricted, repetitive patterns of behavior, interests, or activities.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: In a patient diagnosed with unilateral breast cancer, what potential risk should be considered when initiating treatment with tamoxifen?
options: Breast cancer in the opposite breast
questions.explanation: Tamoxifen is a Selective Estrogen Receptor Modulator (SERM) used to treat hormone-receptor-positive breast cancer. While it acts as an estrogen antagonist in the breast, it acts as an estrogen agonist (stimulator) in the uterus. This stimulatory effect on the uterine lining significantly increases the potential risk of developing endometrial hyperplasia and endometrial cancer (Option B). This is a well-documented long-term side effect that requires regular gynecological monitoring for any abnormal bleeding. Paradoxically, tamoxifen actually reduces the risk of cancer in the opposite (contralateral) breast (Option C), which is one of its primary therapeutic benefits. It is not associated with an increased risk of ovarian cancer (Option A) or cervical cancer (Option D). Therefore, the tissue-specific estrogenic action on the endometrium is the primary oncological risk associated with its use
questions.learning: Tamoxifen is a Selective Estrogen Receptor Modulator (SERM) used to treat hormone-receptor-positive breast cancer. While it acts as an estrogen antagonist in the breast, it acts as an estrogen agonist (stimulator) in the uterus.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Revised A 1.5-year-old child is brought to the hospital with a history of breathlessness, body temperature of less than 37 degrees, cough, and cold. On examination, the respiratory rate was 46/min, and there were no chest retractions. Which is the most appropriate management?
options: Administer IV antibiotics and refer to higher centre
Administer oral antibiotics, warn of danger signs, and send home
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Administer oral antibiotics, warn of danger signs, and send home

This child with a respiratory rate of 46 breaths/min has tachypnea/fast breathing without any danger signs has pneumonia according to IMNCI guidelines. The next best step of management is to administer oral antibiotics, warn of danger signs, and send home.

The treatment for pneumonia for a child between 2 months and 5 years of age is oral amoxicillin and home care advice.

The revised classification of acute respiratory infections is simplified to include only two categories of pneumonia:

* Cough and cold, no pneumonia - requires home remedy

* Pneumonia - with fast breathing and/or chest indrawing, which requires home therapy with oral amoxicillin.

* Severe pneumonia - pneumonia with any general danger sign, which requires a referral and injectable therapy.

Danger signs:

* Not able to drink

* Persistent vomiting

* Convulsions, lethargic or unconscious

* Stridor in a calm child

* Severe malnutrition

Tachypnea or Fast breathing is defined based on the age and respiratory rate:

Age of child
Rate

<2 months
60 breaths/min

2-12 months
50 breaths/min

1-5 years
40 breaths/min
questions.learning: Administer oral antibiotics, warn of danger signs, and send home This child with a respiratory rate of 46 breaths/min has tachypnea/fast breathing without any danger signs has pneumonia according to IMNCI guidelines.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: While performing an endoscopy, a constriction is felt at the oesophageal junction, 25 cm from the upper incisors. Which of the following structures is responsible for this?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Arch of aorta

The constriction is felt due to the arch of aorta and left bronchus crossing the esophagus at 25 cm from the upper incisor teeth.

Normally, the esophagus shows 3 constrictions at the following levels measured from upper incisors:

* Junction of the esophagus with cricopharynx (15 cm from the incisor teeth)

* Crossed by arch of aorta and left bronchus (25 cm from the incisor teeth)

* It pierces the diaphragm (40 cm from the incisor teeth)

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient reports pain in right upper abdomen. FNAC of liver cyst shows parasitic organism. Most likely cause?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Echinococcus granulosus

• Hydatid cyst of liver is caused by Echinococcus granulosus.
• FNAC shows scolices and hooklets.
• Taenia solium causes neurocysticercosis, Taenia saginata and H. nana are intestinal parasites.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following is the most common side effect of cholecystectomy?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Steatorrhea

The most common side effect of cholecystectomy is steatorrhea. Steatorrhea is fecal fat excretion of more than 7 g/24 hours or >6% /24 hours, when on a diet of 100 to 150 g of fat. Gall Bladder is the major source of Bile and Bile plays an important role in the absorption of fats/lipids. Hence Cholecystectomy can lead to steatorrhea.

Digestion of Lipids

* Pancreatic lipase is the most important enzymes involved in lipid digestion. Main products of its action are FFA and 2-monoglycerides (2-monoacylglycerols

* Colipase is an accessory factor secreted in the pancreatic juice that helps to stabilize pancreatic lipase in an active conformation

* Bile acids emulsify the insoluble lipids and make them reach the surface of the mucosal cells. Bile acids also activate another pancreatic lipase called cholesterol esterase.

* Cholesterol esterase hydrolysis cholesterol esters, esters of fat-soluble vitamins, phospholipids, and triglycerides
questions.learning: Steatorrhea — The most common side effect of cholecystectomy is steatorrhea. Steatorrhea is fecal fat excretion of more than 7 g/24 hours or >6% /24 hours, when on a diet of 100 to 150 g of fat.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Renal Electrolytes · Acid Base Electrolyte Disturbances
questions.text: A 23-year-old man with type 1 diabetes mellitus is brought to the emergency department with confusion and generalized weakness. He reports missing multiple doses of insulin over the past few days due to poor oral intake following an episode of diarrhea. On examination, he is dehydrated and has deep, rapid breathing with a fruity odor to his breath. Arterial blood gas analysis reveals metabolic acidosis. Which of the following changes in urine chemistry is most likely to be seen in this patient?
options: Increased urine pH, increased bicarbonate excretion, decreased ammonium excretion
Increased urine pH, decreased bicarbonate excretion, increased ammonium excretion
Decreased urine pH, decreased bicarbonate excretion, decreased ammonium excretion
Decreased urine pH, decreased bicarbonate excretion, increased ammonium excretion
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Decreased urine pH, decreased bicarbonate excretion, increased ammonium excretion

This patient has diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) causing high anion gap metabolic acidosis.

Renal compensation:

• Kidneys try to excrete excess acid (H⁺)
• Increase ammonium (NH₄⁺) excretion to buffer H⁺
• Reabsorb bicarbonate → ↓ urinary HCO₃⁻ loss
• Urine becomes acidic (↓ pH)
questions.learning: Decreased urine pH, decreased bicarbonate excretion, increased ammonium excretion This patient has diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) causing high anion gap metabolic acidosis.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Identify the blue-colored area shown in the image.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Mid-pelvis

The plane through the ischial spines represents the mid-pelvis, the narrowest functional level and key area where rotation and arrest disorders occur. This region is also called the plane of least pelvic dimensions.

| Boundary | Structure

| Anterior | Lower border of pubic symphysis

| Posterior | Sacrum (S4–S5 region)

| Lateral | Ischial spines

The mid-pelvis is crucial because:

• It is the narrowest part of the birth canal
• Determines engagement and descent of the fetal head
• Used to determine fetal station

↓

A) Obstetric outlet ❌

Located at the inferior opening of the pelvis.

B) Anatomical outlet ❌

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following correctly represents the fractional inactivated polio vaccine (fIPV) dosing schedule under the National Immunization Schedule?
options: At birth, 6 weeks, 10 weeks, 14 weeks, 16-24 months, 5 years
questions.explanation: Fractional Inactivated Polio Vaccine (fIPV) is administered as a 0.1 ml intradermal dose. Under the current National Immunization Schedule (NIS), the primary doses are given at 6 weeks and 14 weeks. Recently, a third dose was added to be administered at 9 completed months of age. Option A is incorrect because fIPV is not given at 10 weeks. Option B represents the full schedule for Oral Polio Vaccine (OPV), which is given as 2 drops at birth and subsequently alongside IPV. Option D is not a standard immunization schedule. Unlike the live OPV, fIPV is a killed vaccine that provides safe humoral immunity without the risk of Vaccine-Associated Paralytic Polio (VAPP). The 9-month dose is specifically given in the left upper arm
questions.learning: Fractional Inactivated Polio Vaccine (fIPV) is administered as a 0.1 ml intradermal dose. Under the current National Immunization Schedule (NIS), the primary doses are given at 6 weeks and 14 weeks.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which joint is not formed by the bone shown in the image?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Synchondrosis

Thoracic vertebrae do not form synchondrosis (primary cartilaginous) joints; they are involved in forming plane joints, syndesmosis, and symphysis joints.

Joints formed by a vertebra:

| Joint | Type | Explanation

| ----- | ---- | -----------

| Intervertebral disc joint | Symphysis (secondary cartilaginous) | Between vertebral bodies via fibrocartilage disc

| Zygapophyseal (facet) joints | Plane joint (synovial) | Between superior & inferior articular processes

| Costovertebral joint | Synovial plane joint | Rib head articulates with thoracic vertebra

| Syndesmosis | Fibrous joint | Ligaments connecting vertebrae (supraspinous, interspinous ligaments)

Why NOT Synchondrosis?

Synchondrosis = primary cartilaginous joint, united by hyaline cartilage

• Examples: 1st rib & sternum, epiphyseal growth plates, spheno-occipital joint
• Vertebrae do NOT form any synchondrosis joint in adults
• The intervertebral joint uses fibrocartilage → that's a symphysis, not synchondrosis
questions.learning: Synchondrosis Thoracic vertebrae do not form synchondrosis (primary cartilaginous) joints; they are involved in forming plane joints, syndesmosis, and symphysis joints.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Twin pregnancy where 1 twin is older by 1 month than the other on ultrasound. What is this known as?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Superfetation

Superfetation = twins conceived in different cycles, giving different gestational ages. Superfecundation happens in the same cycle. MCMA twins are identical and same age.

| Feature | Superfetation | Superfecundation

| ------- | ------------- | ----------------

| Timing | Two different ovulation cycles | Same ovulation cycle

| Gestational age | Different ages | Same age

| Fathers | May be same | May be different

A) Superfecundation

• Occurs in same menstrual cycle, so fetuses have same gestational age.

C) Illegitimate

• Not a medical term.

D) Monochorionic monoamniotic

• Twins are same age, not different gestational ages.
questions.learning: Superfetation Superfetation = twins conceived in different cycles, giving different gestational ages. Superfecundation happens in the same cycle.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: In the context of pediatric advanced life support (PALS), which component does not correctly correspond to the ABCD approach?
questions.explanation: The "ABCD" mnemonic is a standardized approach used in emergency medicine and Pediatric Advanced Life Support (PALS) for the primary assessment of a critically ill child. The components are: A : Airway (Option A) – Ensure the airway is clear and maintainable. B : Breathing (Option B) – Assess respiratory rate, effort, and oxygen saturation. C : Circulation (Option C) – Assess heart rate, pulses, and capillary refill. D : Disability – Assess neurological status using GCS or AVPU. "Dehydration" (Option D) is NOT a component of the primary ABCD survey. While assessing hydration status is important in a pediatric history, it is part of the secondary or more detailed systemic assessment, not the initial life-saving survey meant to identify immediate threats to life. Therefore, Disability is the correct fourth component, making "Dehydration" the inaccurate choice in this context
questions.learning: The "ABCD" mnemonic is a standardized approach used in emergency medicine and Pediatric Advanced Life Support (PALS) for the primary assessment of a critically ill child.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Surgery where nostrils are partially or completely occluded is done for which condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Atrophic rhinitis

Complete closure of the nostrils (Young's operation) or partial closure of the nostrils (Modified Young's operation) is done for the treatment of atrophic rhinitis.

In Young's operation, both nostrils are closed completely by raising flaps within the nasal vestibule. They are opened after 6 months. During this time, the mucosa becomes normal, and the crusting is reduced.

In Modified Young's operation, the procedure has been modified to avoid discomfort from complete closure of the nostrils. Here the nostrils are only partially closed. The results are the same when compared to Young's operation.

Atrophic rhinitis (ozaena) is a chronic inflammation of the nose with atrophy of nasal mucosa and turbinate bones. Roomy nasal cavities with foul-smelling crusts are seen. The patient presents with a foul smell from the nose, marked anosmia (merciful anosmia), and paradoxical nasal obstruction (nasal obstruction despite wide nasal passages). Paradoxical nasal obstruction occurs due to degenerative changes in the sensory nerves of the nasal mucosa, leading to an inability to sense airflow.

Medical management includes nasal irrigation and removal of crusts. 25% glucose in glycerine, antibiotics (quinolones or metronidazole), estradiol nasal spray, and mucolytics can be used.
questions.learning: Atrophic rhinitis Complete closure of the nostrils (Young's operation) or partial closure of the nostrils (Modified Young's operation) is done for the treatment of atrophic rhinitis.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which one of the following diseases affects predominantly large arteries?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Giant cell arteritis

Giant cell arteritis (temporal arteritis) is a large-vessel vasculitis affecting the aorta and its major branches, especially the extracranial branches of the carotid artery (e.g., temporal artery). It commonly occurs in patients >50 years and presents with headache, scalp tenderness, jaw claudication, visual symptoms, and is often associated with polymyalgia rheumatica.

Why not the other options?

• A. Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA): Small-vessel vasculitis involving the upper/lower respiratory tract and kidneys.
• B. Polyarteritis nodosa (PAN): Medium-vessel vasculitis affecting renal, mesenteric, and other medium-sized arteries.
• D. Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (EGPA): Small-vessel vasculitis associated with asthma and eosinophilia.
questions.learning: Giant cell arteritis Giant cell arteritis (temporal arteritis) is a large-vessel vasculitis affecting the aorta and its major branches, especially the extracranial branches of the carotid artery (e.g., temporal artery).

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A patient presents with bleeding gums, petechiae, delayed wound healing, and similar clinical features. Which vitamin deficiency is most likely responsible for these symptoms?
questions.explanation: The clinical triad of bleeding gums, petechiae (small red skin spots), and poor wound healing is the classic presentation of scurvy, caused by Vitamin C deficiency. Vitamin C (ascorbic acid) is an essential cofactor for the enzymes prolyl and lysyl hydroxylase, which are required for the cross-linking of collagen fibers. Deficient collagen synthesis leads to fragile blood vessels and weakened connective tissue. Vitamin A deficiency (Option A) primarily causes ocular issues like night blindness and Bitot's spots. Vitamin B6 deficiency (Option B) is associated with neuropathy and seizures. Vitamin B3 deficiency (Option C) causes pellagra, characterized by the "3 Ds": dermatitis, diarrhea, and dementia. Because Vitamin C is uniquely required for structural collagen integrity, its absence directly results in the hemorrhagic and healing defects described in the patient
questions.learning: The clinical triad of bleeding gums, petechiae (small red skin spots), and poor wound healing is the classic presentation of scurvy, caused by Vitamin C deficiency.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A patient has presented with blister on hand followed by axillary lymphadenopathy. What will you ask the patient with regard to history?
options: History of similar complaint in family members
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. History of exposure to cat

Patient with blister on the hand followed by axillary lymphadenopathy is more suggestive of Cat scratch disease, a disease caused by Bartonella henselae, hence we should ask about the history of exposure to cat.

Cat-scratch disease is also known as subacute regional lymphadenitis. It is acquired following contact with infected animals, commonly cats.

Regional lymph nodes demonstrate:

* Follicular hyperplasia with circumscribed central stellate necrosis with neutrophils

* Surrounded by palisading histiocytes (suppurative granulomas)

* Sinuses packed with monocytoid B cells

* Usually, there are no perifollicular and intrafollicular epithelioid cells

Bartonella henselae also causes bacillary angiomatosis and bacillary peliosis in HIV-infected people.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Choose the correct order of suctioning during neonatal resuscitation.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Mouth-nose

During neonatal resuscitation, the mouth is suctioned first and then the nares, in order to decrease the risk of aspiration. A 12 or 14 French suction catheter is used, with the suction pressure kept between 80-100mmHg.

Routine suctioning of the trachea during neonatal resuscitation is not recommended. The suctioning of the esophagus and stomach is avoided if not indicated specifically, as it can produce a vagal response due to stimulation in the posterior pharynx, resulting in apnea and/or bradycardia.

The steps in neonatal resuscitation follow the ABCs, Airway, Breathing, and Circulation.

The neonatal resuscitation algorithm is given below:

Chest compression should be initiated over the lower third of the sternum at a rate of 90/minutes. The ratio of chest compression to ventilation is 3: 1 (90 compressions: 30 breaths). The thumb technique (preferred) and 2 finger technique are the two different techniques used for performing chest compression. Umbilical vein cannulation is the preferred method for the administration of medications.
questions.learning: Mouth-nose During neonatal resuscitation, the mouth is suctioned first and then the nares, in order to decrease the risk of aspiration. A 12 or 14 French suction catheter is used, with the suction pressure kept between 80-100mmHg.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which variety of cartilage generally does not show calcification as a normal age-related change?
questions.explanation: This question reinforces the histological distinction between laryngeal cartilage types and their reaction to the aging process. The thyroid, cricoid, and the base of the arytenoid are hyaline cartilages. Hyaline cartilage is prone to endochondral ossification and calcification beginning in the third decade of life. By contrast, the epiglottis is composed of elastic cartilage, characterized by an abundance of elastic fibers in its matrix. Elastic cartilage is designed for high flexibility and resilience; it does not calcify with age. This property ensures that the epiglottis remains pliable enough to fold over the laryngeal inlet during deglutition throughout a person's lifespan. Options A, B, and D are all hyaline structures that will progressively harden and become more radiopaque over time. Clinically, the calcification of hyaline laryngeal cartilages can sometimes interfere with surgical procedures or be misinterpreted on computed tomography scans of the neck, whereas the epiglottis consistently retains its cartilaginous, non-calcified density
questions.learning: This question reinforces the histological distinction between laryngeal cartilage types and their reaction to the aging process. The thyroid, cricoid, and the base of the arytenoid are hyaline cartilages.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 4-year-old child has a mid–upper arm circumference of 105 mm and eagerly consumes the entire amount of therapeutic food provided. Under which category is this child most appropriately classified?
questions.explanation: Severe Acute Malnutrition (SAM) in children aged 6 to 59 months is diagnosed when the Mid-Upper Arm Circumference (MUAC) is less than 115 mm. This child's MUAC of 105 mm confirms SAM. SAM is further classified as "uncomplicated" or "complicated" based on the presence of medical issues or the "appetite test". Because the child eagerly completed the therapeutic food, they have passed the appetite test. In the absence of severe edema or other danger signs, these patients can be managed at home with therapeutic feeding. Complicated SAM (Option B) would be diagnosed if the child had failed the appetite test, had severe pitting edema, or required immediate inpatient stabilization. Acute malnutrition (Option C) is too broad a term, and "normal nutrition" (Option D) is ruled out by the low MUAC. Thus, the child fits the criteria for Uncomplicated SAM
questions.learning: Severe Acute Malnutrition (SAM) in children aged 6 to 59 months is diagnosed when the Mid-Upper Arm Circumference (MUAC) is less than 115 mm. This child's MUAC of 105 mm confirms SAM.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: What is the role of the marked structure in the given image?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Motor function

The marked structure is the subthalamic nucleus, which is a part of the basal ganglia and is concerned with motor function.

The basal ganglia refers to the mass of grey matter located within the cerebral white matter and is responsible for a number of coordinated functions including the control of extra-pyramidal pathways for motor coordination. There are two major pathways involved which are, the direct and indirect pathways.

The direct pathway stimulates the cortex to produce movement, whereas the indirect pathway inhibits it. The striatal activity in the direct pathway is mediated by D1 dopamine receptors and in the indirect pathway by D2 dopamine receptors. The subthalamic nucleus is a part of the indirect pathway. A lesion at subthalamic nuclei leads to loss of inhibitory effect of the indirect pathway resulting in dopaminergic overactivity responsible for features of hemiballismus.

Other Options:

Option B: Reward-punishment is associated with the prefrontal area and the dopaminergic connections linked to it from the ventral tegmental area.

Option C: Judgement is controlled by the frontal lobe.

Option D: Memory is controlled by the hippocampus.
questions.learning: Motor function — The marked structure is the subthalamic nucleus, which is a part of the basal ganglia and is concerned with motor function. The basal ganglia refers to the mass of grey matter located within the cerebral white matter and is responsible for…

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following drugs is used in GERD?
questions.explanation: Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease (GERD) is managed primarily with drugs that reduce gastric acid secretion and, in selected patients, with agents that improve gastrointestinal motility. Domperidone is a dopamine D₂-receptor antagonist that acts as a prokinetic agent. Domperidone increases the tone of the lower esophageal sphincter (LES) and enhances gastric emptying, thereby reducing the likelihood of gastric contents refluxing into the esophagus. For this reason, it is commonly used as an adjunct therapy in GERD, especially in patients with associated delayed gastric emptying or persistent symptoms despite acid suppression. Ondansetron (Option A) is a 5-HT₃ antagonist used to treat nausea and vomiting and has no role in GERD. Loperamide (Option C) and diphenoxylate (Option D) are antidiarrheal agents that slow intestinal motility and do not treat reflux; they may even worsen symptoms by delaying gastric emptying. Although proton pump inhibitors (PPIs) remain the mainstay of GERD treatment, domperidone is the correct choice among the options given for managing GERD
questions.learning: Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease (GERD) is managed primarily with drugs that reduce gastric acid secretion and, in selected patients, with agents that improve gastrointestinal motility.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A soldier presents to a referral hospital one day after sustaining a high-velocity shrapnel injury to his right thigh. He complains of severe pain at the wound site. On examination, crepitus is present. Which of the following organisms is the most likely cause of his condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Clostridium perfringens

The most likely diagnosis in the given clinical scenario is gas gangrene/ clostridial myonecrosis, which is caused by clostridium perfringens.

Military wounds provide an ideal environment for gas gangrene as the kinetic energy of high-velocity missiles or shrapnel causes extensive tissue damage. Patients who are immunocompromised, diabetic, or have malignant disease are also at greater risk. The usual incubation period is <24 hours of injury.

Gas gangrene wound infections are associated with severe local wound pain and crepitus (gas in the tissues). The wound produces a thin, brown, sweet-smelling exudate, in which Gram staining will reveal bacteria. Edema and spreading gangrene occur due to the release of collagenase, hyaluronidase, other proteases, and alpha-toxin. Early systemic complications like circulatory collapse and organ failure can occur without adequate treatment.

Management includes high doses of intravenous penicillin and aggressive debridement of affected tissues. Amputations should be performed under antibiotic prophylaxis.

Other options:

C. difficile, a gram-positive anaerobic bacillus, causes Clostridioides (formerly Clostridium) difficile infection (CDI) after ingestion of spores of the organism. The more severe form of the condition is known as pseudomembranous colitis (PMC). It is most commonly associated with prolonged antimicrobial use which interferes with the commensal colonic microflora. The most commonly implicated antibiotics are cephalosporins, ampicillin, and clindamycin.
questions.learning: Clostridium perfringens — The most likely diagnosis in the given clinical scenario is gas gangrene/ clostridial myonecrosis, which is caused by clostridium perfringens.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Mechanism of action of botulinum toxin is:
options: Inhibits release of acetylcholine from lower motor neurons
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Inhibits release of acetylcholine from lower motor neurons

Botulinum toxin blocks neuromuscular transmission by inhibiting the release of acetylcholine (ACh) at the presynaptic terminals of lower motor neurons.

Mechanism:

• Botulinum toxin cleaves SNARE proteins (e.g., synaptobrevin, SNAP-25).
• These proteins are essential for fusion of synaptic vesicles with the presynaptic membrane.
• Their inhibition prevents exocytosis of acetylcholine, leading to failure of neuromuscular transmission.

Clinical correlation:

• Causes descending flaccid paralysis (e.g., botulism)
• Used therapeutically in conditions like dystonia, spasticity, and cosmetic procedures

Why other options are incorrect:

• Inhibits NM receptor: Seen with drugs like curare, not botulinum toxin.
• Inhibits reuptake of acetylcholine: ACh is not reuptaken like monoamines; it is degraded by acetylcholinesterase.
• Inhibits synthesis of acetylcholine: Not the mechanism of botulinum toxin.
questions.learning: Inhibits release of acetylcholine from lower motor neurons Botulinum toxin blocks neuromuscular transmission by inhibiting the release of acetylcholine (ACh) at the presynaptic terminals of lower motor neurons.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Rabies virus uses which molecular motor to cause involvement of the central nervous system from the site of the host?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Dynein

Rabies virus uses dyenin for transport from site of inoculation to the central Nervous system.

The rabies virus P protein which is involved in viral transcription and replication binds with the LC8 chain of dynein molecule for retrograde transport of the virus to the CNS.

AXONAL TRANSPORT

* Protein synthesis occurs in the cell body of neuron and proteins and polypeptides are transported to axonal endings by the axoplasmic flow.

* Axonal transport can be Orthograde or Retrograde.

* Orthograde transport

* Can be either fast or slow axonal transport and it occurs along microtubules that run along the length of the axon away from the cell body.

* Fast axonal transport occurs at about 400 mm/day, and slow axonal transport occurs at 0.5 to 10 mm/day.

* Molecular motor involved in orthograde transport is kinesin.

* Retrograde transport,

* In the opposite direction (from the nerve ending to the cell body), occurs along microtubules at about 200 mm/day. Synaptic vesicles, nerve growth factor (NGF) and some viruses (Eg: herpes simplex, rabies, and polio) are transported back to the cell body.

* Molecular motor involed in retrograde transport is dyenin.
questions.learning: Dynein Rabies virus uses dyenin for transport from site of inoculation to the central Nervous system. The rabies virus P protein which is involved in viral transcription and replication binds with the LC8 chain of dynein molecule for retrograde transport…

questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. C5

The deltoid muscle is the main muscle involved in the abduction of the arm. It is innervated by the C5 root of the axillary nerve. So, a lesion involving the C5 causes inability to abduct the arm.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Revised Which of the following is not an indication for cesarean section?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Previous history of macrosomia

Previous history of macrosomia is not an indication of a cesarean section(CS).

Cesarean is needed even with a dead fetus when vaginal delivery is not possible.
The following are the absolute indication:

* Central placenta previa (Option C)

* Contracted pelvis or cephalopelvic disproportion (absolute)(Option A)

* Pelvic mass causing an obstruction (cervical or broad ligament fibroid)

* Advanced carcinoma cervix (Option D)

* Vaginal atresia or stenosis

Relative indications for cesarean section are those where vaginal delivery may be possible but risks to the mother and/or baby are high. They are as follows:

* Nonreassuring FHR

* Dystocia- It may be due to a relatively large fetus (passenger), small pelvis (passage), or inefficient uterine contractions (power)

* Antepartum hemorrhage: Placenta previa and abruptio placenta

* Malpresentation: Breech, shoulder (transverse lie), brow

* Previous cesarean delivery-a) When primary CS was due to recurrent indication (contracted pelvis), (b) Previous two CS,(c) Features of scar dehiscence, (d) Previous classical CS

* Cephalopelvic disproportion (relative)

* Failure to progress in labor

* Hypertensive disorders: Severe pre-eclampsia, eclampsia— uncontrolled fits even with antiseizure therapy.
questions.learning: Previous history of macrosomia Previous history of macrosomia is not an indication of a cesarean section(CS). Cesarean is needed even with a dead fetus when vaginal delivery is not possible.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 23-year-old patient presents with persistent flank pain, fatigue, and episodes of red-colored urine, with no prior history of urinary or renal disease. Laboratory tests show more than 20 red blood cells per high-power field in the urine, and microscopic examination reveals these RBCs to be dysmorphic. What is the most likely diagnosis in this patient?
questions.explanation: The presence of "dysmorphic RBCs" (such as acanthocytes) in the urine is a critical diagnostic clue indicating that the hematuria is of glomerular origin. As RBCs pass through the damaged glomerular basement membrane and navigate the osmotic changes of the renal tubules, they become distorted. Post-Streptococcal Glomerulonephritis (PSGN) is a classic cause of nephritic syndrome presenting with hematuria, flank pain, and systemic symptoms like fatigue. Minimal Change Disease (Option A) is a nephrotic syndrome characterized by massive proteinuria rather than significant hematuria or dysmorphic RBCs. Urinary Tract Infections (UTI, Option C) and Bladder Calculi (Option D) are causes of "extra-glomerular" or post-renal hematuria. In these cases, the RBCs do not pass through the glomerulus and therefore maintain their normal, uniform, biconcave shape. Since this patient's RBCs are specifically described as dysmorphic, a glomerular disease like PSGN is the only plausible diagnosis among the choices provided
questions.learning: The presence of "dysmorphic RBCs" (such as acanthocytes) in the urine is a critical diagnostic clue indicating that the hematuria is of glomerular origin.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 42-year-old man presents with confusion, deep rapid breathing, and a fruity odor on the breath. Investigations reveal severe hyperglycemia, ketonuria, and metabolic acidosis. What is the most common cause of death in this condition?
questions.explanation: This patient is presenting with the classic clinical triad of Diabetic Ketoacidosis (DKA): hyperglycemia, ketosis (indicated by ketonuria and fruity-smelling breath from acetone), and metabolic acidosis (resulting in Kussmaul breathing, which is deep and rapid). While DKA has several potential complications, "cerebral edema" is the most feared and common cause of death, particularly in children and young adults. It often occurs during treatment, potentially due to rapid shifts in osmolality if fluids or insulin are administered too aggressively. Cardiac arrhythmias (Option B) can occur due to severe potassium imbalances but are less frequently the primary cause of death compared to brain swelling. ARDS (Option A) and AKI (Option D) are potential complications of severe sepsis or dehydration associated with DKA but are not the leading cause of mortality. Therefore, the clinical focus during DKA management is careful fluid resuscitation and gradual reduction of blood glucose to prevent the catastrophic development of cerebral edema

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A 28-year-old male is positive for SARS-COV-2. A total of 30 people have been in contact with the patient and show no symptoms or signs of COVID-19. What is the time duration for which they must be quarantined?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Maximum incubation period

Quarantine is the limitation in freedom of movement of healthy contacts of cases, who have been exposed for a period that lasts as much as the maximal incubation period of the disease.

The incubation period is the time interval between the invasion of the infectious agent and the appearance of the first symptom or signs in the body. It is termed as the latent period in non-infectious diseases.

* It is a primary level of prevention, under specific protection.

* Types of quarantine

* Absolute: complete limitation of movement

* Modified: selective partial limitation of movement

* Segregation: observation of a group of persons in a population after separation.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is not caused by food adulteration?
questions.explanation: Fluorosis is a chronic condition caused by excessive intake of fluoride, primarily through contaminated drinking water or dental products, rather than the deliberate or accidental adulteration of food. It results from high geological fluoride concentrations in groundwater. In contrast, the other options are classic examples of health conditions caused by food adulteration. Epidemic dropsy (Option B) is caused by mustard oil adulterated with Argemone oil. Neurolathyrism (Option C) results from consuming pulses adulterated with Lathyrus sativus (Kesari dal), which contains the neurotoxin BOAA. Endemic ascites (Option D) is caused by food contaminated with pyrrolizidine alkaloids from plants like Crotalaria. Since fluorosis is an environmental waterborne issue, it is the correct answer as the exception to the food-adulteration list
questions.learning: Fluorosis is a chronic condition caused by excessive intake of fluoride, primarily through contaminated drinking water or dental products, rather than the deliberate or accidental adulteration of food.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 70-year-old woman presents with severe back pain. CT of the lumbar spine is shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Spondylolisthesis

Spondylolisthesis is defined as anterior displacement of one vertebra over another, often due to degeneration or bilateral defects in the pars interarticularis—seen as a “Scotty dog with a collar” on oblique X-ray views.

Key Radiological Signs:

• Anterior displacement (“step-off”)
• Misalignment of vertebral bodies
• Narrowed disc space (degenerative type)
• Possible osteophytes
