questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: School health service should include all the following except
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Doctor on premises

School health service includes all the above except the presence of a doctor on school premises.

School health service programs function to promote positive health, prevent diseases, diagnose, treat and follow up on defects.

The health appraisal services of the program are administered by doctors in PHCs. Teachers are trained to do daily inspection, first aid and emergency care whenever necessary and a doctor's presence on school premises is not required.

The main aspects of this program includes:

* Screening of general health assessment of anaemia/nutritional status, visual acuity, hearing problem, dental check-up, physical disabilities, learning disorders, behaviour problems, etc.

* Prevention of communicable diseases through immunization

* Providing a healthful school environment

* Nutritional services

* First-aid and emergency care

* Education of handicapped children

* Health education

* Maintenance and use of school health records
questions.learning: Doctor on premises School health service includes all the above except the presence of a doctor on school premises. School health service programs function to promote positive health, prevent diseases, diagnose, treat and follow up on defects.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 50-year-old male presented with progressive blurred vision, photophobia, and eye pain. On examination, there was conjunctival redness, a mid-dilated pupil, and a shallow anterior chamber in the right eye. He has been treated both medically and surgically for the condition but showed no improvement. The following procedure incorporates a device to aid drainage. Identify the device.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Ex-Press™ implant

The clinical vignette points to a diagnosis of glaucoma not responsive to medical treatment and trabeculectomy and the device used is an ex-Press™ glaucoma implant (mini shunt).

It is a form of minimally invasive glaucoma surgery (MIGS) to increase aqueous drainage.

Ex-PRESS glaucoma implant is a small stainless steel device. It is inserted under a scleral flap during a modified trabeculectomy. Complications such as hypotony are lower than with standard trabeculectomy.

Glaucoma drainage devices are devices that allow aqueous outflow by establishing communication between the anterior chamber and sub-Tennon's space/sub-conjunctival space. While these devices were traditionally reserved for high-risk patients, or after trabeculectomy had failed, they are becoming increasingly popular.

The commonly used devices are as follows:

1. Shunts using episcleral explants

• Ahmed glaucoma valve: Silicone
• Molteno implant - Polypropylene plate and silicone plate
• Baerveldt implant - Silicone

2. Mini-shunts

• Ex-Press™ Mini-Shunt: Stainless steel
• iStent® - Titanium
questions.learning: Ex-Press™ implant — The clinical vignette points to a diagnosis of glaucoma not responsive to medical treatment and trabeculectomy and the device used is an ex-Press™ glaucoma implant (mini shunt).

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following autoantibodies is most commonly associated with fetal heart block?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Anti-Ro antibody

Anti-Ro (SSA) antibodies are the autoantibodies most strongly associated with congenital heart block (CHB) in the fetus. These maternal IgG antibodies cross the placenta and can damage the fetal atrioventricular (AV) node, leading to irreversible congenital complete heart block. They are classically seen in mothers with Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE) or Sjögren syndrome, although they may also be present in asymptomatic women.

• Anti-Ro (SSA) antibodies are the most common cause of immune-mediated congenital heart block.
• Fetal manifestations include:

• Congenital complete heart block
• Fetal bradycardia
• Neonatal lupus syndrome

Why not the other options?

• A. Anti-dsDNA antibody: Highly specific for SLE and correlates with disease activity, especially lupus nephritis, but is not associated with fetal heart block.
• C. Anti-Smith antibody: Highly specific for SLE, but has no association with congenital heart block.
• D. Anti-Jo antibody: Associated with polymyositis/dermatomyositis (antisynthetase syndrome), not neonatal lupus.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: A skeletal muscle biopsy is examined under an electron microscope before and during contraction. As actin filaments slide over myosin filaments, which of the following changes is expected in the sarcomere?
options: A band shortens while the I band remains unchanged
H zone and I band decrease in length, while the A band remains constant
A band decreases in length, while the H zone remains unchanged
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. H zone and I band decrease in length, while the A band remains constant

According to the sliding filament theory, muscle contraction occurs because thin (actin) filaments slide inward over thick (myosin) filaments. The filaments themselves do not shorten; instead, the degree of overlap between them increases.

As contraction occurs:

• H zone decreases or disappears because the region containing only myosin becomes smaller.
• I band decreases because the region containing only actin shortens.
• A band remains constant because the length of the myosin thick filament does not change.
• Z lines move closer together, resulting in shortening of the sarcomere.

Why not the other options?

• A. A band shortens while the I band remains unchanged: Incorrect. The A band remains constant, while the I band shortens.
• B. H zone and I band decrease in length, while the A band remains constant✅: Correct.
• C. A band decreases in length, while the H zone remains unchanged: Incorrect. The opposite occurs: A band remains unchanged, whereas the H zone decreases.
• D. Z lines move farther apart: Incorrect. During contraction, Z lines move closer together, shortening the sarcomere.
questions.learning: H zone and I band decrease in length, while the — A band remains constant According to the sliding filament theory, muscle contraction occurs because thin (actin) filaments slide inward over thick (myosin) filaments.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 20-year-old patient presents with pain and swelling involving the proximal phalanx of the middle finger. Considering the patient’s age and the location of the lesion, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: An enchondroma is a benign cartilaginous tumor that develops in the medullary cavity of bones. It is the most common tumor of the small bones of the hand (phalanges and metacarpals). On X-ray, it appears as a well-defined, radiolucent area often containing "stippled" or "popcorn-like" calcifications. While often asymptomatic, they can cause swelling or a pathological fracture. Osteosarcoma (Option A) and Ewing’s sarcoma (Option B) are highly aggressive, malignant tumors that rarely primary involve the small phalanges and would show significant bone destruction and periosteal reaction. Osteoclastoma (Option C), or Giant Cell Tumor, is typically found in the epiphysis of large long bones and would appear as an expansile "soap-bubble" lesion. Given the specific location in a finger phalanx and the well-defined lucency, enchondroma is the most statistically and radiographically probable diagnosis
questions.learning: An enchondroma is a benign cartilaginous tumor that develops in the medullary cavity of bones. It is the most common tumor of the small bones of the hand (phalanges and metacarpals).

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: Give the diagnosis of the condition shown in the image given below.
questions.explanation: The provided clinical image shows a child with an abnormally high-riding, undescended scapula on one side. This congenital condition is known as Sprengel's deformity (Option D). It occurs due to the failure of the scapula to descend from its embryonic cervical position to its final thoracic position. It is often associated with a bony or fibrous "omovertebral" bar and limited shoulder abduction. Ankylosing spondylitis (Option A) is a systemic inflammatory disease of the spine and SI joints. Facioscapulohumeral dystrophy (Option B) is a muscular dystrophy that would show scapular "winging" due to muscle weakness rather than a high-riding bone. Cervical fracture (Option C) would present with acute pain and trauma history. Sprengel's deformity is often part of the Klippel-Feil syndrome. Surgical intervention (like the Woodward or Green procedure) is used to improve both cosmetics and function. Thus, the undescended scapula is diagnostic
questions.learning: The provided clinical image shows a child with an abnormally high-riding, undescended scapula on one side. This congenital condition is known as Sprengel's deformity (Option D).

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 45-year-old lady complains of post-coital bleeding. She has a positive pap smear. What is the next line of management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Colposcopy directed biopsy

The appropriate management of a 45-year-old with a positive pap smear and post-coital bleeding is a colposcopy-directed biopsy.

A per speculum examination must be done whenever a female comes with post-coital bleeding in order to evaluate for carcinoma of the cervix. If growth is visible, a punch biopsy should be done, and else if no growth is visible, then a pap smear is done. A pap smear is a screening test for cervical cancer. The presence of abnormal cells/ a positive test requires further evaluation by colposcopy, cervical biopsy, or fractional curettage.

Cervical cancer screening should start at age 21. Women aged 21-29 should have a pap smear every 3 years, while women aged 30-65 should have both HPV and pap co-test every 5 years. Women should stop having cervical cancer screening after the age of 65 years. If a pap smear is suspicious, then screening is continued till 75 years. HIV+ve women should have annual checkups until three consecutive negative tests followed by testing every 3 years for life.

Pap testing should be done prior to vaginal examination. Lubricants should not be used and the patient should not be menstruating during the pap test. The patient should not have intercourse 24hrs prior to the test. The ideal time is around ovulation.
questions.learning: Colposcopy directed biopsy — The appropriate management of a 45-year-old with a positive pap smear and post-coital bleeding is a colposcopy-directed biopsy.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which type of genetic transfer is performed by the organism shown in the image below?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Transduction

The bacteriophages (bacterial viruses) mediate transduction, a mechanism of horizontal gene transfer in which bacterial DNA is transferred from one bacterium to another via a phage. Transduction is an important mechanism for the spread of virulence factors and antibiotic resistance genes among bacteria.

Why not the other options?

• A. Conjugation: Direct transfer of plasmid DNA through a sex pilus between two bacteria (requires cell-to-cell contact).
• C. Transformation: Uptake of naked DNA from the environment by competent bacteria (e.g., Streptococcus pneumoniae, Neisseria, Haemophilus).
• D. Translocation: Movement of DNA segments within the genome; not a mechanism of horizontal gene transfer between bacteria.

Exam pearls:

• Bacteriophage → Transduction
• Sex pilus (F plasmid) → Conjugation
• Naked DNA uptake → Transformation

High-yield associations:

• Generalized transduction: Lytic phages transfer any bacterial gene.
• Specialized transduction: Lysogenic phages transfer specific genes adjacent to the prophage insertion site (e.g., Corynebacterium diphtheriae, Vibrio cholerae, Clostridium botulinum acquire toxin genes through lysogenic phage conversion).
questions.learning: Transduction — The bacteriophages (bacterial viruses) mediate transduction, a mechanism of horizontal gene transfer in which bacterial DNA is transferred from one bacterium to another via a phage.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Which of the following is not an etiological factor for head and neck malignancies?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Vitamin A deficiency

Vitamin A deficiency is not a risk factor for head and neck malignancies. Vitamin A deficiency is a risk factor for esophageal cancer.

The head and neck cancers include cancers of the oral cavity, pharynx, larynx, paranasal sinuses, nasal cavity, and salivary glands. Squamous cell cancer is the most common head and neck malignancy, often linked to tobacco and alcohol use. Non-squamous malignancies include thyroid cancer, salivary gland cancer, and sarcomas.

The risk factors for head and neck malignancies are listed below:

Oral cavity cancer:

• Tobacco, smokeless tobacco like Bidi, Chutta, Paan (oral tobacco mixed with betel leaf, areca nut, and salted lime), Khaini, and marijuana
• Alcohol, poor oral hygiene, and intake of red meat and salted meat
• Infections with human papillomavirus, and HIV
• Genetic conditions like  Li-Fraumeni, ataxia telangiectasia, Bloom syndrome, and Fanconi's anemia.

Oropharyngeal cancer:

• Smoking and alcohol
• HPV 16 and 18

Cancer of the larynx and hypopharynx:

• Tobacco and alcohol
• Nickel, mustard gas, and asbestos exposure
• Long-term exposure to sulphuric acid and hydrochloric acid in battery plant workers.
• Postcricoid carcinoma is associated with previous radiation and sideropenic dysphagia
• HPV infection and immunosuppression

Nasopharyngeal cancer:

• Chinese population
• Epstein Barr virus infection
• Nitrosamines in salted fish and meat
• Vitamin C deficiency

Cancers of the nasal cavity and paranasal sinus:

• Tobacco
• Occupational exposure to dust from wood, textiles, and leather. Nickel and chromium dust and mustard gas exposure.
• HPV 16 and 18

Thyroid cancer:

• Females
• Previous radiation
• Inherited conditions like Gardner syndrome, familial polyposis, and Cowden syndrome. Medullary thyroid cancer associated with MEN-2 syndrome

Salivary gland carcinoma:

• Previous radiation
• Exposure to nickel alloy dust, and silica dust
• Smoking and heavy alcohol consumption were linked to a higher risk of salivary gland cancer in men but not in women
• Early menarche and nulliparity
questions.learning: Vitamin — A deficiency Vitamin A deficiency is not a risk factor for head and neck malignancies. Vitamin A deficiency is a risk factor for esophageal cancer.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A newly joined teacher develops rice water stools. The causative agent acts on which of the following receptors?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. GM1 ganglioside receptor

The given clinical scenario of rice-water stools is suggestive of cholera, caused by Vibrio cholerae. The toxin produced by the organism acts on GM1 ganglioside receptors.

Vibrio cholerae is a comma-shaped, gram-negative bacillus with darting motility. It has a single polar flagellum. It causes cholera, an acute diarrheal disease. It is marked by painless, profuse, watery diarrhea with flecks of mucus (rice water stools) associated with effortless vomiting. Pulmonary edema and arrhythmias are some of the complications.

Infection is acquired by ingestion of contaminated food and water. The organisms produce an enterotoxin known as cholera toxin (CT). It has 1 A and 5 B subunits. The B subunit (binding units) fixes to the GM1 ganglioside receptors on jejunal epithelial cells. The A subunit dissociates into the A2 fragment, which attaches the A1 fragment to the B subunit. This results in prolonged accumulation of cAMP, which causes an outpouring of large amounts of water and electrolytes into the intestinal lumen. Ultimately, it results in profuse watery diarrhea.

In addition to the cholera toxin, additional toxins such as zona occludens toxin and accessory cholera toxin are also produced. The former alters intestinal permeability by its action on intestinal epithelial cells.

The characteristic darting mobility and its hindrance by antiserum can be used for rapid microscopic diagnosis.

Fluid resuscitation by rice-based ORS is recommended. Medical management includes erythromycin or azithromycin.
questions.learning: GM1 ganglioside receptor — The given clinical scenario of rice-water stools is suggestive of cholera, caused by Vibrio cholerae. The toxin produced by the organism acts on GM1 ganglioside receptors.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A child is brought to the hospital with respiratory distress and biphasic stridor. The radiograph is shown below. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Acute laryngotracheobronchitis

The diagnosis in this child with respiratory distress and biphasic stridor is acute laryngotracheobronchitis, which is caused by the parainfluenza virus. The x-ray finding is the 'steeple sign' due to subglottic narrowing.

The age of presentation of laryngotracheobronchitis ranges from 6 months to 6 years. The clinical features include barking cough, inspiratory stridor, hoarseness, and low-grade fever.

Management:

• Racemic epinephrine nebulization leads to the rapid improvement of upper airway obstruction. Epinephrine constricts pre-capillary arterioles in the upper airway mucosa and decreases capillary hydrostatic pressure, leading to fluid resorption and improvement in airway edema.
• Dexamethasone is administered by the least invasive route (Oral > IV > IM ) for all the grades of croup.
• Oxygen should be administered to children who are hypoxemic (SpO2 <92 %)

Antibiotics are not indicated in acute laryngotracheobronchitis.

Other options:

Option A: Acute epiglottitis is a medical emergency presenting in children with a rapidly progressive course of fever, sore throat, dyspnea, and respiratory obstruction, followed by a toxic appearance and drooling. The neck is hyperextended and stridor is a late finding. Radiography shows a classic thumb sign.

Option C: Foreign body aspiration initially presents with a paroxysm of cough, choking, and gagging, accompanied by new-onset wheezing and asymmetric breath sounds.

Option D: Laryngomalacia is a congenital laryngeal anomaly presenting in children with low-pitched inspiratory stridor exacerbated by exertion.
questions.learning: Acute laryngotracheobronchitis — The diagnosis in this child with respiratory distress and biphasic stridor is acute laryngotracheobronchitis, which is caused by the parainfluenza virus.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A 28-year-old male is brought to the emergency. On examination, his PR is 50 bpm, BP is 80/60 mmHg, RR is 7 breaths/min and his temperature is 95 F. He has pin point pupils and is disoriented. What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Opioid intoxication

Opioid intoxication is the most probable diagnosis in the above given clinical scenario. Opioids include morphine, heroin, codeine, etc.

Symptoms of opioid overdose:

* Triad of coma, respiratory depression, and pinpoint pupils(miosis)

* Hypotension

* Bradycardia

* Shallow breathing

* Hypothermia

Characteristics of opioid toxicity:

* Opioid intoxication toxidrome - respiratory and mental status depression, analgesia, miosis, orthostatic hypotension, nausea and vomiting, histamine release resulting in localized urticaria and bronchospasm, ileus secondary to decreased GI motility, and urinary retention secondary to increased vesical sphincter tone.

* Miosis is not universally present from intoxication with every opioid; normal or even enlarged pupils have been documented secondary to diphenoxylate, meperidine, morphine, pentazocine, and propoxyphene toxicity.

* Opioid-induced acute lung injury, previously known as non-cardiogenic pulmonary edema, is an uncommon complication associated with heroin overdose.

Airway protection and ventilatory maintenance are the most important treatment steps for opioid intoxications, because respiratory depression is the major morbidity and the cause of essentially all the mortality.

* After adequate ventilation is ensured, administer naloxone.

* Single-dose activated charcoal can be administered in case opioid ingestion occured within one hour.

Opioid withdrawal symptoms (mnemonic- O MY WITHDRAWALS):

* Mydriasis

* Yawning

* Weakness

* Insomnia, irritability

* Tremors, tachycardia

* Hyperthermia, hypertension

* Diarrhea

* Rhinorrhoea

* Apnoeic attacks

* Weight loss

* Anxiety

* Lacrimation

* Sweating

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A patient presents with recurrent episodes of severe generalized pain, often triggered by vigorous physical activity. Blood examination reveals anemia and elongated, sickle-shaped red blood cells instead of the normal biconcave shape, confirming a diagnosis of sickle cell anemia. Which specific amino acid substitution is responsible for this condition?
options: Substitution of valine by glutamic acid at the 6th position
Substitution of glutamic acid by valine at the 6th position
Substitution of valine by glutamic acid at the 5th position
Substitution of glutamic acid by valine at the 5th position
questions.explanation: Sickle cell anemia is a molecular disease caused by a single point mutation in the -globin gene. Specifically, it involves the substitution of the amino acid glutamic acid by valine at the 6th position of the -polypeptide chain. This change from a polar, hydrophilic amino acid (glutamate) to a non-polar, hydrophobic one (valine) creates a "sticky" patch on the hemoglobin molecule. When oxygen levels are low (e.g., during vigorous exercise), these hemoglobin S (HbS) molecules polymerize into long fibers, distorting the red blood cell into a sickle shape. Options A, C, and D describe incorrect substitutions or positions. The sickle cells are rigid and block small blood vessels, leading to the "excruciating pain" of a vaso-occlusive crisis. This specific biochemical detail is a hallmark of genetic medicine, illustrating how a minute change in a protein's primary structure can lead to profound systemic illness and anemia
questions.learning: Sickle cell anemia is a molecular disease caused by a single point mutation in the -globin gene. Specifically, it involves the substitution of the amino acid glutamic acid by valine at the 6th position of the -polypeptide chain.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following agency provides seed and manure in applied nutrition programs in schools?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. UNICEF

UNICEF provides seed and manure in applied nutrition programs in schools.

Applied Nutrition Program is implemented with the aim of producing various types of productive food by the community for the community itself.

UNICEF assists the program by providing implements, seeds, manure, and water supply equipment. If free land is available in schools, the facilities provided by UNICEF should be used in developing school gardens.

The produce obtained from the gardens can be utilized for school feeding programs and for nutrition education.

Another strategy called GOBI was also implemented by UNICEF with the aim of a child health revolution.

Other options:

Option A- CARE- Cooperative for Assistance and Relief Everywhere aims at providing food for children in the age group of 6-11 years. It is also helping in projects like integrated nutrition and health project, better health and nutrition projects, anemia control projects, etc.

Option B- UNDP- The United Nations Development Program provides funds for technical assistance. Its main objective is to help poorer nations in developing their human and natural resources.

Option D- WHO- World Health Organization aims at the attainment of the highest level of health by all people, which helps them to lead a socially and economically productive life.
questions.learning: UNICEF UNICEF provides seed and manure in applied nutrition programs in schools. Applied Nutrition Program is implemented with the aim of producing various types of productive food by the community for the community itself.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A pregnant lady with PIH was being monitored with bed rest in supine position. Which of the following is a complication of the below representation?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Supine venacava syndrome

Supine vena cava syndrome is the complication of the given representation. The image shows compression of the inferior vena cava by the gravid uterus which can sometimes lead to supine hypotension.

During late pregnancy, the gravid uterus compresses the great vessels against the hard spine, when the patient is in the supine position. Of the two vessels, the vena cava is compressed, but the aorta, owing to its structure is relatively resistant.

Normally, the vena cava compression results in opening up collateral circulation by means of paravertebral and azygous veins but in some cases, when the collateral circulation fails to open up, the venous return of the heart may be seriously curtailed resulting in hypotension, tachycardia, and syncope and is called supine vena cava syndrome.

The normal blood pressure is quickly restored by turning the patient to the lateral position.
questions.learning: Supine venacava syndrome Supine vena cava syndrome is the complication of the given representation. The image shows compression of the inferior vena cava by the gravid uterus which can sometimes lead to supine hypotension.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A veterinarian presents with several weeks of intermittent fever, myalgia, arthralgia, fatigue, and weight loss, with symptoms showing temporary remission before recurring. Given his occupational exposure, blood is cultured on a specific medium to identify the causative organism. Which pathogen is most likely responsible for this presentation?
questions.explanation: The patient’s symptoms describe an undulant fever—intermittent fever that comes and goes over weeks—accompanied by joint and muscle pain. This pattern, combined with the patient's occupation as a veterinarian, is classic for Brucellosis. Brucella is a zoonotic infection transmitted through contact with infected animals (cattle, goats, pigs) or unpasteurized dairy products. Burkholderia (Option A) causes Melioidosis, typically in farmers exposed to soil/water. Mycobacterium (Option C) causes tuberculosis, which presents with a more persistent, non-undulant fever and cough. Coxiella (Option D) causes Q fever, another zoonosis, but it usually presents as an acute pneumonia or hepatitis rather than a chronic undulant fever with joint involvement. Brucella requires a specialized culture medium (e.g., Castaneda’s medium) and a long incubation period. The specific occupational risk for veterinarians and the cyclical nature of the fever make Brucella the most probable diagnosis
questions.learning: The patient’s symptoms describe an undulant fever—intermittent fever that comes and goes over weeks—accompanied by joint and muscle pain. This pattern, combined with the patient's occupation as a veterinarian, is classic for Brucellosis.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: The test shown below is performed to assess the integrity or function of which anatomical structure?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Anterior cruciate ligament

Sudden deceleration / pivot injury

↓

Twisting of knee

↓

ACL tear

↓

Anterior instability of tibia

The anterior draw test, performed with the knee at 90 degrees flexion, specifically tests the anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) by assessing anterior translation of the tibia relative to the femur. The Lachman test at 20 degrees flexion is more sensitive for ACL injuries.

Function of ACL

• Prevents anterior displacement of tibia
• Prevents hyperextension
• Provides rotational stability

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A chronic alcoholic patient came to the emergency with pain in the epigastrium radiating to the back and recurrent vomiting. On examination, guarding was present in the upper epigastrium. The erect chest X-ray was normal. What is the next step?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Serum lipase

The clinical scenario of the patient presenting with abdominal pain, recurrent vomiting, and upper epigastric guarding in a chronic alcoholic is highly suggestive of acute pancreatitis. The normal erect chest X-ray indicates that there is no pneumoperitoneum (effectively ruling out perforation). The next step is to send blood samples for serum lipase levels.

While contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CECT) of the abdomen (option D) is the best investigation to rule out a case of acute pancreatitis, it is not the next step after an abdominal X-ray.

Acute pancreatitis is often caused by gallstones (70%) or alcoholism (25%). The cardinal symptom is acute-onset severe pain in the upper quadrant of the abdomen. The patient usually presents in shock (hypotension and tachycardia) and tachypnoea. Some may also present with signs of bleeding into the fascial planes leading to discoloration of the sites involved:

1. Cullen’s sign: Around the umbilicus
2. Grey Turner’s sign: Flanks
3. Fox sign: Inguinal region
4. Bryant’s sign: Scrotum

The diagnosis is often clinical with a laboratory diagnosis of serum lipase preferred over serum amylase. The severity of the acute pancreatitis is assessed using the Ranson and Glasgow scoring system ( ≥3 at 48h of onset of pain ). APACHE, SOFA, SAPS, and MODS can also be used to assess the severity of pancreatitis in intensive care (ICU) settings.

Pancreatitis is managed conservatively with initial nasogastric drainage followed by intravenous fluids, analgesia, and frequent monitoring of vital signs, urine output, and blood gases.

Other options:

Option A: Upper gastrointestinal intestinal (GI) endoscopy is performed by passing a flexible endoscope and is the best method for examining the upper gastrointestinal mucosa. It doesn't help us diagnose pancreatitis.

Option B: The alcohol breath test is used as a screening test to measure the concentration of alcohol in a person's breath, but doesn't help us diagnose pancreatitis.
questions.learning: Serum lipase — The clinical scenario of the patient presenting with abdominal pain, recurrent vomiting, and upper epigastric guarding in a chronic alcoholic is highly suggestive of acute pancreatitis.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: The resting membrane potential(RMP) of the nerve is -70mV. Increased permeability of which ion is responsible for the RMP?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Potassium

Increased permeability of potassium ions(K+) is responsible for the RMP of a nerve as there are more K+ channels open at rest, facilitating the flow of potassium ions across the membrane.

Resting membrane potential (RMP) is the difference in the electrical potentials between the cytoplasm of the cell and the extracellular space.

At rest, there are more open K+ channels compared to Na+ channels, thus the membrane permeability of K+ is greater. As a result of this, the intracellular and extracellular K+ concentrations are the major determinants of the RMP. Furthermore, the RMP is close to the equilibrium potential of K+ in general.

Clinical Significance: In hyperkalemia, the extracellular level of K+ is increased. Thus the RMP moves closer to the threshold to elicit an action potential leading to a more excitable nerve. The excitable nerve, stimulates the muscle repeatedly causing fasciculations, exhaustion of muscle, and weakness. In hypokalemia, the extracellular level of K+ is reduced. Thus the RMP is reduced and the neuron is hyperpolarized.
questions.learning: Potassium Increased permeability of potassium ions(K+) is responsible for the RMP of a nerve as there are more K+ channels open at rest, facilitating the flow of potassium ions across the membrane.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: The Hallpike (Dix–Hallpike) maneuver is used to evaluate which of the following conditions?
questions.explanation: The Dix-Hallpike maneuver is a diagnostic clinical test specifically used to assess vestibular function, specifically to confirm a diagnosis of Benign Paroxysmal Positional Vertigo (BPPV). It involves moving the patient from a sitting to a supine position with the head turned 45 degrees to one side and extended 20 degrees back. A positive test is indicated by the elicitation of vertigo and a characteristic rotatory nystagmus, which signifies that loose calcium carbonate crystals (otoconia) have entered the posterior semicircular canal. Audiometry (Option B) and cochlear function tests (Option C) assess hearing thresholds rather than balance. Corneal tests (Option D) evaluate cranial nerve function (V and VII) or ocular health. The Hallpike maneuver is the gold standard bedside test for differentiating positional vertigo from other balance disorders. Thus, it is a primary tool for evaluating the peripheral vestibular apparatus
questions.learning: The Dix-Hallpike maneuver is a diagnostic clinical test specifically used to assess vestibular function, specifically to confirm a diagnosis of Benign Paroxysmal Positional Vertigo (BPPV).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A 45-year-old patient presents with gait instability, particularly noticeable when standing on one leg. On examination, standing on the left leg causes the right side of the pelvis to drop. Paralysis of which muscle group is responsible for this finding?
options: Right gluteus maximus and gluteus medius
Left gluteus maximus and gluteus medius
Right gluteus medius and gluteus minimus
Left gluteus medius and gluteus minimus
questions.explanation: The physical exam finding described is a positive Trendelenburg sign. In this case, the drooping of the right pelvis when standing on the left leg indicates that the hip abductors of the stance leg (left) are paralyzed or weak. These abductors are the gluteus medius and gluteus minimus, innervated by the superior gluteal nerve. Normally, these muscles contract on the weight-bearing side to prevent the pelvis from tilting toward the unsupported side. Paralysis of the right-sided muscles (Options A and C) would cause the left pelvis to sag. The gluteus maximus (Option B) is primarily an extensor of the hip rather than an abductor, and its weakness leads to a "lurching" gait but not pelvic sagging in the coronal plane. Instability while walking, or a "waddling gait," is common when these muscles are compromised. Therefore, the sag on the right side while weight-bearing on the left side definitively localizes the pathology to the left gluteus medius and minimus
questions.learning: The physical exam finding described is a positive Trendelenburg sign. In this case, the drooping of the right pelvis when standing on the left leg indicates that the hip abductors of the stance leg (left) are paralyzed or weak.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A young patient presents with recurrent seasonal conjunctivitis marked by intense itching and excessive watering of the eyes. Given that this is an immediate hypersensitivity reaction, which cell type primarily mediates these symptoms?
questions.explanation: The clinical presentation of seasonal conjunctivitis, characterized by recurring intense itching and tearing, is a classic Type I hypersensitivity reaction. Mast cells are the primary mediators in this immediate allergic response. When a sensitized individual is exposed to seasonal allergens like pollen, IgE antibodies already bound to the surface of mast cells trigger degranulation. This release of pre-formed inflammatory mediators, most notably histamine, causes the characteristic symptoms of redness, itching, and chemosis. While eosinophils (Option A) are often recruited later in the allergic cascade and contribute to chronic inflammation, they are not the primary cells responsible for the immediate, acute symptoms. Neutrophils (Option C) are typically associated with acute bacterial infections and are not central to the allergic pathway. Lymphocytes (Option D), particularly T-cells, play roles in delayed hypersensitivity but are not the primary drivers of the rapid, IgE-mediated symptoms seen in seasonal allergic conjunctivitis. Therefore, mast cell stabilization and histamine blocking are key therapeutic strategies for these patients
questions.learning: The clinical presentation of seasonal conjunctivitis, characterized by recurring intense itching and tearing, is a classic Type I hypersensitivity reaction.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Researchers plan to study the relationship between maternal smoking during pregnancy, reported at antenatal visits, and newborn birth weight recorded immediately after delivery. Which study design is most suitable for analyzing this association?
questions.explanation: A prospective cohort study is the most appropriate design because the researchers start with a defined exposure (maternal smoking status reported during antenatal visits) and follow the participants forward in time to observe the outcome (birth weight recorded at delivery). This design allows for the direct calculation of incidence and establishes a clear temporal relationship between exposure and outcome. A retrospective cohort (Option B) would involve looking back at historical records for both exposure and outcome, which is not the case here as the data is collected sequentially. A case-control study (Option C) would start with the outcome (e.g., low birth weight infants) and look backward to find exposures, which is less efficient for a common exposure like smoking. A cross-sectional study (Option D) measures exposure and outcome at a single point in time, failing to provide temporal evidence. Therefore, the longitudinal nature of tracking the pregnancy from early visits to birth identifies this specifically as a prospective cohort study

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A child presents with the findings shown in the image below. What is the true statement regarding this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Kwashiorkor due to protein malnutrition

This malnourished child with a distended abdomen has kwashiorkor due to protein malnutrition.

Kwashiorkor is a form of severe acute malnutrition (SAM) characterized by edema and apathy. It usually affects infants and children, most often around the age of weaning till the age of 5.

It is due to an overall deficiency in protein and calories, with a much more severe protein deficit. It is due to a deficiency of proteins, such as albumin that exerts oncotic pressure in the blood that there is such extensive pitting edema which starts in the legs, and feet and then spreads to hands, face and later becomes generalized.

Skin changes occur over the swollen limbs and include dark, crackled peeling patches with pale skin underneath forming patches of hyper and hypopigmentation called flaky paint dermatosis or crazy paving. The skin gets easily infected.

The hair is dull, brittle, sparse, and can easily be pulled out. It may lose its curl. In dark-haired children, the hair may turn pale or reddish. Alternating bands of light and normal color hair may be seen, known as the flag sign. Children are miserable, apathetic, and often refuse to eat. There is marked muscle atrophy and growth retardation.

Marasmus is another form of SAM that occurs as a result of a calorie deficiency primarily. It is characterized by severe wasting that occurs due to the consumption of fat and muscle to release energy. The child has monkey facies and baggy pants appearance due to the loss of fat pad in the face and buttocks without edema.

Clinical features seen in marasmus are:

* Simian facies

* Lethargic and irritable,apathetic

* Bradycardia

* Thin, dry skin

* Thin and brittle hair, easily pluckable

* hypotension, and hypothermia

* The reduction of buccal fat pad gives rise to a wrinkled or aged look, while the term “baggy pants appearance” describes sagging skin of the buttocks that hangs downward.

questions.learning: Kwashiorkor due to protein malnutrition — This malnourished child with a distended abdomen has kwashiorkor due to protein malnutrition. Kwashiorkor is a form of severe acute malnutrition (SAM) characterized by edema and apathy.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A farmer from South East India presents with fever, respiratory distress and neurological deficits. The vector of the causative organism is shown below. what is the associated organism?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Nipah virus

The given clinical scenario along with the vector bat is suggestive of infection from the nipah virus.

Nipah virus is an RNA virus that belongs to the family Paramyxoviridae, genus Henipavirus. It is a zoonotic virus that shows both animal-to-human (bats, pigs) and human-to-human transmission. The natural hosts are fruit bats of the Pteropodidae family.

The clinical manifestations include asymptomatic subclinical infection, acute respiratory infection, and fatal encephalitis. There is no treatment or vaccine available for either people or animals. The primary treatment for humans is supportive care. Nipah virus is on the WHO list of Blueprint priority diseases.

The life cycle of nipah virus is shown below:

Other options

Option A: Ebola virus belongs to the family Filoviridae and is transmitted by African fruit bats. Human-to-human transmission through blood or body fluids can occur. It causes fever, abdominal pain, diarrhoea, and haemorrhage

Option B: Zika virus is transmitted to human beings by the bite of an infected Aedes mosquito. It can also be transmitted trans-placentally, causing microcephaly and other severe fetal brain defects.

Option C: Malaria is a parasitic infection caused by the plasmodium species and is transmitted by the female anopheles mosquito. Symptoms include fever, chills, and myalgia with periodicity differing for each species. The fever returns every two days for P. ovale, P. vivax, and P. falciparum and every three days for P. malariae.
questions.learning: Nipah virus — The given clinical scenario along with the vector bat is suggestive of infection from the nipah virus. Nipah virus is an RNA virus that belongs to the family Paramyxoviridae, genus Henipavirus.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A woman with no history of pregnancy, a BMI of 23, and complaints of hirsutism is evaluated, and an ultrasound image is provided. Based on these findings, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The ultrasound image displays a classic "string of pearls" appearance, characterized by multiple small, peripheral follicles surrounding a dense central stroma. This radiographic finding, combined with the clinical symptom of hirsutism (excessive hair growth due to high androgens), is highly diagnostic of Polycystic Ovarian Syndrome (PCOS) (Option A). PCOS can occur even in women with a normal BMI (23 in this case), often referred to as "lean PCOS". Multiple fibroids (Option C) would appear as solid, hypoechoic masses within the uterine wall rather than the ovary. A tubal block (Option B) would be diagnosed via hysterosalpingography, not a standard pelvic ultrasound. Mesenteritis (Option D) is an inflammatory condition of the bowel mesentery and is unrelated to these gynecological symptoms. Therefore, the characteristic combination of hyperandrogenic signs and pathognomonic ovarian morphology confirms PCOS as the definitive diagnosis
questions.learning: The ultrasound image displays a classic "string of pearls" appearance, characterized by multiple small, peripheral follicles surrounding a dense central stroma.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient presents with dyspnea and distended neck veins that increase on inspiration. There is no murmur. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Constrictive pericarditis

The patient presenting with dyspnea and Kussmauls signs as evidenced by the distended neck veins that increase on inspiration, likely has underlying constrictive pericarditis.

Constrictive pericarditis: It is a condition where a thickened, fibrotic, and often calcified pericardium restricts the diastolic filling of the heart.

In developing countries, infectious etiologies like tuberculosis or viral infections are the most common cause of this condition. Cardiac surgery and radiation therapy are also common causes. Other causes include connective tissue disease, uremia, neoplasm, or idiopathic.

Clinically the patients may present with dyspnea, orthopnea, fatigue, ascites. On examination neck veins may be distended and will show a positive Kussmauls sign. On auscultation, heart sound smay be distant and a pericardial knock at the cardiac apex may be heard. This occurs due to the abrubt cessation of ventricular filling.

JVP findings - There is a rapid 'x' and 'y' descent. The rapid 'y' descent is more prominent and reflects rapid early ventricular diastolic filling. This occurs due to the constricting pericardium, increasing the atrial pressures.

Diagnosis: Diagnosis is difficult and is confirmed by multiple investigations

* Hallmark findings of pericardial constriction are pericardial thickening, calcification, and abnormal ventricular diastolic function.

* The X-ray can be normal or there may be non-specific cardiac enlargement, calcification, and roughened cardiac outline.

* CT and MRI are more sensitive investigations.

Constrictive pericarditis will have prominent y descent, prominent x descent, and Kussmaul's sign. Normally, the venous pressure should fall by at least 3 mmHg with inspiration. Kussmaul’s sign is defined by either a rise or a lack of fall of the JVP with inspiration.

Other options:

Option B: Aortic regurgitation would present with a diastolic murmur.

Option C: Tricuspid stenosis may also present similarly with congestive hepatomegaly, and venous distention, however, in this patient the absence of a murmur makes the diagnosis unlikely. Tricuspid stenosis will have prolonged y wave on JVP.

Option D: Pulmonary arterial hypertension would present with a prominent jugular "a" wave, palpable left parasternal lift, and loud S2 which are not seen in this patient.
questions.learning: Constrictive pericarditis — The patient presenting with dyspnea and Kussmauls signs as evidenced by the distended neck veins that increase on inspiration, likely has underlying constrictive pericarditis.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 45-year-old man presents to the emergency department with intense abdominal pain radiating to the back. Laboratory tests show markedly elevated serum amylase and lipase levels. In the management of this condition, which of the following interventions should be avoided?
options: Nil per oral to avoid pancreatic stimulation
Parenteral nutrition is preferred for 2-3 days over the nil per oral (NPO) approach
questions.explanation: The patient is suffering from acute pancreatitis, indicated by severe abdominal pain radiating to the back and elevated serum amylase and lipase levels. The mainstay of management in acute pancreatitis is aggressive fluid resuscitation, pain control, and supportive care. The preferred fluids for resuscitation are isotonic crystalloids, especially Ringer lactate or normal saline, as they effectively restore intravascular volume and correct fluid losses due to third spacing. In contrast, 5% dextrose should be avoided because it is not an effective volume expander and does not adequately replenish electrolytes or circulating volume. Nil per oral (NPO) is appropriate initially to rest the pancreas. Early enteral feeding is now recommended once the patient stabilizes, as it reduces complications. Although parenteral nutrition is not preferred routinely, it may be used when enteral feeding is not feasible. Thus, among the given options, administration of 5% dextrose is inappropriate in the management of acute pancreatitis
questions.learning: The patient is suffering from acute pancreatitis, indicated by severe abdominal pain radiating to the back and elevated serum amylase and lipase levels.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which is the best graft for a femoropopliteal bypass?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Great saphenous vein

The great saphenous vein (GSV) is the best as it lasts longer than polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE), dacron, and human umbilical vein as a graft in a femoropopliteal bypass.

The GSV is the conduit of choice for arterial bypass grafts below the inguinal ligament.

For bypass above the inguinal ligament, while both GSV and PTFE grafts have similar patency rates in the first 2 years, the GSV is superior thereafter and hence preferred over PTFE or any other grafts.

The ipsilateral GSV is the conduit of choice for femoropopliteal bypass. When it is not available, contralateral GSV should be used. Other veins are preferred when both ipsilateral and contralateral GSV is not available and they include a small saphenous vein, cephalic vein, and basilic vein.

Non-autogenous grafts are used for patients who lack a suitable venous conduit. The most commonly used prosthetic conduit is PTFE. Recent studies have shown that heparin-bonded PTFE is superior to compared to PTFE without heparin.
questions.learning: Great saphenous vein — The great saphenous vein (GSV) is the best as it lasts longer than polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE), dacron, and human umbilical vein as a graft in a femoropopliteal bypass.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A young male is brought in for age estimation for medico-legal purposes. Based on the X-ray provided, what is the estimated age?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 15–17 years

The age estimation in medicolegal practice relies on the appearance and fusion of ossification centers. In this X-ray, the proximal humeral epiphysis is fused with the shaft, while the medial end of the clavicular epiphysis is not yet fused, indicating an age of approximately 15–17 years. Correlation with other skeletal radiographs and dental examination improves accuracy.

Why not the other options?

• A. 10–12 years: Proximal humeral epiphysis is not yet fused at this age.
• B. 12–15 years: Epiphyseal fusion around the shoulder is still incomplete.
• D. >18 years: By this age, most shoulder epiphyses are fused, and the medial clavicular epiphysis is approaching or has completed fusion (typically 22–25 years, the last epiphysis to fuse).

| Ossification Center | Fusion Age (Approx.)

| ------------------- | --------------------

| Elbow | 14–16 years

| Proximal humerus | 16–18 years

| Distal radius & ulna | 17–19 years

| Iliac crest | 19–21 years

| Medial end of clavicle (last epiphysis) | 22–25 years

Exam Tip:

• Medial clavicular epiphysis is the last epiphysis in the body to fuse and is frequently used for medicolegal age estimation around 18–25 years.
• Shoulder X-rays showing fused proximal humerus but unfused medial clavicle generally indicate late adolescence (≈15–17 years in exam-based interpretation).

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Which of the following is typically not seen in allergic rhinitis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Otto Veraguth folds

Otto Veraguth folds are not seen in allergic rhinitis.

Otto Veraguth fold is a physical sign of depression wherein there is a triangular fold in the nasal corner of upper eyelid.

Allergic rhinitis is an IgE-mediated immunological response of the nasal mucosa to allergens in the environment.

Patients typically present with recurrent bouts of sneezing, nasal obstruction, watery nasal discharge, and itching.

Clinical signs include:

• Allergic shiners: dark circles around the eyes.
• Allergic salute: black transverse nasal crease on the dorsum of the nose due to repeated upward rubbing.
• Dennie-Morgan lines - transverse skin creases in the infraorbital area.

Allergic rhinitis can be classified into intermittent and persistent, based on the duration of the disease:

• Intermittent- Symptoms are present for less than 4 days a week, or less than 4 weeks
• Persistent- Symptoms are present for more than 4 days a week, or more than 4 weeks

It can be classified as mild, moderate, or severe based on the severity of the disease:

• Mild- None of the following symptoms are present- sleep impairment, impairment of daily activities, school, or work, troublesome symptoms.
• Moderate- severe: If at least one of the symptoms mentioned above are present.

A step-care approach is recommended for allergic rhinitis and its impact on asthma (ARIA) for the treatment of allergic rhinitis includes the following:

• Oral antihistamines or intranasal cromolyn sodium are recommended for mild, intermittent disease. (option A).
• Intranasal corticosteroids are used for moderate disease as monotherapy. (option B).
• Oral antihistamines and intranasal steroids can be used in combination to treat severe diseases. (option C).
• A short course of oral corticosteroids and immunotherapy can be used for severe, persistent disease in case the above intervention fails

In the given image, Otto Veraguth's sign or Veraguth's fold is shown, a diagonal palpebral fold running from the lateral corners of the eyes, medially upward to the medial end of the eyebrows. It is a physical sign of depression.

Another physical sign of depression is the Omega sign. In this, there is vertical wrinkling between the eyebrows joined at the top by a horizontal crease.
questions.learning: Otto Veraguth folds Otto Veraguth folds are not seen in allergic rhinitis. Otto Veraguth fold is a physical sign of depression wherein there is a triangular fold in the nasal corner of upper eyelid.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A clinician touched the eyes of a patient with a piece of cotton, and rapid blinking of the eyes occurred in response. What is the structure responsible for carrying the above sensation?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Trigeminal nerve

The response of blinking when the clinician touches the patient's eye with a piece of cotton is known as the corneal reflex. The sensation is transmitted by the ophthalmic branch of the trigeminal nerve (CN V), while the motor response is controlled by the facial nerve (CN VII).

The corneal reflex is an involuntary, protective response that causes blinking when the cornea is stimulated, such as by a light touch. It serves as a defence mechanism to prevent foreign objects from entering the eye and causing damage. The reflex involves two main components: sensory input and motor output. The sensation of touch or irritation on the cornea is detected by the ophthalmic branch of the trigeminal nerve (CN V), specifically its nasociliary branch, which sends the signal to the brainstem.

The motor response, which is the blinking of the eyelids, is mediated by the facial nerve (Option B). The facial nerve innervates the orbicularis oculi muscle, which is responsible for closing the eyelids. This reflex is important for protecting the eye from potential damage, and any disruption to the trigeminal or facial nerves can impair the corneal reflex, leading to difficulty in protecting the eye from injury.

Other options:

Option B: The Facial Nerve (CN VII) is a major nerve responsible for controlling the muscles of facial expression including orbicularis oculi, which is responsible for forced closing of the eyelid. Although orbicularis oculi and facial nerve is a part of corneal reflex, its is not responsible for carrying the sensation and hence cannot be the answer.

Option C: The oculomotor nerve (CN III) plays a key role in several eye reflexes, particularly in the pupillary light reflex and the accommodation reflex. The pupillary light reflex mediates pupil constriction in response to light exposure by controlling the sphincter pupillae muscle. In the accommodation reflex, it coordinates the convergence of the eyes and the constriction of the pupils when focusing on a near object.

Option D: The optic nerve (CN II) plays a crucial role in sensory input for several reflexes. In the pupillary light reflex, it detects light entering the eye and sends the signal to the brain, triggering pupil constriction via the oculomotor nerve (CN III). Additionally, the optic nerve is involved in the accommodation reflex, where it helps detect the visual stimulus, prompting changes in eye focus and pupil constriction

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A 22-year-old college student presents with multiple small depigmented skin lesions that have been present for over two years, as shown in the accompanying image. Based on this clinical presentation, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Vitiligo is a common acquired chronic depigmenting disorder characterized by the loss of functional melanocytes from the epidermis. This results in the "milky-white," well-demarcated macules and patches seen in the image. It often affects the hands, face, and genital areas. Melasma (Option A) presents as hyperpigmented (dark) brown patches, typically on the face, and is related to hormonal changes or UV exposure. Psoriasis (Option C) features erythematous plaques with silvery scales, not depigmentation. Dermatitis herpetiformis (Option D) presents with intensely itchy, grouped vesicles on an erythematous base, often associated with celiac disease. Vitiligo can have a significant psychological impact on young adults like this college student. Diagnosis is clinical, though Wood’s lamp examination can help highlight the areas of depigmentation. Management options include topical corticosteroids, calcineurin inhibitors, and phototherapy (NB-UVB), aimed at inducing repigmentation and stabilizing the disease
questions.learning: Vitiligo is a common acquired chronic depigmenting disorder characterized by the loss of functional melanocytes from the epidermis. This results in the "milky-white," well-demarcated macules and patches seen in the image.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 55-year-old woman is being counseled for surgery for her long-standing dacryocystitis. Which of the following is the surgery of choice?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Dacryocystorhinostomy

The treatment of choice for chronic dacryocystitis is dacryocystorhinostomy (DCR) as it re-establishes the lacrimal drainage.

One of the sequelae of chronic dacryocystitis is mucocele formation, which when infected, leads to pyocele formation and finally lacrimal fibrosis. Treatment of lacrimal sac fibrosis is dacryocystectomy.

Streptococcus hemolyticus and Staphylococcus aureus are the most common etiological agents for acute and chronic dacryocystitis

Initially, the inflammation is controlled with antibiotics and anti-inflammatory agents. Sequelae of acute dacryocystitis is a lacrimal fistula, which is treated with is dacryocystorhinostomy (DCR).
questions.learning: Dacryocystorhinostomy — The treatment of choice for chronic dacryocystitis is dacryocystorhinostomy (DCR) as it re-establishes the lacrimal drainage. One of the sequelae of chronic dacryocystitis is mucocele formation, which when infected, leads to pyocele…

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A patient present with symptoms of dermatitis, diarrhea, and cognitive decline. Which micronutrient deficiency is most likely responsible?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Niacin

The image shows Casal necklace—a photosensitive hyperpigmented dermatitis around the neck, which is characteristic of pellagra due to niacin (Vitamin B3) deficiency.

Niacin is a precursor of NAD⁺ and NADP⁺, essential for oxidation–reduction reactions and energy metabolism.

Deficiency → impaired cellular energy production, especially in skin, GI tract, and brain.

Classic triad (3 D’s):

• Dermatitis (photosensitive, Casal necklace)
• Diarrhea
• Dementia

(+ Death if untreated)

Why other options are incorrect:

• Thiamine: Beriberi, Wernicke’s encephalopathy
• Pyridoxine: Neuropathy, sideroblastic anemia
• Retinol (Vitamin A): Night blindness, xerophthalmia
questions.learning: Niacin — The image shows Casal necklace—a photosensitive hyperpigmented dermatitis around the neck, which is characteristic of pellagra due to niacin (Vitamin B3) deficiency.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Identify the mode of inheritance from the pedigree chart given below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Autosomal dominant

The pedigree chart shows an autosomal dominant mode of inheritance.

Autosomal dominant conditions are manifested in the heterozygous state, hence at least one parent of an index case is usually affected. In this mode of inheritance, both males and females are affected and both can transmit the condition. When an affected person marries an unaffected one, every child has one in two chance of having the disease.
questions.learning: Autosomal dominant — The pedigree chart shows an autosomal dominant mode of inheritance. Autosomal dominant conditions are manifested in the heterozygous state, hence at least one parent of an index case is usually affected.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Which of the following has the worst prognosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Partial B/L RLN palsy

Semon’s Law – RLN (Recurrent Laryngeal Nerve) Palsy

• In progressive (compressive) lesions of the Recurrent laryngeal nerve:

• Abductors are affected first
• Adductors are affected later

Reason: Abductor fibers (posterior cricoarytenoid) are more vulnerable than adductors.

B/L Partial RLN palsy: Only abductors paralyzed

• Vocal cord position → Paramedian
• Clinical features: Abductors lost, adductors intact
• Airway → severely compromised

Most dangerous situation

While in Complete B/L palsy:

• Both cords → cadaveric (more lateral)
• Airway → relatively better

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which of the following hormones play a permissive role in the attainment of puberty?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Leptin

The hormone that plays a permissive role in the attainment of puberty is leptin.

It now appears that leptin may be the link between body weight and puberty. Leptin is a satiety-producing hormone secreted by adipocytes. High leptin levels reduce appetite and increase energy expenditure.

Evidence for which is given by:

• Obese ob/ob mice that cannot make leptin are infertile, and their fertility is restored by injections of leptin.
• Leptin treatment also induces precocious puberty in immature female mice.
• However, the way that leptin fits into the overall control of puberty remains to be determined.

Leptin also accelerates GnRH pulsatility in neurons, fastening puberty.
questions.learning: Leptin — The hormone that plays a permissive role in the attainment of puberty is leptin. It now appears that leptin may be the link between body weight and puberty.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following is most likely to be seen due to rupture of a saccular aneurysm?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Subarachnoid hemorrhage

Subarachnoid hemorrhage is most likely to be seen due to the rupture of a saccular aneurysm.

Saccular aneurysms are thin-walled outpouchings measuring 2 or 3 cm in diameter with a bright, red, translucent wall. These are mainly seen at the arterial branching points along the circle of Willis.

The absence of smooth muscle and internal elastic lamina is the main pathogenesis in saccular aneurysms. Female sex, smoking, cocaine abuse, and family history are some other risk factors.

Genetic conditions predisposing to subarachnoid hemorrhage are:

• Adult polycystic kidney disease
• Fibromuscular dysplasia
• Neurofibromatosis type 1
• Ehler Danlos syndrome and Marfan's syndrome.

Clinically, subarachnoid hemorrhage presents with a sudden and severe headache commonly referred to as thunderclap headache. It may be associated with seizures, unresponsiveness, and vomiting.

CT scan is the imaging method of choice. It shows blood in basal cisterns and aneurysms appear as round enhancing lesions. Management includes craniotomy and clipping or coiling by endovascular embolization. Medical management includes fluid replacement with normal saline, oral nimodipine 60 mg every 4 hours, and supportive measures.

Hyponatremia can be a frequent complication in subarachnoid hemorrhage. The below image shows a CT of subarachnoid hemorrhage with blood in basal cisterns.

Other options:

Option A: Subdural hemorrhage or subdural hematoma occurs mainly due to rupture of the cortical bridging veins. Symptoms of raised intracranial pressure (ICP)  such as headache, vomiting, blurring of vision, as well as focal deficits are seen.

Option C: Intracerebral hemorrhages may spontaneously occur in patients with hypertension, amyloid angiopathy, coagulation disorders, or as a complication of ischemic stroke. Headache, raised ICP, and focal neurological deficits can be present.

Option D: Hydrocephalus is a condition where the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) circulation is obstructed or there is a failure to resorb thereby leading to an increase in CSF volume with enlargement of the ventricles. Symptoms of raised ICP are seen.
questions.learning: Subarachnoid hemorrhage Subarachnoid hemorrhage is most likely to be seen due to the rupture of a saccular aneurysm. Saccular aneurysms are thin-walled outpouchings measuring 2 or 3 cm in diameter with a bright, red, translucent wall.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Out of a total of 2000 patients assessed for HIV, 200 were confirmed positive. A new ELISA screening test was conducted on the same group, identifying 260 positive cases, but only 130 of them actually had the disease. What is the specificity of this test?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 93%

The specificity based on the given clinical scenario is 93%.

Specificity refers to the test’s ability to correctly identify HIV-negative individuals (true negatives) out of all who do not have the disease. The formula for specificity is:

In the given scenario,

Total patients tested = 2000
True HIV-positive cases (confirmed) = 200
ELISA test positive cases = 260
True positives (correctly identified by ELISA) = 130

Positive results:

Out of the 260 positive results, 130 had the disease
So, the number of true positives = 130
The remaining 130 people are false positives because they had positive results but did not have the disease

Negative results:

Total actual negatives = Total patients - Confirmed positive cases, 2000−200=1800.
True negatives (TN) = Total actual negatives - False positives, 1800−130=1670.

Specificity= True Negatives / True Negatives (TN) + False Positives (FP) ×100.

Specificity = 1670 / (1670+130) ×100

Specificity = 1670 / (1800) ×100 = 92.8% ≈ 93%

Pearl PF0045: Validity of a Screening Test

* Validity/ Accuracy of a screening test depends upon the sensitivity, specificity, and predictive accuracy of the test.

* It represents the closeness to a true value/ actual value.

* These are the inherent properties of a screening test.

* PPV and NPV are dependent on the Prevalence of disease.

* Sensitivity & Speciifity are independent of prevalence of disease.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A child presents to your outpatient department with the findings shown in the image below. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Kwashiorkor

The image showing flaky paint dermatosis is seen characteristically in Kwashiorkor.

Kwashiorkor is a form of severe acute malnutrition (SAM) characterized by edema and apathy. It usually affects infants and children, most often around the age of weaning till the age of 5.

Children with kwashiorkor have moon-shaped faces. Edema is most likely to appear first in the feet and then in the lower legs soon developing into generalized edema. Abdominal distension occurs with or without dilated bowel loops and hepatomegaly and fatty infiltrate.

Skin changes occur over the swollen limbs and include dark, crackled peeling patches with pale skin underneath forming patches of hyper and hypopigmentation called flaky paint dermatosis or crazy paving. The skin gets easily infected.

The hair is dull, brittle, sparse, and can easily be pulled out. It may lose its curl. In dark-haired children, the hair may turn pale or reddish. Alternating bands of light and normal color hair may be seen, known as the flag sign. Children are miserable, apathetic, and often refuse to eat. There is marked muscle atrophy and growth retardation.

Clinical features seen in marasmus are:

* Simian facies

* Lethargic and irritable,apathetic

* Bradycardia

* Thin, dry skin

* Thin and brittle hair,easily pluckable.

* hypotension, and hypothermia

* The reduction of buccal fat pad gives rise to a wrinkled or aged look, while the term “baggy pants appearance” describes sagging skin of the buttocks that hangs downward.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A child presents with elevated liver enzyme levels, and ocular examination reveals a golden to greenish-brown ring at the periphery of the cornea. What is the underlying cause of this clinical finding?
questions.explanation: The clinical description points toward the Kayser-Fleischer (KF) ring, a pathognomonic sign of Wilson's disease (hepatolenticular degeneration). This condition is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by mutations in the ATP7B gene, leading to defective copper transport and its subsequent accumulation in various tissues. In the eye, copper deposits in the Descemet's membrane at the periphery of the cornea, creating the characteristic golden-brown or greenish ring. The child's concurrent elevated liver enzymes reflect the primary hepatic involvement of Wilson's disease, where copper toxicity causes cirrhosis and chronic hepatitis. Glucose (Option B), galactose (Option C), and mannose (Option D) are sugars. While galactose is associated with early-onset "oil droplet" cataracts, it does not cause corneal rings. KF rings are best visualized using a slit-lamp examination and are present in nearly all patients with the neurological form of the disease and about 50-60% of those with primarily hepatic presentation. Early identification is crucial as the disease is treatable with copper-chelating agents like penicillamine

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: Identify the disease shown in the image below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Elephantiasis

The given clinical picture is suggestive of lymphatic filariasis (elephantiasis).

Lymphatic filariasis is caused by Wuchereria bancrofti and Brugia malayi.

Elephantiasis is a delayed sequel to repeated lymphangitis, obstruction, and lymphedema. Repeated leakage of lymph into tissues first results in lymphedema, then to elephantiasis.

The characteristic manifestations of filariasis are due to obstruction of lymph vessels and nodes. The essential features are lymphadenopathy, lymphangitis, lymphangiovarix, lymphorrhagia or chylorrhagia, hydrocoele, lymphoedema and elephantiasis, and chyluria. Sometimes the swelling involves the whole leg, the whole arm, the scrotum, the vulva, or the breast.

Occult Filariasis is a term given to hypersensitivity reactions to filarial antigens.Wuchereria bancrofti infection is usually asymptomatic.

Microfilaria of the Wuchereria bancrofti has a pointed tail that is free of nuclei.

The lymphatic vessels of the male genitalia are most commonly affected in bancroftian filariasis, producing episodic funiculitis, epididymitis, and orchitis. Adenolymphangitis of the extremities is less common.

DEC provocation test is used to demonstrate microfilaria during the day.

Diethylcarbamazine is the drug of choice.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: In the case of rape of a young child, the hymen is usually:
options: Ruptured since it is superficially situated
Ruptured since it is very thin
Unruptured since it is deeply situated
Unruptured since it is highly elastic
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Unruptured since it is deeply situated

In the case of a young child, the hymen is deeply situated and usually intact after intercourse. As the vagina is very small, it is impossible for the penetration of the adult organ to take place.

In children, there are few or no signs of general violence, as the child is unaware of the assault and incapable of resisting. A few indicators for inquiry are:

• Pain on urination and/or defecation
• Abdominal pain
• Inability to sleep
• Sudden withdrawal from peers/adults
• Feelings of anxiety
• Nervousness
• Helplessness
• A feeling of ending one’s life
questions.learning: Unruptured since it is deeply situated — In the case of a young child, the hymen is deeply situated and usually intact after intercourse. As the vagina is very small, it is impossible for the penetration of the adult organ to take place.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Cardiovascular System · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 72-year-old man is evaluated during a routine clinic visit after experiencing intermittent palpitations over the past month. He has a history of hypertension and mild COPD and remains hemodynamically stable. His pulse is irregular at 90/min, and ECG is shown. The arrhythmia has likely been present for more than 48 hours. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Initiate oral rivaroxaban

The ECG is diagnostic of atrial flutter, which carries a thromboembolic risk similar to atrial fibrillation.

Since the arrhythmia has been present for >48 hours (or duration is uncertain):

• Anticoagulation for at least 3 weeks is required before cardioversion or catheter ablation (unless TEE excludes atrial thrombus).
• A DOAC (eg, rivaroxaban, apixaban, dabigatran) or warfarin is appropriate.

Why the other options are incorrect?

• A. Admit for intravenous ibutilide: Can chemically cardiovert atrial flutter but should not be used before adequate anticoagulation because of embolic risk.
• B. Oral amiodarone: May restore sinus rhythm and precipitate thromboembolism before anticoagulation.
• C. Synchronized electrical cardioversion: Contraindicated before adequate anticoagulation when flutter has lasted >48 hours.

High-yield pearl:

• AF and atrial flutter of >48 hours require ≥3 weeks of anticoagulation (or TEE-guided exclusion of thrombus) before cardioversion.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: What is the dose of carbetocin used in the prevention of postpartum hemorrhage?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 100 mcg

100 mcg of carbetocin is used in the prevention of postpartum hemorrhage (PPH).

The use of carbetocin (100 µg, IM/IV) is recommended for the prevention of PPH. It is a long-acting synthetic analog of oxytocin with agonist properties. It binds to oxytocin receptors in the uterine smooth muscle, and results in rhythmic contractions, increased frequency of existing contractions, and increased uterine tone.

To effectively prevent PPH, the WHO recommends the use of only one of the following uterotonic agents:

• Oxytocin - (10 IU - IM/IV)
• Carbetocin - (100 μg - IM/IV)
• Misoprostol - (400 μg or 600 μg, per-oral)
• Ergometrine/methylergometrine - (200 μg - IM/IV)
• Oxytocin and ergometrine fixed-dose combination - (5 IU,500μg - IM)

Of these, oxytocin is used as the first-line agent in preventing postpartum hemorrhage. When oxytocin is not available, the other drugs mentioned above can be used based on the clinical condition and availability of the drug.
questions.learning: 100 mcg 100 mcg of carbetocin is used in the prevention of postpartum hemorrhage (PPH). The use of carbetocin (100 µg, IM/IV) is recommended for the prevention of PPH.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A 23-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department unconscious after a motor vehicle accident. NCCT is shown here. A branch of which of the following arteries is most likely severed in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Maxillary

A biconvex (lens-shaped) hyperdense collection on NCCT following head trauma is characteristic of an epidural hematoma. This usually occurs due to rupture of the middle meningeal artery, most commonly after a temporal bone (pterion) fracture.

Key anatomical correlation:

• Middle meningeal artery is a branch of the maxillary artery.
• It runs between the skull and dura mater.
• Trauma can tear this artery → rapid arterial bleeding → epidural hematoma.

Classic clinical features:

• Head trauma
• Brief loss of consciousness → lucid interval → rapid deterioration
• Expanding hematoma causing increased intracranial pressure and brain compression
