questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Allopurinol and vitamin C are used to reduce uric acid levels and prevent gout-like symptoms. Which of the following factors plays a key role in the maturation of collagen?
questions.explanation: Ascorbic acid (Vitamin C) is essential for the maturation of collagen. It acts as a vital cofactor for the enzymes prolyl hydroxylase and lysyl hydroxylase, which are responsible for the hydroxylation of proline and lysine residues in the procollagen chain. This post-translational modification is necessary for the formation of stable hydrogen bonds that hold the collagen triple helix together. A deficiency in Vitamin C leads to scurvy, characterized by fragile connective tissue, bleeding gums, and poor wound healing. Proline (Option A) is an amino acid component of collagen, but not the "maturing" agent. Copper and zinc (Option B) are cofactors for other enzymes (like lysyl oxidase for cross-linking), but the primary "maturation" step of hydroxylation is Vitamin C-dependent. Phenylalanine (Option D) is unrelated to collagen synthesis. In the context of the question, Vitamin C serves dual roles: aiding collagen health and facilitating the excretion of uric acid. Thus, ascorbic acid is the indispensable factor for collagen structural integrity
questions.learning: Ascorbic acid (Vitamin C) is essential for the maturation of collagen. It acts as a vital cofactor for the enzymes prolyl hydroxylase and lysyl hydroxylase, which are responsible for the hydroxylation of proline and lysine residues in the procollagen chain.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 35-year-old woman takes aspirin for a headache, later she presented with wheezing and breathlessness. These symptoms are likely to be associated with which of the following conditions?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Nasal polyp

This clinical vignette is suggestive of aspirin intolerance. It is most likely to be associated with nasal polyps.

In a patient with Samter's triad, aspirin should be avoided due to the risk of the development of aspirin intolerance.

Samter triad is a non-IgE mediated hypersensitivity reaction associated with the intake of aspirin or other cyclooxygenase inhibitors. Samter's triad is also known as aspirin-induced asthma or aspirin-sensitive asthma. It consists of:

* Nasal polyposis

* Bronchial asthma

* Aspirin intolerance

Patients with Samter's triad will have persistent nasal congestion, rhinorrhea, anosmia, nasal polyps, and recurrent chronic rhinosinusitis. Asthma and aspirin intolerance develop later.

Acute asthma attacks usually occur 3 hours after intake of aspirin or NSAIDs. Severe rhinorrhea, conjunctival injection, facial flushing, and periorbital edema are also seen. Aspirin-induced hypersensitivity reactions also may occur.

Patients should avoid aspirin and NSAIDs that inhibit COX-1. Treatment may involve aspirin desensitization and endoscopic sinus surgery.

Pearl PF1083: Ethmoidal polyps

* Main etiological factor is allergy

* Usually affects the middle-aged

* Site of origin: Lateral wall of the nose

* Clinical features: Nasal stuffiness, headache (due to sinusitis), sneezing, watery nasal discharge, anosmia/ hyposmia, mass protruding from the nasal cavity

* Findings:

* Anterior rhinoscopy: Multiple, bilateral polypi that are smooth, glistening, grape-like masses often pale in color

* They may be sessile or pedunculated, insensitive to probing and do not bleed on touch

* Investigation of choice: NCCT

* Treatment of choice: FESS
questions.learning: Nasal polyp — This clinical vignette is suggestive of aspirin intolerance. It is most likely to be associated with nasal polyps.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 32-year-old pregnant woman at 28 weeks of gestation presents with hypertension and has a history of well-controlled asthma. She is currently not on any medications, and her blood pressure is 150/95 mmHg. Which treatment option is most appropriate for managing her hypertension?
questions.explanation: This 32-year-old pregnant woman at 28 weeks’ gestation has mild–moderate hypertension (150/95 mmHg) with a history of asthma. When selecting antihypertensive therapy in pregnancy, it is essential to choose a drug that is safe for the fetus and does not exacerbate maternal comorbidities. Although labetalol is commonly used as a first-line agent for hypertension in pregnancy, it has β-blocking activity. Even though it is relatively β₁-selective, labetalol can still precipitate bronchoconstriction, making it less suitable in patients with asthma, including those with well-controlled disease. This concern applies to both IV labetalol (Option A) and oral labetalol (Option D). Additionally, IV labetalol is mainly reserved for hypertensive emergencies, which this patient does not have. ACE inhibitors (Option C) are contraindicated in pregnancy because they can cause fetal renal dysgenesis, oligohydramnios, and neonatal renal failure. Nifedipine, a calcium channel blocker, is safe and effective in pregnancy, does not affect bronchial smooth muscle, and is therefore the best choice for managing hypertension in a pregnant patient with asthma

questions.text: A diabetic patient's fasting blood glucose level is found to be 160 mg/dL. What will you advise the patient regarding non-pharmacological management?

Correct answer: C. < 30% of the calories should come from fat

Solution - Standard Dietary Recommendations

| --------- | --------------

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following growth hormone analogue that is not used for treatment of GH deficiency but is used in the treatment of HIV-associated lipodystrophy?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Tesamorelin

Tesamorelin is a GHRH analogue used to reduce visceral adiposity in HIV-associated lipodystrophy by stimulating endogenous GH release. It is not used for routine treatment of GH deficiency.

| Drug | Type | Main Use

| ---- | ---- | --------

| Somatropin | Recombinant GH | ⭐ GH deficiency

| Sermorelin | GHRH analogue | GH deficiency (stimulates GH)

| Pegvisomant | GH receptor antagonist | Acromegaly

| Tesamorelin ⭐ | GHRH analogue | HIV lipodystrophy

Somatropin is recombinant GH for deficiency states, while pegvisomant is a GH receptor antagonist used in acromegaly. Sermorelin is used diagnostically or for GH deficiency, not lipodystrophy.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: A new resident to a high-altitude area develops hypoxia. What is the causative factor?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Low partial pressure of 02

Hypoxia in high altitude is due to the low partial pressure of O2.

Adaptation at High Altitudes:

* The work capacity is reduced at high altitudes and is directly proportional to the decrease in O2 uptake.

* Immediate exposure to low PO2 at higher altitudes stimulates the arterial chemoreceptors, and this stimulation increases alveolar ventilation.

* This immediate increase in pulmonary ventilation upon rising to a high altitude blows off large quantities of CO2, reducing the PCO2 and increasing the pH of the body fluids causing respiratory alkalosis. This raised pH inhibits the brain stem respiratory center and opposes the increased ventilation. So, respiratory alkalosis will hinder maximal exercise effort.

* To compensate for this respiratory alkalosis, kidneys reduce hydrogen ion secretion and increase bicarbonate excretion. This reduces plasma and cerebrospinal fluid bicarbonate concentration, bringing the pH to normal. It removes the inhibitory effect of alkalosis on respiration. Hence fall in blood bicarbonate facilitates the exercise effort.

* Lactic acid levels increase which causes extreme fatigue. When there is insufficient oxygen (at high altitudes), most of the pyruvic acid is converted into lactic acid, which diffuses out of the muscle cells into the interstitial fluid and blood.

Pearl PF1303: Acclimatization to high altitude

questions.text: Match the following with the nerve supply of external ear:
options: A - Auriculotemporal nerve; B - Greater auricular nerve; C - Facial and Vagus nerve
A - Greater auricular nerve; B - Auriculotemporal nerve; C - Facial and Vagus nerve
A - Greater auricular nerve; B - Facial and Vagus nerve; C - Auriculotemporal nerve
A - Facial and Vagus nerve; B - Greater auricular nerve; C - Auriculotemporal nerve
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. A - Greater auricular nerve; B - Auriculotemporal nerve; C - Facial and Vagus nerve

The correctly matched option regarding the nerve supply of the pinna is option B: A - Greater auricular nerve; B - Auriculotemporal nerve; C - Facial and Vagus nerve.

The nerve supply of the pinna is provided by the following:

• Greater auricular nerve (A) supplies most of the medial surface of the pinna and the posterior part of the lateral surface.
• Lesser occipital nerve supplies the upper part of the medial surface.
• Auriculotemporal nerve  (B) supplies the tragal area and crus helix.
• Arnold's nerve (C) i.e. the auricular branch of the vagus nerve (CN X) supplies the concha and the corresponding area on the medial surface.
• Facial nerve (CN VII) (C) which is distributed along with Arnold's nerve also supplies the concha and the retro auricular groove.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A tall male presents with sparse pubic and axillary hair, underdeveloped genitalia, and laboratory findings of elevated LH and FSH levels. Karyotype analysis reveals an XXY chromosomal pattern. Based on these features, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The combination of a tall stature, signs of androgen deficiency (scant hair, small genitalia), and the pathognomonic 47, XXY karyotype is diagnostic of Klinefelter's syndrome (Option B). This is the most common cause of primary hypogonadism in males. The elevated LH and FSH levels occur due to the lack of negative feedback from the failing testes (hypergonadotropic hypogonadism). Vanishing testis syndrome (Option A) would result in a similar hormonal profile but would lack the specific XXY genetics and tall stature. Noonan syndrome (Option C) presents with characteristic facial features and heart defects, usually with a 46, XY karyotype. Congenital adrenal hyperplasia (Option D) typically presents with ambiguous genitalia in females or precocious puberty in males. Therefore, the specific chromosomal finding of XXY confirms Klinefelter's syndrome as the definitive diagnosis
questions.learning: The combination of a tall stature, signs of androgen deficiency (scant hair, small genitalia), and the pathognomonic 47, XXY karyotype is diagnostic of Klinefelter's syndrome (Option B).

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: What dose of epinephrine is used in anaphylactic shock?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1:1000 I.M. - 0.5 ml

Epinephrine (1:1000 solution) 0.5 ml via intramuscular route is preferred in the treatment of anaphylactic shock.

For intravenous use, 1:1000 adrenaline must be further diluted to 1:10,000 and should be used very cautiously as slow bolus.

There is a much greater risk of causing harmful side effects by either inappropriate dosage or misdiagnosis of anaphylaxis when using IV adrenaline. Hence, IM injection is preferred over intravenous (IV) bolus because it is faster in many situations and safer (lower risk of cardiovascular complications, such as severe hypertension and ventricular arrhythmias).

For intramuscular, subcutaneous, and inhalational (nebulization) routes of administration, 1:1000 dilution can be used.

In cardiac arrest, the 1:1000 adrenaline must be diluted to 1:10,000 for IV use. The recommended dose of epinephrine is 1mg = 10 mL of 1:10,000 solution IV administered every 3 to 5 minutes during resuscitation as per the CPR guidelines.

Epinephrine is also used in the treatment of hypotension, to induce local vasoconstriction to reduce the diffusion of local anaesthetics and to induce bronchodilation in asthma and COPD.
questions.learning: 1:1000 I.M. - 0.5 ml Epinephrine (1:1000 solution) 0.5 ml via intramuscular route is preferred in the treatment of anaphylactic shock. For intravenous use, 1:1000 adrenaline must be further diluted to 1:10,000 and should be used very cautiously as slow bolus.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following diseases is characterized by destructive lymphoid infiltration of the thyroid gland leading to fibrosis and enlargement of the thyroid gland with an increased risk of developing thyroid lymphoma?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Hashimoto’s thyroiditis

Hashimoto’s thyroiditis is the most common cause of hypothyroidism in iodine-sufficient areas and is an autoimmune thyroid disorder characterized by destructive lymphocytic infiltration of the thyroid gland, leading to progressive fibrosis and thyroid enlargement (goiter). Patients with Hashimoto’s thyroiditis have a significantly increased risk of developing primary thyroid lymphoma, particularly Diffuse Large B-cell Lymphoma (DLBCL) and MALT lymphoma.

• D. Hashimoto’s thyroiditis:

• Autoimmune destruction of the thyroid by T-lymphocyte-mediated inflammation.
• Associated with anti-thyroid peroxidase (anti-TPO) and anti-thyroglobulin antibodies.
• Increases the risk of primary thyroid lymphoma.

Why are the other options incorrect?

• A. de Quervain’s thyroiditis: Subacute granulomatous thyroiditis, usually post-viral, presents with a painful, tender thyroid and transient thyrotoxicosis.
• B. Multinodular goitre: Non-inflammatory enlargement of the thyroid with multiple nodules; not associated with thyroid lymphoma.
• C. Riedel’s thyroiditis: Rare fibrosing thyroiditis causing a hard, “woody” thyroid, but not associated with lymphoid infiltration or increased lymphoma risk.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: In the given image, the physician is trying to palpate which of the following arteries?
questions.explanation: The image illustrates the clinical assessment of the posterior tibial artery pulse. This artery is routinely palpated posterior to the medial malleolus and anterior to the Achilles tendon. Assessment of this pulse is essential for evaluating peripheral arterial disease (PAD) in the lower extremities. The anterior tibial artery (Option A) is located deep in the leg and is not easily palpable. The dorsalis pedis artery (Option C) is palpated on the dorsum of the foot, lateral to the extensor hallucis longus tendon. The lateral plantar artery (Option D) is a terminal branch of the posterior tibial artery and is also too deep for routine clinical palpation. Clinicians must be familiar with these anatomical landmarks to accurately perform a vascular examination, especially in diabetic patients where peripheral circulation must be monitored closely to prevent ulcers and gangrene

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 58-year-old patient presents with a history of multiple chalazia over the past year. Examination reveals several nodules on the eyelids, some of which have required incision and drainage. Which type of cancer should be suspected in this patient?
questions.explanation: Sebaceous cell carcinoma is a rare but highly malignant eyelid tumor that characteristically masquerades as benign conditions. In a patient over 50 with a history of recurrent or "multiple" chalazia in the same location, or chronic unilateral blepharitis that fails to respond to standard treatment, this cancer must be the primary suspicion. This "great masquerader" originates from the Meibomian glands or glands of Zeis. Squamous cell carcinoma (Option B) and Basal cell carcinoma (Option C) typically present as discrete nodules or ulcers with distinct margins (e.g., pearly edges in BCC) rather than mimicking chalazia. Kaposi’s sarcoma (Option D) appears as violaceous lesions, usually in immuno compromised individuals. Diagnosis of sebaceous cell carcinoma requires a full-thickness biopsy. It is notoriously aggressive, often exhibiting "pagetoid spread" along the conjunctival surface and metastasizing to regional lymph nodes. Early surgical excision with wide margins or Mohs micrographic surgery is essential. Clinicians must biopsy any chalazion that recurs after surgery

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 25-year-old patient presents with abdominal pain and fever for 3 days duration. The chest X-ray in the erect position is given below. What will be the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Hollow viscus perforation

The given clinical scenario of acute abdominal pain and fever with chest X-ray in an erect position showing air under the diaphragm (pneumoperitoneum) is a characteristic of hollow viscus perforation.

The most common cause of pneumoperitoneum is bowel perforation (>90% of the cases). Gastric and posterior duodenal perforations are seen in long-standing cases of peptic ulcers. Intestinal perforations are seen with ischemia, inflammation, diverticula, or obstruction (E.g:- colonic carcinoma). Other causes also include iatrogenic, penetrating injuries, prolonged mechanical ventilation, peritoneal dialysis, etc.

Perforation of a viscus is a life-threatening condition due to leakage of the enteric contents which can lead to acute bacterial peritonitis.

Clinical features of hollow viscous perforation are due to the developed peritonitis. They include abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting. On examination, the patient has tachycardia, tenderness, rebound tenderness, decreased or absent bowel sounds, and guarding on palpation. Fever may be present.

The patient is initially investigated with an upright chest X-ray which typically shows air beneath the diaphragm. Various other signs for pneumoperitoneum in the supine abdominal X-rays are Rigler’s sign, Cupola sign, falciform ligament sign, football sign, and Doge’s cap sign. However, CECT is the most sensitive investigation to detect minimal/ suspected pneumoperitoneum along with the cause and site of perforation.

Other options:

Option A: Gastric volvulus is a twisting or axial rotation of the stomach along its longitudinal axis (organo-axial) or vertical axis (mesentero-axial). The sudden onset of constant and severe upper abdominal pain, recurrent retching with the production of little vomitus, and the inability to pass an NG tube constitute the Borchardt triad. Plain films of the abdomen reveal a gas-filled viscus in the chest or upper abdomen.

Option C: Liver abscess will mostly have the classic presenting symptoms of fever, jaundice, and right upper quadrant pain, with a tenderness to palpation. Chest X-ray findings generally reflect subdiaphragmatic diseases, such as an elevated right hemidiaphragm, right pleural effusion, or atelectasis.

A chest radiograph shows an air-fluid level in the right upper abdomen (arrow) and multiple nodular opacities in the bilateral lungs (arrowheads)

Option D: Empyema thoracis is an infection of the pleural space. An empyema thoracis on a chest X-ray can mimic a pleural effusion or a lung abscess.The fluid is commonly drained completely with a chest tube or small-bore catheter.

The chest radiograph showing pleural empyema.

* The proximal row is made up of the talus and calcaneum.

* The distal row from medial to lateral contains, the medial, intermediate, and lateral cuneiforms and the cuboid.

* Medially the navicular bone is interposed between the head of the talus and the cuneiforms.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A woman presents with fever and a typical malar rash. Echocardiographic examination reveals vegetations on both surfaces of the heart valves. Based on these clinical and investigative findings, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The patient exhibits systemic signs of Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE), specifically the fever and the characteristic "malar (butterfly) rash". In the context of SLE, the specific type of cardiac involvement described—small, sterile vegetations located on "both sides" (surfaces) of the heart valves or chordae tendineae—is known as Libman-Sacks endocarditis. Infective endocarditis (Option A) typically presents with larger, friable vegetations and positive blood cultures, usually only on the flow-facing side of the valve. Non-bacterial thrombotic endocarditis (Option C) involves sterile vegetations but is usually associated with advanced cancers (marantic endocarditis) rather than SLE and rashes. Rheumatic heart disease (Option D) typically shows "verrucae" along the lines of closure of the valves and is preceded by a streptococcal infection. Libman-Sacks vegetations are composed of immune complexes and fibrin; while often asymptomatic, they can occasionally lead to valve dysfunction or embolic events. This association with "both sides of the valves" is a classic pathognomonic description in pathology exams

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A boy is severely beaten by 4 to 5 people and arrives at the hospital with serious injuries. A dying declaration is recorded. Which of the following statements about dying declarations in India is false?
options: It must always be recorded by a magistrate
An oath is not administered before recording a dying declaration.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. It must always be recorded by a magistrate

The statement that is not applicable to the dying declaration is it must be always recorded by a magistrate.

While it is ideal for a Magistrate to record a dying declaration, there is no legal provision that states that it must always be recorded by a magistrate. The statement can be recorded by a magistrate, the doctor, the village headman, a police officer, or any member of the public.

A dying deposition, on the other hand, must always be recorded by a Magistrate.

A dying declaration (Sec. 32 IEA) is a form of a written or oral statement made by a person whose imminent death is a result of an unlawful act. The statement made relates to the facts of the cause of death and the circumstances surrounding it.

Procedure:

* As soon the severely injured person is brought to the hospital, the medical officer should inform the magistrate to have a dying declaration recorded. The fitness of the declarant to make the statement should be examined first.

* The doctor can record it himself or herself if he thinks that the person will not survive till the arrival of the magistrate. In such a case, the police or the doctor concerned must note down the reason as to why waiting for the magistrate for recording this statement was not feasible.

* Treatment should not be delayed while recording dying declaration.

* An oath is not administered in these circumstances because of the belief that the dying person tells the truth. (Option D)

* Before documenting a dying declaration, the doctor has to ascertain that the person is conscious and of sound mind with normal mental faculties (compos mentis).(Option A)

* If the person dies or becomes unconscious while recording the dying declaration, the doctor must record the information obtained upto that point.

* Usually recorded in the form of a simple narrative in the patient's own language.

* No suggestions, prompting, help, or leading questions from other people are allowed. (Option C)

* No outsider is allowed to be present

* After completing writting, it has to be read back to the patient who has to approve it by signing/thumb impression. The signature of two witnesses is also mandatory.

A dying deposition is a form of oral evidence that is recorded in the presence of the accused or their lawyer, with the provision of cross-examination. There is no legal provision for a dying deposition in the Indian Evidence Act (it is not followed in India).
questions.learning: It must always be recorded by a magistrate — The statement that is not applicable to the dying declaration is it must be always recorded by a magistrate.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 7-year-old male child weighing 40 kg presents with thermal burns involving 22% of the total body surface area. What is the approximate amount of fluid that should be administered in the first 8 hours of resuscitation?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 1,320 mL

The amount of fluid that needs to be administered in the first 8 hours in this case is 1,320 mL

Hartmann’s solution or Ringer’s lactate is the crystalloid most commonly used for burn resuscitation, as it closely matches the osmolality of plasma. It is cheaper compared to colloid solutions and is effective in maintaining intravascular volume.

The modified Parkland formula is the standard method for fluid calculation, expressed as:

* TBSA% burn × weight (kg) × 3 = Volume in mL.

* substituiting the given values, 22 ✖️ 3 ✖️ 40 = 2,640 mL.

To complete 24-hour resuscitation, half (1,320 mL) of this is given in the first 8 hours and the other half over the remaining 16 hours. Urine output serves as a reliable endpoint to guide resuscitation and should be maintained at 0.5–1.0 mL/kg/hour in children. Urine output greater than 2 mL/kg/hour indicates the need to reduce the infusion rate.

Resuscitation fluids in burn patients must always be commenced from the time of burn injury, and if there is any delay, the deficit should be compensated. Intravenous fluid therapy is indicated for adults with burns exceeding 15% of total body surface area (TBSA) and for children with burns exceeding 10% TBSA.

In children, maintenance fluids are required in addition to resuscitation fluids, usually in the form of dextrose–saline. The regimen is weight-based:

* 100 mL/kg for 24 hours for the first 10 kg

* 50 mL/kg for the next 10 kg

* 20 mL/kg for each kilogram above 20 kg body weight

Pearl PF2125: Burns – Formulae for Fluid Calculation(Updated according to ATLS 10th edition 2018 guidelines)

Parkland’s formula gives the total fluid requirement for 24hours. Half of this volume is infused in the first 8 hours, and the remaining half is infused in the next 16 hours.

This formula is recommended for those who have sustained large deep partial-thickness or full-thickness burns that cover more than 20% of the TBSA in adults and more than 10% in children.

Formulas provide a starting target rate; Subsequently, the amount of fluid provided should be adjusted based on urine output.

Dextrose maintenance:

* 100 ml/ kg in 24 hours for 10 kg

* 50 ml/kg for next 10 kg

* 20 ml/kg for every kg after 20 kg

Evan’s formula is used for normal saline.

For the first 24 hours:

* Amount of NS administered = weight in kgs x % TBSA

* Amount of colloid administered = weight in kgs x % TBSA

* 5% Dextrose administered= 2000 ml

After 24 hours, the amount of NS and colloid administered is half. 2000 ml of dextrose is maintained.

Muir and Barclay’s formula for colloids:

* 1 portion of colloid = (weight in kgs x % TBSA)/2

* 6 portions of colloid are administered over 36 hours

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 4-year-old boy presents with low-grade fever, inspiratory stridor, and barking cough for the past 5 days. Examination reveals a hoarse voice, a moderately inflamed pharynx, and a slightly increased respiratory rate. His chest X-ray showed subglottic narrowing appearing like a steeple. Which among the following is not indicated in the treatment of this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Parenteral cefotaxime

The clinical scenario of a child with a barking cough, inspiratory stridor, hoarseness, low-grade fever, and increased respiratory rate and an X-ray showing subglottic narrowing appearing like a steeple is suggestive of croup (laryngotracheobronchitis). Parenteral cefotaxime is not indicated in its treatment.

The median age for laryngotracheobronchitis is 3 months to 5 years. It is caused due to viral infection of the glottic and subglottic regions. Patients present with low-grade fever,  barking cough, hoarseness of voice, and inspiratory stridor.

The image below shows a steeple sign, seen in croup.

Treatment of croup involves:

* Racemic epinephrine nebulization - It constricts pre-capillary arterioles in the upper airway mucosa and decreases capillary hydrostatic pressure, leading to fluid resorption from the interstitial space and reduction of edema. The indications for the administration of nebulized epinephrine are:

* moderate to severe stridor at rest

* the possible need for intubation

* respiratory distress

* hypoxia

* Oral dexamethasone - Indicated in all the grades of croup. Corticosteroids reduce laryngeal edema through their anti-inflammatory action. IM dexamethasone and nebulized budesonide have an equal clinical effect. Corticosteroids should not be administered to children with varicella or tuberculosis as they may worsen the disease.

* A helium-oxygen mixture (heliox) may be considered for severe croup when intubation is being considered. Oxygen should be administered to children who are hypoxemic (SpO2 <92 %)

* Antibiotics are not indicated.

Most children that have croup can be managed safely at home. Indications for hospitalization:

* Progressive stridor

* Severe stridor at rest

* Respiratory distress

* Hypoxia

* Cyanosis

* Depressed mental status

* Poor oral intake

* Need for reliable observation

NOTE:

As the duration of action of racemic epinephrine is only less than 2 hours, it is mandatory to place the patient on observation for 2-3 hours to watch for the reappearance of symptoms. The patient can be discharged home if he has:

* No stridor at rest

* Normal air entry

* Normal O2 saturation

* Normal level of consciousness

* Received steroids
questions.learning: Parenteral cefotaxime — The clinical scenario of a child with a barking cough, inspiratory stridor, hoarseness, low-grade fever, and increased respiratory rate and an X-ray showing subglottic narrowing appearing like a steeple is suggestive of croup…

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text:
Blood examination shows pancytopenia, which can be correct?

A. Megaloblastic anemia

B. Hairy cell leukemia

C. Hypocellular MDS

D. APML
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. A, B, C

Megaloblastic anemia (hypocellular phase), hairy cell leukemia, and hypocellular MDS can show pancytopenia. Acute promyelocytic leukemia is not associated with pancytopenia.

Causes of pancytopenia with hypocellular bone marrow:

• Acquired aplastic anemia
• Hypocellular myelodysplastic syndrome
• Rare aleukemic leukemia
• Some acute lymphoid leukemia
• Rare lymphomas of bone marrow
• Copper deficiency

Causes of pancytopenia with cellular bone marrow:

• Myelodysplastic syndromes
• Systemic lupus erythematosus
• Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (PNH)
• Hypersplenism
• B12, folate deficiency, Copper deficiency
• Myelofibrosis
• Aleukemic leukemia
• HIV, Brucellosis, Leishmaniasis, Tuberculosis Sepsis
• Myelophthisis
• Bone marrow lymphoma
• Sarcoidosis
• Hairy cell leukemia
questions.learning: A, B, C Megaloblastic anemia (hypocellular phase), hairy cell leukemia, and hypocellular MDS can show pancytopenia. Acute promyelocytic leukemia is not associated with pancytopenia.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A 23 year old patient presents with lesions in the groin as shown in the image below. Which of the following cannot be a cause of these lesions?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Aspergillus

The image shows a well-circumscribed, annular plaque in the groin region which is characteristic of tinea cruris. Tinea cruris is a dermatophytosis. Trichophyton, Microsporum and Epidermophyton are dermatophytes whereas Aspergillus is not.

Dermatophytes include 3 genera:

1. Trichophyton species infect skin, hair, and nails and include T. rubrum, T. mentagrophytes, T. tonsurans, T. schoenleinii, and T. violaceum.
2. Microsporum contains M. gypseum, M. canis, and M. nanum. These infect only hair and skin (not nails).
3. Floccosum is the only species in the genus Epidermophyton, It infects only skin and nails (not hair).

Aspergillus spp. produce large necrotic lesions like ecthyma gangrenosum, and sometimes small papules and cold abscesses.
questions.learning: Aspergillus — The image shows a well-circumscribed, annular plaque in the groin region which is characteristic of tinea cruris. Trichophyton, Microsporum and Epidermophyton are dermatophytes whereas Aspergillus is not.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: According to McKeown’s theory, the major reason for the decline in tuberculosis prevalence is due to:
options: Improvement in social and environmental factors
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Improvement in social and environmental factors

McKeown’s theory states that the major decline in mortality from infectious diseases (including tuberculosis) occurred before the advent of effective medical therapy. The primary driver was improvement in social and environmental conditions, such as:

• Better nutrition
• Improved housing
• Reduced overcrowding
• Improved sanitation and living standards
questions.learning: Improvement in social and environmental factors McKeown’s theory states that the major decline in mortality from infectious diseases (including tuberculosis) occurred before the advent of effective medical therapy.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which among the following logos will be seen in a contaminated biomedical waste management plant?
questions.explanation: Biohazard symbol A contaminated biomedical waste management plant handles infectious, hazardous materials and must be prominently marked with the Biohazard symbol (Option A). This logo is the international standard for labeling materials that pose a biological threat to humans or the environment. The Universal Recycling symbol (Option B) indicates that materials are suitable for recycling and is not a warning for infectious hazards. The Radiation hazard symbol (Option C) is used strictly for radioactive materials, such as those found in oncology or radiology departments. The High Voltage symbol (Option D) is a safety warning for electrical hazards and is not used to categorize clinical waste. Thus, the biohazard logo is the specific identifier for the presence of infectious biomedical waste.
questions.learning: Biohazard symbol — A contaminated biomedical waste management plant handles infectious, hazardous materials and must be prominently marked with the Biohazard symbol (Option A).

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A patient presented with diarrhea, memory loss, and a characteristic rash as below. What is the most likely deficient vitamin here?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Niacin

This is an image of Casal's necklace which is seen in case of Pellagra which occurs in Niacin deficiency.

Casal's necklace:

* So called as it forms a ring around the neck.

* Characteristic skin rash that is pigmented and scaling, particularly in skin areas exposed to sunlight.

* It is seen in advanced cases.

Pellagra:

* Due to deficiency of Niacin (Vitamin B3).

Causes of Pellagra:

* Dietary deficiency like corn based diet- maize and jowar

* Alcoholics

* Hartnup disease -  Congenital defects of intestinal and kidney absorption of tryptophan

* Deficiency of micronutrients (e.g., iron, riboflavin, and pyridoxine)

* Isoniazid can precipitate pellagra deficiency

Symptoms:

The primary manifestations of this syndrome are referred to as “the four D’s”:

* Dermatitis

* Diarrhea

* Dementia

* Death (if not treated)

* Other features:

* Bright red glossitis

* Casals Necklace

Treatment:

Oral supplementation with 100 - 200 mg of nicotinamide or nicotinic acid - 5 days.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is a non-parametric test?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Friedman test

Friedman test is a non-parametric test. It is used to test for differences between groups when the dependent variable being measured is ordinal.

Other options:

Student t-test, analysis of variation (ANOVA) test, and pearson correlation are all based on quantitative data and hence grouped under parametric tests.
questions.learning: Friedman test Friedman test is a non-parametric test. It is used to test for differences between groups when the dependent variable being measured is ordinal.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 22y type 1 DM is in the post operative ward following a cesarean done for failed induction (for preeclampsia with severe features). She complains of drowsiness and altered sensorium. She is on maintenance MgSO4 infusion and on IV infusion of insulin. On examination, her PR is 70/ min. BP is 140/ 98 mmHg. RR is 10/min. Auscultation of lungs reveals bilateral normal air entry. Abdominal examination reveals a firm uterus with normal tenderness. Pfannenstiel scar is intact and there is no significant vaginal bleeding. B/l patellar reflexes are absent. A urine dipstick for protein and sugar is negative and a capillary glucose sample is 270 mg%. The suspected diagnosis is?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Magnesium sulphate toxicity

Magnesium sulfate is widely used in Preeclampsia to prevent seizures.

However, excess magnesium can depress the neuromuscular and respiratory systems. Classic signs of MgSO₄ toxicity include:

| Sign  | Explanation

| ----- | ------------

| Loss of deep tendon reflexes  | Earliest sign

| Respiratory depression  | RR < 12/min

| Drowsiness / confusion  | CNS depression

| Cardiac arrest  | Severe toxicity

Loss of patellar reflex is the earliest sign of magnesium toxicity.

| Serum Mg level  | Effect

| --------------- | -------

| 4–7 mEq/L  | Therapeutic level

| >10 mEq/L  | Loss of reflexes

| >12 mEq/L  | Respiratory depression

| >15 mEq/L  | Cardiac arrest

Treatment is immediate administration of: Calcium Gluconate

Dose: 10 ml of 10% calcium gluconate IV slowly

Other steps:

•

Stop MgSO₄ infusion

•

Support respiration

•

Monitor urine output

To prevent toxicity, monitor:

| Parameter  | Safe level

| ---------- | -----------

| Respiratory rate  | >12/min

| Urine output  | >25–30 ml/hr

| Patellar reflex  | Present
questions.learning: Magnesium sulphate toxicity Magnesium sulfate is widely used in Preeclampsia to prevent seizures. However, excess magnesium can depress the neuromuscular and respiratory systems.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Hepcidin inhibits iron transfer from the enterocyte to the plasma by binding to _____
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Ferroportin

Hepcidin inhibits iron transfer from the enterocytes into the plasma by binding to ferroportin, which is an iron efflux channel in the enterocyte.

Iron metabolism is regulated by hepcidin, a protein and acute phase reactant produced by the liver. It binds to ferroportin and degrades it. This inhibits the transfer of iron from the enterocyte to the plasma via ferroportin. As a result, iron becomes trapped within the duodenal cells (enterocytes) in the form of mucosal ferritin and is lost in feces when these cells are shed off.

Transcription of hepcidin is increased by the following factors:

• Increased levels of iron
• Inflammatory cytokines

Transcription of hepcidin is decreased by the following factors:

• Iron deficiency
• Hypoxia
• Ineffective erythropoiesis

Hepcidin is encoded by the HAMP gene and its mutations are associated with hereditary hemochromatosis.
questions.learning: Ferroportin Hepcidin inhibits iron transfer from the enterocytes into the plasma by binding to ferroportin, which is an iron efflux channel in the enterocyte.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Name the international agency that aids India in the construction of sanitary latrines.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. FORD

Ford Foundation takes part in designing and constructing sanitary latrines in rural areas.

Ford Foundation is assisting more in developing rural health services and family planning. They do this by

* Setting up orientation centers to train the medical and paramedical personal

* Projects to solve basic problems in environmental sanitation

* Projects in rural health services

* Established National institute of health administration and education

* Projects to solve water issues in Calcutta

* Family planning fellowship programs

Other options

USAID: United States Agency for International Development is one of the three US agencies extending support to India by giving grants and loans. They have been assisting in improving overall health

CARE: Cooperative for Assistance and Relief everywhere. In India, they primarily take part in providing food to children and now work in conjunction with ICDS for the same

Red Cross: Initially begun to help with war survivors, now it provides help in all sorts of humanitarian crises be it natural or otherwise. In India, they offer healthcare facilities via their hospitals.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which of the following drug binds to CD4 receptors and is used for both CCR-5 as well as CXCR-4 tropic HIV?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Ibalizumab

Ibalizumab is a monoclonal antibody that binds the CD4 receptor post-attachment and blocks HIV entry. Because it targets CD4 rather than the co-receptor, it is effective against both CCR5- and CXCR4-tropic HIV strains. Maraviroc blocks only CCR5, not CXCR4 virus. CD4-directed entry inhibition is the key distinguishing feature.

Entry Inhibitors

| Attachment ⊖ | Gp120 (Fostemsavir)

| ------------ | -------------------

| Post Attachment ⊖ | CD4 Receptors (Ibalizumab)

| Fusion⊖ | Gp41 (Enfuvirtide)

| Co-Receptor ⊖ | CCR-5 (Maraviroc)
questions.learning: Ibalizumab Ibalizumab is a monoclonal antibody that binds the CD4 receptor post-attachment and blocks HIV entry. Because it targets CD4 rather than the co-receptor, it is effective against both CCR5- and CXCR4-tropic HIV strains.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: A patient with a long history of chronic smoking presents with breathlessness. Pulmonary function tests reveal a reduced FEV₁%. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: A history of chronic smoking combined with an obstructive pattern on spirometry—specifically a decrease in FEV1 and a reduced FEV1/FVC ratio (<70%)—is characteristic of COPD. COPD includes chronic bronchitis and emphysema, both of which involve irreversible airflow limitation. In contrast, pulmonary fibrosis (Option B) and interstitial lung disease (Option C) are restrictive lung diseases; they typically show a normal or even increased FEV1/FVC ratio because the forced vital capacity (FVC) decreases more than the FEV1. While asthma (Option D) also causes an obstructive pattern, it is distinguished from COPD by its significant reversibility after bronchodilator use and is less directly linked to chronic smoking in late adulthood compared to COPD. Therefore, given the specific risk factor of smoking and the obstructive findings, COPD is the most likely clinical diagnosis
questions.learning: A history of chronic smoking combined with an obstructive pattern on spirometry—specifically a decrease in FEV1 and a reduced FEV1/FVC ratio (<70%)—is characteristic of COPD.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Heart of sewage disposal plant:
questions.explanation: The aeration tank is called the “heart of a sewage disposal plant” because it is the main site of biological treatment. Here, activated sludge (microorganisms) breaks down organic matter in sewage using oxygen supplied by aeration. This process significantly reduces biochemical oxygen demand (BOD) and removes most of the pollutants. Why other options are incorrect: (A) Primary sedimentation tank:Removes suspended solids by settling, but no major biological treatment occurs. (C) Secondary sedimentation tank:Used for settling of activated sludge after aeration, not the main treatment step. (D) Sludge digestion tank:Handles sludge stabilization (anaerobic digestion), not primary sewage purification. Since the maximum purification occurs in the aeration tank, it is considered the heart of the sewage treatment plant
questions.learning: The aeration tank is called the “heart of a sewage disposal plant” because it is the main site of biological treatment. Here, activated sludge (microorganisms) breaks down organic matter in sewage using oxygen supplied by aeration.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following is not a boundary of the Gastrinoma triangle? (NEET PG 2016)
options: Second and third part of duodenum
Spleen vein and inferior mesenteric vein
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Spleen vein and inferior mesenteric vein

The Gastrinoma triangle (Passaro's Triangle) is an anatomical region where gastrinomas are most commonly found. This triangle is formed by specific anatomical boundaries that define the area where these tumors typically develop. The splenic vein and inferior mesenteric vein are not components of this triangle's boundaries, making this the incorrect option.
questions.learning: Spleen vein and inferior mesenteric vein — The Gastrinoma triangle (Passaro's Triangle) is an anatomical region where gastrinomas are most commonly found.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Consider the following pairs with respect to muscle channelopathies. Which of the pairs given below are correctly matched?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 1, 2 and 4 only

• 1. Sodium → Paramyotonia congenita ✓

• Caused by mutations in the SCN4A gene, encoding the skeletal muscle voltage-gated Na⁺ channel.
• Produces paradoxical worsening of stiffness with repeated activity.

• 2. Calcium → Malignant hyperthermia ✓

• Malignant hyperthermia is associated with abnormal Ca²⁺ release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum, classically due to RYR1 mutations.
• Excess intracellular Ca²⁺ → sustained muscle contraction → hypermetabolism, hypercapnia, hyperthermia, and rigidity.
• Strictly speaking, the relevant channel is the ryanodine receptor (RyR1), a Ca²⁺-release channel.

• 3. Ryanodine receptor → Becker disease ✗

• Becker muscular dystrophy is caused by mutations in the DMD gene, resulting in abnormal/deficient dystrophin.
• RyR1 mutations are associated with malignant hyperthermia and certain congenital myopathies, not Becker dystrophy.

• 4. Chloride → Thomsen disease ✓

• Thomsen disease is autosomal dominant myotonia congenita, caused by CLCN1 (Cl⁻ channel) mutations.
• Defective Cl⁻ conductance → membrane hyperexcitability → myotonia.
questions.learning: Sodium → Paramyotonia congenita ✓ • Caused by mutations in the SCN4A gene, encoding the skeletal muscle voltage-gated Na⁺ channel. • Produces paradoxical worsening of stiffness with repeated activity. • 2.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: A capnograph obtained from an intubated patient undergoing controlled ventilation is given below. Which of the following is a likely cause of the finding seen?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Spontaneous respiratory effort

The curare notch in the plateau phase of the capnograph indicates that the patient is trying to breathe spontaneously. The patient's inspiratory effort causes some fresh gas to be sucked in the capnometer, resulting in a lower carbon dioxide concentration and a notch.

Image below shows a capnograph with clefts during phase III which indicates spontaneous breathing efforts by the patient during controlled mechanical ventilation. It is also known as a curare notch or cleft.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A forensic expert receives a summons from the district court to record evidence in a criminal case, but two days earlier, he had already received a summons for a civil case in the same court. What is the appropriate course of action for him?
options: Attend the court for which the summons came first.
Attend the court for the criminal case.
questions.explanation: When a witness receives conflicting summons (subpoenas) for the same day, legal protocol dictates a specific order of priority. Criminal cases always take precedence over civil cases due to their public importance and the urgency of justice in criminal law. The forensic expert is legally mandated to attend the criminal court and must formally notify the civil court of the conflict, requesting a rescheduled date. Regarding the distractors, informing both and waiting (Option A) is insufficient as it risks contempt of court for non-attendance. The order of receipt (Option B) does not determine priority; only the nature and level of the court do. Ignoring both (Option D) is a serious legal offense that can result in fines, imprisonment, or arrest warrants. If both summons were for the same type of case, the expert would attend the higher court first, or if at the same level, the one received first
questions.learning: When a witness receives conflicting summons (subpoenas) for the same day, legal protocol dictates a specific order of priority. Criminal cases always take precedence over civil cases due to their public importance and the urgency of justice in criminal law.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A couple has given birth to their first child. Based on the nuclear family cycle, which phase is the family entering into?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Extension

The phase of a nuclear family cycle from the birth of their first child to the birth of their last child is called extension.

Pearl PF0595: The Family as a Social Organization

* A family is a group of biologically related individuals living together under the same roof and eating from a common kitchen.

* It is the most primary and basic unit of all societies.

* The basic and arbitrary model of a family cycle has six phases:

Phase

Beginning

1

2

Birth of 1st child

Birth of last child

4

Contraction

1st child leaves home

Last child leaves parental home

5

Completed contraction

Last child leaves parental home

6

Dissolution

Death of 1st spouse

Death of survivor

* Types of families:

* A nuclear family or elementary family consists of only the married couple and their offspring while they are dependants.

* The term new family is applied when nuclear families are younger than 10 years and consist of parents and children.

* A joint family or extended family consists of a number of married couples and their children who live together in the same household with usually the men being related by blood. All property in joint families is held in common with the family income going into a common pocket. A senior male member is usually the head of the family who makes decisions.

* A three generation family is one where there are representatives from three different generations in one house.

* A communal family is one in which all the members play a part in its management.

* Functions of the family:

* Residence (patrilocal and matrilocal)

* Division of labour

* Reproduction and raising children

* Socialization and social care

* Economic functions

* Problems families are those that lag behind the rest of the community in terms of standard and quality of life of its members.

* Broken families are those in which the parental or family system has been disrupted by separation, divorce or death.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which international agency supports the construction of sanitary latrines (toilets) in India?
questions.explanation: The United States Agency for International Development (USAID) has been actively involved in supporting water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH) programs in India. One of its key contributions includes promoting the construction of sanitary latrines, improving access to safe sanitation, and reducing open defecation. USAID collaborates with the Government of India and various NGOs under initiatives such as the Swachh Bharat Mission, aiming to improve public health by enhancing sanitation infrastructure and hygiene practices. These efforts help in preventing waterborne diseases and improving overall community health. Why Other Options Are Wrong (B) CURE: Not a major international agency involved in sanitation programs in India (C) Red Cross: Focuses more on disaster relief and emergency health services (D) Ford Foundation: Works in development sectors but not specifically known for latrine construction programs
questions.learning: The United States Agency for International Development (USAID) has been actively involved in supporting water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH) programs in India.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Radioisotope used in PET-CT scan?
questions.explanation: The most common and standard radioisotope used in PET-CT scanning for oncological and metabolic imaging is Fluorine-18, typically attached to a glucose analog known as 18F-FDG (Fluorodeoxyglucose). As established in Q.281, cancer cells uptake this glucose analog at high rates, which the PET scanner detects as "hot spots." Iodine (Option B, typically I-131) is used primarily for the diagnosis and treatment of thyroid conditions. Radium (Option C) and Cesium-131 (Option D) are used in brachytherapy for cancer treatment, not as diagnostic tracers for PET imaging. 18F-FDG has a half-life of approximately 110 minutes, allowing enough time for production, transport, and imaging while ensuring a relatively low radiation dose to the patient. PET-CT is an essential tool for staging malignancies, monitoring therapy response, and identifying hidden metastases. Clinicians must consider physiological uptake in the brain and heart when interpreting FDG-PET results
questions.learning: The most common and standard radioisotope used in PET-CT scanning for oncological and metabolic imaging is Fluorine-18, typically attached to a glucose analog known as 18F-FDG (Fluorodeoxyglucose).

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient presents with a daily urine output of 7 liters, urine osmolality of 260 mOsm/L, an ADH level of 0.8 pg/mL, and MRI findings showing absence of the posterior pituitary bright spot on T1-weighted images. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The patient has marked polyuria (7 L/day) with dilute urine (urine osmolarity = 260 mOsm/L), indicating Diabetes Insipidus (DI). The ADH level is very low (0.8 pg/mL), which points toward a defect in ADH production or release rather than renal unresponsiveness. The key diagnostic clue is the absence of the posterior pituitary “bright spot” on T1-weighted MRI, which normally represents stored vasopressin granules. Loss of this bright spot is characteristic of central (pituitary) DI. Why other options are incorrect: 1 Nephrogenic DI: ADH levels are normal or elevated, as the kidneys fail to respond. 2 Primary polydipsia: ADH may be suppressed, but the posterior pituitary bright spot is usually preserved. 3 Mannitol infusion: Causes osmotic diuresis without low ADH or MRI changes

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A young man suddenly collapses at a railway station and is rushed to the emergency department. He is found to be pulseless, with ventricular fibrillation noted on cardiac monitoring. Immediate defibrillation is carried out. According to ACLS guidelines, what should be the next step in his management?
questions.explanation: According to the current Advanced Cardiovascular Life Support (ACLS) guidelines, the absolute next step immediately after delivering a shock (defibrillation) is to resume chest compressions. You should not stop to check for a pulse (Option A) or analyze the rhythm until 2 minutes (5 cycles) of high-quality CPR have been completed. This "resume immediately" protocol ensures that the heart receives maximal perfusion, which is critical for a shock to be successful in restoring a perfusing rhythm. Epinephrine (Option C) is typically administered after the second shock, and Amiodarone (Option D) is considered after the third shock if VF persists. Defibrillation causes a brief period of asystole or non-perfusing rhythm; therefore, providing immediate mechanical support through compressions is the highest priority step to maintain organ viability. Consequently, resuming CPR is the definitive life-saving next action
questions.learning: According to the current Advanced Cardiovascular Life Support (ACLS) guidelines, the absolute next step immediately after delivering a shock (defibrillation) is to resume chest compressions.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient presents with a swelling in the groin region and it is diagnosed as a direct inguinal hernia. Weakness in which of the following structures is most likely to cause this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Conjoint tendon

A direct inguinal hernia is caused due to weakness in the conjoint tendon.

The innermost layers of the lateral abdominal wall contain two muscles, namely internal oblique and transverse abdominis. These muscle fibers arch over the deep inguinal ring from lateral to medial, fuse, and become tendinous forming the conjoint tendon. The area below this arch lacks muscle and contains external oblique aponeurosis and fascia transversalis, making it weak.

Direct inguinal hernia is common in elderly patients. It is seen medial to the inferior epigastric vessels, in Hesselbach’s triangle. This area lacks muscle and contains only fascia.

Other options:

Option A: Pectineal ligament also known as Cooper's ligament is a strong fibrous band that extends laterally along the pectineal line from the pectineal attachment of the lacunar ligament.

Option C: The inguinal ligament is external oblique aponeurosis that extends between the anterior superior iliac spine and the pubic tubercle. On the point of attachment to the pubic tubercle, some fibers pass upwards behind the superficial inguinal ring and external oblique aponeurosis to join the rectus sheath and linea alba. These form the reflected part of the inguinal ligament.

Option D: Lacunar ligament is formed from the fibers of the medial end of the inguinal ligament and the fibers from the fascia lata of the thigh. It forms the medial wall of the femoral canal.
questions.learning: Conjoint tendon — A direct inguinal hernia is caused due to weakness in the conjoint tendon. The innermost layers of the lateral abdominal wall contain two muscles, namely internal oblique and transverse abdominis.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A 4-year-old boy presents with a history of facial edema that has now progressed to total body swelling involving the face, abdomen, scrotum, and feet. Urinalysis revealed protein 4+ and a urine protein:creatinine ratio of 3. What is the initial treatment of choice for this child?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Prednisolone

The clinical picture and investigations are highly suggestive of minimal change nephrotic syndrome and the initial treatment of choice is corticosteroids such as prednisolone.

Minimal change nephrotic syndrome is the most common cause of nephrotic syndrome. It is seen in ages 2-6 years. Its features include heavy proteinuria, oedema, hypoalbuminemia and hyperlipidemia. They may be asymptomatic or can present with peripheral edema. Renal biopsy is not required for confirmation and treatment can be initiated if the child fits the standard clinical picture of nephrotic syndrome.

They show excellent response to steroid therapy with prednisone or prednisolone. A daily dose of 2mg/kg (max 60mg) for 6 weeks followed by an alternate day dose of 1.5mg/kg (max 40mg) for the next 6-8 weeks is recommended.

Alternative drugs used in steroid-dependent patients, frequent relapsers, steroid-resistant patients, and those with severe corticosteroid toxicity are as follows:

* Cyclophosphamide

* Calcineurin inhibitors: Cyclosporine and Tacrolimus

* Mycophenolate

* Levamisole

* Rituximab (chimeric monoclonal antibody against CD20)

These syndromes, however, are not mutually exclusive. Some glomerular diseases may progress from one pattern to another or may present with considerable overlap between them, as a nephritic–nephrotic syndrome; features of nephrotic syndrome can concurrently occur with any form of nephritic syndrome but are most commonly seen with diffuse proliferative glomerulonephritis (seen in systemic lupus erythromytosus) and membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A patient comes with a history of high fever for 5 days and altered sensorium. On further probing, it was found that he had two seizures one day ago. Peripheral smear shows the following findings. How will you manage this patient?
options: Clindamycin 600 mg intravenously 8 hourly for 7 days
Artesunate 2.4 mg/kg intravenously at 12 and 24 hours, followed by daily once
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Artesunate 2.4 mg/kg intravenously at 12 and 24 hours, followed by daily once

The given scenario and image from the peripheral smear showing rings (headphones appearance) point towards the diagnosis of severe Plasmodium falciparum malaria, and the treatment of choice for this condition is artesunate 2.4 mg/kg IV at 12 and 24 hours, followed by daily once for 4 days.

Major manifestations of severe falciparum malaria include more than two convulsions in 24 hours, unarousable coma/ cerebral malaria (failure to localize or respond appropriately to stimuli or coma persisting for >30 min after generalized convulsion), acidosis, severe normocytic normochromic anemia, renal failure, pulmonary edema, hypoglycemia, shock, and disseminated intravascular coagulation.
Other manifestations include hemoglobinuria, hyperparasitemia, jaundice, and extreme weakness.

The treatment of choice is artesunate given at a dose of 2.4 mg/kg stat IV, followed by 2.4 mg/kg at 12 and 24 hours, and then daily if necessary.

If artesunate is unavailable, artemether is given at a dose of 3.2 mg/kg stat IM, followed by 1.6 mg/kg QD, or quinine dihydrochloride given at a dose of 20 mg of salt/kg infused over 4 hours, followed by 10 mg of salt/kg infused over 2–8 hours.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 49-year-old man presents with recurrent episodes of profuse watery diarrhea, dehydration, hypokalemia, and achlorhydria. Which type of neuroendocrine tumor is most likely responsible for these symptoms?
questions.explanation: The clinical constellation of symptoms described—Watery Diarrhea, Hypokalemia, and Achlorhydria—is known as the WDHA syndrome or Verner-Morrison syndrome. It is caused by a VIPoma, a rare neuroendocrine tumor (usually pancreatic) that secretes excessive Vasoactive Intestinal Peptide (VIP). VIP stimulates intestinal secretion of water and electrolytes and inhibits gastric acid secretion, leading to "achlorhydria" (lack of stomach acid). The diarrhea is typically voluminous (often >3 liters/day) and persists even with fasting, earning it the name "pancreatic cholera." This leads to severe dehydration and significant potassium loss (hypokalemia). Insulinoma (Option A) presents with fasting hypoglycemia. Somatostatinoma (Option B) causes a triad of diabetes, gallstones, and steatorrhea. Glucagonoma (Option D) presents with necrolytic migratory erythema and mild diabetes. Given the specific biochemical findings of low potassium and no stomach acid coupled with profuse watery diarrhea, VIPoma is the most likely diagnosis. Treatment involves fluid resuscitation, somatostatin analogs like octreotide, and surgical resection
questions.learning: The clinical constellation of symptoms described—Watery Diarrhea, Hypokalemia, and Achlorhydria—is known as the WDHA syndrome or Verner-Morrison syndrome.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: What is the preferred method for inducing anesthesia through inhalation in children?
questions.explanation: In pediatric anesthesia, inhalation induction is often preferred over intravenous induction to avoid the distress of needle sticks in an awake child. Sevoflurane (Option A) is the gold standard for this purpose. It has a non-pungent odor and does not irritate the airway, which minimizes complications like breath-holding, coughing, and laryngospasm. Furthermore, its low blood-gas solubility allows for rapid induction and quick emergence. Desflurane (Option B) and Isoflurane (Option D) are highly pungent and irritating to the respiratory tract, making them unsuitable for induction in an awake child. Halothane (Option C) was the historical choice but has been largely replaced due to risks of halothane hepatitis and cardiac arrhythmias (sensitization to catecholamines). Therefore, sevoflurane's combination of airway safety and rapid pharmacokinetics makes it the most appropriate and preferred inhalational induction agent in the pediatric population
questions.learning: In pediatric anesthesia, inhalation induction is often preferred over intravenous induction to avoid the distress of needle sticks in an awake child. Sevoflurane (Option A) is the gold standard for this purpose.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Identify the stage of bed sore in the sacral region.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Stage 4

The given image shows a pressure sore with extensive tissue destruction, including damage to the muscle layer and thus it belongs to stage 4.

Pressure sores also known as bed sores, pressure ulcers and decubitus ulcers are ulcers that occur due to prolonged pressure on certain sites thereby leading to tissue necrosis. The commonest sites involved are ischium, greater trochanter, sacrum, heel, malleolus (lateral >medial), and occiput. Paraplegic patients, elderly patients, and severely ill patients are at a higher risk of developing pressure sores.

Management is primarily proper skin care with pressure dispersion cushions, air-fluidized beds, and urinary or fecal diversion if required. Patients who are bed-bound should be turned once in 2 hours. Those in a wheelchair should lift themselves off the seat for 10 seconds every 10 minutes.

Surgery is the last resort and is done after a proper initial debridement and vacuum-assisted closure. Vacuum-assisted closure is a wound closure technique in which negative pressure is applied to the wound which leads to a decrease in edema. This hastens the debridement and formation of granulation tissue. Skin flaps with a muscle are also used for closure.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Identify the radiological image of the condition given below.
questions.explanation: The skull X-ray demonstrates a classic “cotton wool appearance,” characterized by patchy areas of sclerosis interspersed with lytic regions. This pattern is highly suggestive of Paget’s disease of bone, a disorder involving abnormal bone remodeling. In this condition, there is excessive and disorganized activity of osteoclasts followed by osteoblasts, leading to thickened, enlarged, and structurally weak bone. The skull vault often appears widened with irregular dense patches, giving the typical cotton wool look. Clinically, Paget’s disease may present with bone pain, deformities, increased head size, and sometimes hearing loss due to involvement of skull bones. Why other options are incorrect: (B) Multiple myeloma: Produces multiple punched-out lytic lesions without surrounding sclerosis, giving a “raindrop skull” appearance. (C) Hyperparathyroidism: Causes a “salt and pepper skull” due to diffuse demineralization and loss of trabecular pattern. (D) Sickle cell anemia: Shows a “hair-on-end” appearance due to marrow hyperplasia and vertical trabeculations. Thus, the presence of patchy sclerosis forming a cotton wool pattern confirms Paget’s disease
questions.learning: The skull X-ray demonstrates a classic “cotton wool appearance,” characterized by patchy areas of sclerosis interspersed with lytic regions. This pattern is highly suggestive of Paget’s disease of bone, a disorder involving abnormal bone remodeling.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: In a 46XY female complete gonadal dysgenesis was noted. Complete gonadal dysgenesis is caused by what in the SRY gene?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Point mutation

Amongst the given options, a point mutation in the SRY gene is most likely to result in complete gonadal dysgenesis but this answer remains controversial as some other sources mention SRY deletion is more commonly associated. The most common cause attributable to about 85% of cases is still idiopathic.

Pure gonadal dysgenesis results from a point mutation in SRY/ SRY deletion or point mutations in another gene with testis-determining effects (DAXJ, SF-1, CBX2). This leads to underdeveloped dysgenetic gonads that fail to produce androgens or AMH. This is characterized by a normal prepubertal female phenotype and a normal mullerian system due to absent AMH.

The child usually presents with failure in the development of secondary sexual characteristics at puberty and amenorrhea. Investigations reveal the absence of estrogen production and they have elevated levels of FSH (>40 miU/mL) and low oestradiol levels (<25 pg/mL).

Women with streak ovaries are infertile, but they can bear children with oocyte donation. They must be treated with cyclic estrogen and progestogen to promote feminization and secondary sexual characteristics and prevent osteoporosis.
questions.learning: Point mutation Amongst the given options, a point mutation in the SRY gene is most likely to result in complete gonadal dysgenesis but this answer remains controversial as some other sources mention SRY deletion is more commonly associated.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 30-year-old woman presents with progressive fatigue, anorexia, and weight loss over the past 3 months. She has a history of type 1 diabetes mellitus and reports that her insulin requirements have decreased recently. On examination, there is diffuse hyperpigmentation, especially over the palmar creases. Laboratory evaluation shows that serum cortisol levels do not increase after administration of exogenous ACTH. Which of the following patterns of electrolyte abnormalities is most likely in this patient?
options: Normal sodium, decreased potassium, decreased chloride, increased bicarbonate
Decreased sodium, increased potassium, increased chloride, decreased bicarbonate
Decreased sodium, decreased potassium, decreased chloride, increased bicarbonate
Normal sodium, increased potassium, normal chloride, normal bicarbonate
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Decreased sodium, increased potassium, increased chloride, decreased bicarbonate

This patient has primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison disease), suggested by:

• Hyperpigmentation → ↑ ACTH (POMC → MSH)
• No response to ACTH stimulation → adrenal gland failure
• Associated autoimmune condition (type 1 DM)

Pathophysiology:

• ↓ Aldosterone

• ↓ Na⁺ reabsorption → hyponatremia
• ↓ K⁺ excretion → hyperkalemia
• ↓ H⁺ excretion → metabolic acidosis (↓ bicarbonate)

• ↑ Chloride to maintain electroneutrality → hyperchloremia

Why not other options?

A. Patterns with hypokalemia → suggest hyperaldosteronism

C. Metabolic alkalosis (↑ bicarbonate) → seen in vomiting/diuretics

D. Normal electrolytes → not consistent with adrenal failure

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 40-year-old patient with peptic ulcer disease is prescribed proton pump inhibitors for four weeks but continues the medication for several months due to fear of recurrence. He later presents with pallor and fatigue. What is the most likely explanation for this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. HCl deficiency

Long-term proton pump inhibitor (PPI) therapy suppresses gastric acid (HCl) secretion, which reduces the conversion of dietary ferric iron (Fe³⁺) to the absorbable ferrous form (Fe²⁺). As a result, iron absorption decreases, predisposing patients to iron deficiency anemia, which presents with pallor and fatigue. Prolonged PPI use may also reduce the absorption of vitamin B₁₂, calcium, and magnesium.

Why not the other options?

• A. Gastrin deficiency: Incorrect. PPIs actually cause hypergastrinemia due to loss of acid-mediated negative feedback.
• B. Secretin overactivity: Incorrect. Secretin regulates pancreatic bicarbonate secretion and has no significant role in iron absorption or PPI-induced anemia.
• D. Intrinsic factor deficiency: Incorrect. Intrinsic factor is produced by parietal cells and is required for vitamin B₁₂ absorption. PPIs do not directly reduce intrinsic factor production, although prolonged acid suppression can impair the release of vitamin B₁₂ from dietary proteins.
questions.learning: HCl deficiency Long-term proton pump inhibitor (PPI) therapy suppresses gastric acid (HCl) secretion, which reduces the conversion of dietary ferric iron (Fe³⁺) to the absorbable ferrous form (Fe²⁺).

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: ICER is a unit for which of the following economic analysis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Cost effectiveness

ICER is a unit for Cost-effectiveness.

Incremental cost-effectiveness analysis (ICER) is a difference in cost/difference in effectiveness. Effectiveness is usually measured in Quality Adjusted Life Years (QALYs), which reflect both the quality and quantity of life.

The Cost-effectiveness analysis measures the costs and outcomes of different interventions and calculates the cost-effectiveness ratio. The benefits of the health care system are expressed in terms of results achieved (Eg, the number of lives saved or the number of days free from disease). This is a more promising tool in the health field than cost-benefit analysis. However, in many cases, it is not possible to use cost-effective analysis.

Other options:

Option B: Cost-benefit analysis: Here, the economic benefits of any program are compared with the cost of the program. The benefits are expressed in monetary terms (whereas in cost-effectiveness analysis, it is expressed in terms of results achieved)to identify whether it is economically sound and to select the best one from several alternate programs. The main drawback of this technique is that the benefits of a particular program in the health field cannot always be expressed in monetary terms. Usually, the benefits are expressed in terms of births or deaths prevented or illnesses avoided or overcome.

Option C: Cost-utility: compares the cost of a program to the health improvement it provides.

Option D: Cost margin: the difference between a product's revenues and how much it costs to make.
questions.learning: Cost effectiveness ICER is a unit for Cost-effectiveness. Incremental cost-effectiveness analysis (ICER) is a difference in cost/difference in effectiveness.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which of the following methods of measuring intraocular pressure is based on the Imbert–Fick principle?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Applanation tonometry

Applanation tonometry, particularly Goldmann applanation tonometry (GAT), is based on the Imbert–Fick law.

According to this principle:

P = F/A

where:

• P = Pressure
• F = Force required to flatten the surface
• A = Area flattened

The Imbert–Fick principle states that the pressure inside an ideal, thin-walled sphere is equal to the force required to flatten a portion of its surface divided by the area flattened.

In Goldmann applanation tonometry, a known area of the cornea is flattened (applanated), and the force required to achieve this is used to determine the intraocular pressure (IOP).

Fluorescein is instilled into the tear film and the mires are viewed under cobalt-blue illumination. The endpoint is reached when the inner margins of the two fluorescein semicircles just touch.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A case of gestational trophoblastic neoplasm is detected to have metastasis in the lungs. It is considered as stage _____.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. III

Metastases in the lungs are considered stage III GTN (gestational trophoblastic neoplasia) in FIGO classification.

International Federation of Gynecology and Obstetrics (FIGO) staging for GTN is as follows:

Stage
Description

I
GTN confined to the uterus

II

GTN extends outside of the uterus but is limited to the genital structures

(adnexa, vagina, broad ligament)

III
GTN extends to the lungs, with or without known genital tract involvement

IV
All other metastatic sites i.e. kidney, liver, brain, bowel, etc.

The chest X-ray below shows lung metastasis - stage III GTN.

Gestational trophoblastic neoplasia (GTN) refers to the aggressive invasion of the endometrium and myometrium by trophoblast cells. It includes invasive mole, gestational choriocarcinoma, placental site trophoblastic tumors, and epithelioid trophoblastic tumors. GTN is diagnosed based on elevated β-hCG levels. FIGO criteria for diagnosis of GTN:

• Persistence of β-hCG level plateau in 4 measurements for 3 weeks or longer
• Rise in β-hCG levels in 3 or more consecutive measurements done weekly, over a period of 2 weeks or longer
• Elevated β-hCG level for 6 months or more
• Histologic diagnosis of choriocarcinoma

Treatment for low-risk disease is chemotherapy with methotrexate, while those with high-risk disease are treated with etoposide, methotrexate, and dactinomycin alternating with cyclophosphamide and vincristine (EMA/CO) chemotherapy.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: At term pregnancy, the normal amniotic fluid appearance is __________.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Cloudy with white specks

At term, the amniotic fluid is cloudy and contains a large number of white flakes of vernix.

Amniotic fluid appearance is determined by the proportion of cloudiness and the number of flakes released from the fetal skin over the period of pregnancy. This is summated by the amniotic fluid macroscore.

At the end of the 32 nd week of pregnancy, the amniotic fluid is clear and does not have any flakes (Option C). By the 36 th week, the amniotic fluid starts to have some flakes (Option A) and gradually we will begin to see traces of cloudiness also. By 42 nd week.i.e. term of pregnancy, the amniotic fluid has a large number of flakes and is very cloudy (Option D).
