questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Causes for expanding blind spot are all except __________
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Hypoplasia of optic disc

Optic disc hypoplasia does not cause enlargement of the blind spot.

The physiological blind spot is an area of absolute scotoma in the visual field, seen in the region of optic disc. It is due to the absence of photoreceptors (rods and cones) in that region. Enlarged blind spot is seen in primary open-angle glaucoma (POAG) (Option A), papilledema (Option C), medullated nerve fibers (Option D), optic disc drusen, coloboma of optic disc and
myopic disc with a crescent.

Optic nerve hypoplasia is the most common congenital optic disc anomaly. There is underdevelopment of the optic disc in the disease and it typically presents with a small disc that is surrounded by a yellowish pigmented ring, called the 'double ring sign'.

Option A: In primary open-angle glaucoma(POAG), the optic disc enlargement is seen secondary to increased intra-ocular pressure (IOP) in the eye.

Option C: Papilledema is a passive disc swelling seen with raised intracranial pressure. The blind spot is enlarged due to the edema of the optic disc.

Option D: Medullated or opaque nerve fibers are the abnormal myelination of nerve fibers of the retina. Normally, optic nerve myelination stops at the level of lamina cribrosa. If the myelination continues beyond the optic disc it leads to the expansion of the blind spot.  On ophthalmoscopic examination, these are seen as a whitish patch with feathery margins.
questions.learning: Hypoplasia of optic disc Optic disc hypoplasia does not cause enlargement of the blind spot. The physiological blind spot is an area of absolute scotoma in the visual field, seen in the region of optic disc.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 26-year-old man presents with an 8-month history of chronic diarrhea. CT shows the following. Based on these findings, what is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Ulcerative colitis

Loss of haustrations on barium study produces a classic “lead pipe colon”, characteristic of chronic ulcerative colitis. Normally, the colon has:

• Sacculations → called haustra

In UC:

• Chronic inflammation → fibrosis + muscle damage
• Colon becomes smooth, rigid, tubular

This gives the classic: “Lead Pipe Appearance”

UC causes continuous mucosal inflammation starting from the rectum with long-standing disease leading to colonic shortening and smooth walls. Crohn disease shows skip lesions and cobblestoning, not uniform haustral loss. Chronic diarrhea with this radiologic sign strongly supports UC.

| Distribution | Continuous | Skip lesions

| Depth | Mucosal | Transmural

| Haustra | Lost | Preserved

| Classic sign | Lead pipe colon | String sign

| Granulomas | Absent | Present

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: What does the term "tracking" refer to in relation to blood pressure?
options: Observing changes in blood pressure throughout a 24-hour period
Recording and analyzing blood pressure levels over an extended period to identify patterns and predict future readings
Comparing blood pressure values between different populations based on demographics
Assessing blood pressure during exercise to evaluate cardiovascular health
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Recording and analyzing blood pressure levels over an extended period to identify patterns and predict future readings

"Tracking" in relation to blood pressure refers to recording and analyzing blood pressure levels over an extended period to identify patterns and predict future readings.

When blood pressure levels are observed from childhood through to adulthood, individuals with higher blood pressure early on typically maintain higher levels, while those with lower levels tend to stay lower as they age. This consistent ranking of blood pressure over time is called "tracking." This helps identify children and adolescents who are at risk of developing hypertension in the future.

Although blood pressure is known to increase with age in both sexes, some communities have been identified, whose mean blood pressure does not rise with age. This is because their salt intake and calorie consumption are at a subsistence level.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A 5-year-old boy is brought to the ophthalmology OPD with complaints of intense eye itching and marked photophobia. His parents also report the presence of thick ocular discharge. Based on these symptoms, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical presentation of a young boy with severe itching, photophobia (light sensitivity), and a thick ropy discharge is pathognomonic for Vernal Keratoconjunctivitis (VKC). VKC is a seasonal, bilateral allergic inflammation common in young males living in warm, dry climates. Hallmark signs include "cobblestone" papillae on the superior tarsal conjunctiva or Horner-Trantas dots at the limbus. Trachoma (Option A) involves chronic scarring and is caused by Chlamydia trachomatis. Phlyctenular conjunctivitis (Option C) presents with a localized nodule (phlycten) usually due to hypersensitivity to TB or staphylococcal proteins. Xerophthalmia (Option D) is caused by Vitamin A deficiency and presents with dryness and Bitot's spots, not intense itching and thick discharge. VKC is managed with topical mast cell stabilizers and antihistamines. Therefore, based on the specific allergic symptoms and demographic, VKC is the most likely diagnosis

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following is complementary to the active site of the enzyme?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Substrate

The substrate is complementary to the active site of the enzyme.

The Lock and Key concept was put forth by Emil Fischer. This model is the initial proposition aimed at elucidating the mechanism of an enzymatic catalytic process. Based on this concept, it can be inferred that the enzyme's structure or conformation exhibits a state of rigidity. The substrate effectively conforms to the binding site, which is now referred to as the active site, in a manner analogous to a key fitting precisely into its corresponding lock or a hand fitting snugly into a well-fitting glove. The active site of an enzyme can be described as a stiff and pre-configured template that selectively accommodates a certain substrate for binding.

The induced fit or Koshland theory states that the active site does not possess a firm and pre-determined conformation. The emerging active site exhibits the fundamental characteristics of the substrate binding site. The substrate's contact with the enzyme elicits a conformational change in the enzyme, leading to the establishment of a robust binding site for the substrate. Moreover, as a result of induced fit, the enzyme undergoes conformational changes that lead to the repositioning of the specific amino acids involved in the formation of the active site, hence facilitating the catalytic process. The induced fit model has garnered substantial empirical support through X-ray diffraction studies. Koshland's model additionally elucidates the mechanisms by which allosteric modulators and competitive inhibition exert their effects on enzymes.

The substrate strain theory states that the substrate experiences strain as a result of the conformational alteration generated by the enzyme. It is plausible that upon the binding of a substrate to the preexisting active site, the enzyme elicits a strain on the substrate. The presence of a stressed or strained substrate facilitates the generation of the desired product. The enzymatic action is believed to involve a combination of the induced fit model and substrate strain.

Other options:

Option A: The complementary active site of the enzyme binds to the substrate to form the product.

Option C: The active site of the enzyme is not complementary to the allosteric activator. Allosteric sites are separate and specific sites on the enzyme that are modulated with allosteric effect modifiers and hence are complementary to them.

Option D: The active site of the enzyme binds to the substrate which form a transitional state which is unstable and later dissociates to form a product.
questions.learning: Substrate — The substrate is complementary to the active site of the enzyme. The Lock and Key concept was put forth by Emil Fischer.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: During an appendectomy in a 2-year-old child, the surgeon incidentally discovers a 2-inch long structure located approximately 2 feet proximal to the ileocecal valve. What is the most likely diagnosis of this finding?
questions.explanation: The "Rule of 2s" is the classic aid for identifying Meckel's diverticulum (Option C): it is found in 2% of the population, is approximately 2 inches long, is located 2 feet (60 cm) proximal to the ileocecal valve, and often presents by 2 years of age. This incidental finding during abdominal surgery matches these exact dimensions. Meckel's is a remnant of the vitelline duct. Sarcoma (Option A) is a malignant tumor and would not present as a uniform diverticular structure. Appendicitis (Option B) refers to the inflammation of the appendix itself, not an additional small bowel structure. Zenker's diverticulum (Option D) is a pharyngeal pouch found in the neck, not the abdomen. Meckel's can contain ectopic gastric or pancreatic tissue, leading to painless lower gastrointestinal bleeding or intestinal obstruction. Therefore, based on the specific anatomical location and the "rule of 2s," it is the definitive diagnosis
questions.learning: The "Rule of 2s" is the classic aid for identifying Meckel's diverticulum (Option C): it is found in 2% of the population, is approximately 2 inches long, is located 2 feet (60 cm) proximal to the ileocecal valve, and often presents by 2 years of age.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: DNA packing is done by which of the following ?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Histone

The proteins involved in DNA packing are histones.

Chromatin contains double-stranded DNA molecules and small basic proteins known as histones. In addition, nonhistone proteins are present that are involved in DNA replication and repair, and RNA synthesis. Histones play a role in condensing the DNA.

Nucleosomes are the organizational unit of chromatin and contain an octamer of histones around which 150 base pairs of DNA are packed. There are various types of histone proteins. H2A, H2B, H3, and H4 groups are components of nucleosomes and are known as core histones. They undergo post-translational modifications such as acetylation and methylation. This plays a critical part in chromatin structure and function.

The DNA in the nucleosome is arranged in a left-handed helical configuration over the histone octamer.

Other options:

Option B - Glycoproteins are proteins with oligosaccharide chains (glycans) bound to amino acids. Certain plasma proteins, peptide hormones, and cell membrane proteins are examples. Structural changes in the glycoproteins present in cancer cells may play a role in metastasis.

Option C - Nucleic acids can be either DNA or RNA. DNA is thought to be arranged in a double-stranded helix model. RNA on the other hand exists as a single strand. There are different types of RNA such as mRNA (messenger RNA), tRNA (transfer RNA), and rRNA (ribosomal RNA).

Option D - Adenine is a purine base that when linked to ribose forms adenosine, a nucleoside. When a nucleoside is esterified with a phosphate group a nucleotide is formed. Guanine is the other purine base. Cytosine is the pyrimidine base common to DNA and RNA. Thymine is present only in DNA and Uracil in RNA.
questions.learning: Histone — The proteins involved in DNA packing are histones. Chromatin contains double-stranded DNA molecules and small basic proteins known as histones.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which therapy is given for cervical cancer?
questions.explanation: Platinum-based chemotherapy, specifically Cisplatin, is the gold standard for treating advanced, recurrent, or metastatic cervical cancer. It is most commonly used in "concurrent chemoradiation," where Cisplatin is administered alongside radiotherapy to act as a radiosensitizer, significantly improving survival rates in locally advanced cases. Option B (Hormonal therapy) is incorrect because cervical cancer is not hormone-dependent, unlike breast or endometrial cancers. While targeted therapy (Option C, e.g., Bevacizumab) and immunotherapy (Option A, e.g., Pembrolizumab) are increasingly used as adjuncts for specific indications, they are not the primary, first-line systemic treatment across all advanced stages. Carboplatin may also be used in patients who cannot tolerate Cisplatin due to renal issues. Therefore, because of its foundational role in standard chemoradiation protocols, platinum-based therapy is the most accurate answer for general cervical cancer management

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following glucose lowering agent can be given as an injectable drug?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Semaglutide

Semaglutide is a Glucagon-Like Peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonist used in the treatment of type 2 diabetes mellitus and obesity. It is administered as a subcutaneous injection once weekly, where it improves glycemic control by enhancing glucose-dependent insulin secretion, suppressing glucagon release, delaying gastric emptying, and promoting satiety.

Why is D correct?

• D. Semaglutide: A GLP-1 receptor agonist available as a once-weekly subcutaneous injection (an oral formulation is also available, but the injectable form is the classic exam answer). It also provides cardiovascular and weight-loss benefits.

Why are the other options incorrect?

• A. Pioglitazone: An oral thiazolidinedione (TZD) that improves insulin sensitivity.
• B. Metformin: An oral biguanide and the first-line drug for type 2 diabetes.
• C. Sitagliptin: An oral DPP-4 inhibitor that increases endogenous incretin levels.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient with a history of consumption of 2-3 drinks per week comes with complaints of right upper quadrant discomfort. He has grade 2 steatosis. His BMI was 29kg/m2 and AST and ALT levels were slightly elevated. What would you advise him?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Lifestyle modification and vitamin E

This patient with a history of consumption of 2-3 alcoholic drinks per week(acceptable limit is <5 per week for men)presents with right upper quadrant discomfort with a BMI of 29kg/m2 and slightly elevated AST and ALT most likely has nonalcoholic fatty liver disease(NAFLD). The first line for management of this condition is to advise him on lifestyle modifications and vitamin E. All the other options include drugs that are used off-label but are not FDA-approved for use in NAFLD.

Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) is associated with diabetes and obesity. The fatty change may also be caused due to the effect of toxins (including certain medications), protein malnutrition, dyslipidemia, and anoxia. Bleomycin, methotrexate, doxycycline, and l-Asparaginase are other drugs causing hepatic steatosis.

Most of the patients with NAFLD and NASH are asymptomatic. They are usually diagnosed incidentally on routine blood work. Some patients with NASH can present with right upper quadrant pain due to stretching of the liver capsule from hepatomegaly, or acanthosis nigricans due to insulin resistance or with signs like palmar erythema, spider telangiectasia, jaundice, splenomegaly, and ascites if they have liver cirrhosis. Currently, a biopsy is the gold standard investigation to establish the diagnosis.

The current approach to NAFLD management focuses on treatment to avoid or decrease the risk factors for NASH (like obesity, insulin resistance, metabolic syndrome, and dyslipidemia). For patients with morbid obesity, bariatric surgery can be done. In patients with decompensated cirrhosis, liver transplantation is can be considered.

Note: The FDA in 2024 has approved Resmetirom, a thyroid hormone receptor-beta (THR-beta) agonist for noncirrhotic NASH with moderate to advanced fibrosis.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: An alcoholic patient is admitted to the hospital 48 hours after his last alcohol intake. He presents with altered consciousness, disorientation, and marked agitation. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Delirium tremens (DT) is the most severe form of alcohol withdrawal, typically peaking 48–72 hours after the last drink. It is characterized by severe agitation, disorientation, altered consciousness, and autonomic instability (hypertension, tachycardia). This is a medical emergency with a significant mortality rate if untreated. Simple alcohol withdrawal symptoms (Option B) include milder tremors and anxiety that typically appear 6–12 hours after cessation. Cocaine intoxication (Option C) causes agitation but usually occurs immediately after use and presents with dilated pupils (mydriasis). Korsakoff psychosis (Option D) is a chronic thiamine deficiency complication involving permanent memory loss and confabulation rather than acute disorientation and severe agitation. Given the 48-hour timeline and the severity of the mental status changes, DT is the definitive diagnosis requiring ICU monitoring and benzodiazepine therapy

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: According to the RCH (Reproductive and Child Health) program guidelines, when should CuT 380A ideally be inserted to ensure maximum compliance? 1. Within 48 hours of delivery 2. Immediate post-partum 3. Within first 5-7 days of menstrual cycle 4. Within 7 days of next menstrual cycle
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 1, 2, 3

CuT-380A is a long-acting reversible contraceptive (LARC) widely promoted under India’s Reproductive and Child Health Programme and National Health Mission. It is a copper intrauterine contraceptive device (IUCD) effective for up to 10 years. IUCD is part of spacing methods in family planning.

As per RCH guidelines, CuT 380A insertion is ideal immediate post-partum, within 48 hours of delivery (PPIUCD), and within 5–7 days of the menstrual cycle, as these timings ensure high acceptance, convenience, and compliance.

Insertion within 7 days of the next menstrual cycle is not an ideal recommended window.

Advantages of CuT-380A are that it is long lasting, reversible, hormone free and cost effective.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A woman has been diagnosed with the congenital uterine malformation shown below. This condition occurs due to
options: Failure of fusion of Mullerian ducts
Failure of resorption of the uterine septum
Failure of development of one Mullerian duct
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Failure of development of one Mullerian duct

The given image shows a single developed half of the uterus with a rudimentary horn, consistent with a unicornuate uterus (non-communicating), which results from the failure of development of one Müllerian duct.

In the unicornuate uterus, the formation of the uterus and fallopian tube occurs entirely from one Müllerian duct due to the developmental arrest of the other Müllerian ducts. In this condition, a fully functional uterus, a normal cervix (option D), and a typical round ligament and fallopian tube are present on one side. On the opposite side, the Müllerian structures develop abnormally, often resulting in the absence (agenesis) or, more commonly, the presence of a rudimentary uterine horn.

A unicornuate uterus lacking a rudimentary horn presents as a compact, well-defined, elliptical uterus that tilts to one side. The upper part, or fundus, exhibits a concave shape. Three-dimensional imaging reveals a characteristic "banana" configuration for the unicornuate uterus. On Hysterosalpingography, the endometrial cavity usually appears in a fusiform shape tapering at the apex and draining into a single fallopian tube. The uterus generally appears shifted off the midline.

The ASRM (American Society of Reproductive Medicine) classification of Mullerian duct anomalies is as follows:

* Class I—Mullerian agenesis or hypoplasia.

* Class II—Unicornuate uterus, with absent or defective development of one Mullerian duct.

* Class III—Uterus didelphys

* Class IV—Bicornuate uterus

* Class V—Septate uterus

* Class VI—Arcuate uterus

* Class VII— DES related

Other options:

Option A: Failure of fusion of mullerian ducts leads to Uterus didelphys and Uterus bicornis.

Option B: Failure of resorption of the uterine septum leads to septate uterus.

Option C: In utero diethylstilbestrol exposure leads to type VII mullerian anomaly (DES related).

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which type of renal calculus is most commonly encountered?
questions.explanation: Renal calculi (kidney stones) are composed of various mineral crystals. Globally, calcium oxalate stones are the most prevalent type, accounting for roughly 75% to 80% of all cases. These stones are radio-opaque and can form in both acidic and alkaline urine. Triple phosphate (struvite) stones (Option C) are associated with urea-splitting bacterial infections (like Proteus) and can form large "staghorn" calculi. Uric acid stones (Option D) are unique because they are typically radiolucent (invisible on plain X-ray) and are linked to high purine intake or gout. Cystine stones (Option B) are rare and result from an inherited defect in amino acid transport. Factors promoting calcium oxalate formation include dehydration, hypercalciuria, and hyperoxaluria. Management focuses on adequate hydration and dietary modifications. Because calcium oxalate is the predominant mineral composition found in the majority of patients worldwide, it is the correct answer to this epidemiological question
questions.learning: Renal calculi (kidney stones) are composed of various mineral crystals. Globally, calcium oxalate stones are the most prevalent type, accounting for roughly 75% to 80% of all cases.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 24-year-old woman presents with a 3-day history of fever, headache, ataxia, nausea, and vomiting. On examination, she has neck stiffness and a positive Brudzinski’s sign. Lumbar puncture reveals cerebrospinal fluid with a markedly elevated white blood cell count predominantly composed of neutrophils, low glucose levels, and a positive latex agglutination test. Based on these findings, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The patient presents with the classic clinical triad of meningitis: fever, headache, and meningeal signs such as Brudzinski’s sign. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis is diagnostic and is consistent with acute pyogenic (bacterial) meningitis. Key CSF findings include a markedly elevated white blood cell count (>1000 cells/mm³) with neutrophil predominance and significantly reduced CSF glucose (<40 mg/dL or <50% of blood glucose). In addition, a positive latex agglutination test supports the diagnosis by detecting specific bacterial antigens, commonly Streptococcus pneumoniae or Neisseria meningitidis. Tubercular meningitis (Option B) and fungal meningitis (Option D) typically show lymphocytic pleocytosis, moderately reduced glucose, and a more subacute or chronic course. Viral meningitis (Option C) is characterized by normal CSF glucose, lymphocytic predominance, and a lower total WBC count. Therefore, the presence of neutrophilic pleocytosis with low glucose confirms a bacterial etiology, making Option A: Acute bacterial meningitis the definitive diagnosis. Immediate intravenous antibiotic therapy is essential to reduce morbidity and mortality
questions.learning: The patient presents with the classic clinical triad of meningitis: fever, headache, and meningeal signs such as Brudzinski’s sign. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis is diagnostic and is consistent with acute pyogenic (bacterial) meningitis.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 20-year-old man presents to the outpatient department with a swelling over the wrist that varies in size, associated with mild hand numbness and occasional pain. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical presentation of a wrist swelling that fluctuates in size and causes occasional pain or numbness is highly characteristic of a ganglion cyst. These are benign, fluid-filled sacs that typically arise from joint capsules or tendon sheaths, most commonly on the dorsal aspect of the wrist. Numbness may occur if the cyst compresses an adjacent nerve. A lipoma (Option A) is a soft, fatty mass that does not typically fluctuate in size or arise directly from joint structures. A dermoid cyst (Option C) is usually congenital, midline, and contains ectodermal elements like hair or sebum. A hematoma (Option D) follows acute trauma and presents with bruising and initial pain that subsides as it resolves. Diagnosis of a ganglion is confirmed by its translucent nature on transillumination and clinical location
questions.learning: The clinical presentation of a wrist swelling that fluctuates in size and causes occasional pain or numbness is highly characteristic of a ganglion cyst.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: A young patient sustained a head injury following a road traffic accident. His family members complain that his behavior has changed following the incident. He is extremely curious and tries touching everything. He forgets everything rapidly, and he tries to keep everything in his mouth. He even tried to eat the plates. They have also noticed him squeezing his genitals. Which of the following structures is most likely to be damaged in this patient?
options: Gray matter around aqueduct of Sylvius
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Amygdala

Increased curiosity, hyperorality, memory loss, and increased sex drive are the features of Kluver Bucy syndrome. This occurs due to the damage to the amygdala.

Features of Kluver Bucy syndrome are:

* Fearlessness

* Increased curiosity

* Memory loss

* Patient tries to keep everything in the mouth, even the solid objects that are not meant for eating

* Increased sex drive

Functions of amygdala:

It receives neuronal signals from the neocortex of the temporal, parietal, and occipital lobes, especially from the auditory and visual association areas. It transmits signals to the same cortical areas, thalamus, hypothalamus, and hippocampus. Stimulation of the amygdala leads to alterations in arterial pressure, heart rate, gastrointestinal motility, piloerection, and abnormal tonic circling and clinic movements. It also has role in olfaction.

Other options:

Option A- Gray matter around the aqueduct of Sylvius is the punishment center. Stimulation of punishment centers leads to the inhibition of reward and pleasure centers completely. Punishment and fear will be more prominent than pleasure and reward.

Option C- Lateral nuclei of hypothalamus primarily control hunger and feeding behavior. Stimulation of this area gives a sense of reward

Option D- Damage to the anterior cingulate gyri releases the rage centers of septum and hypothalamus from the prefrontal inhibitory influence. Therefore the patient becomes very aggressive.
questions.learning: Amygdala Increased curiosity, hyperorality, memory loss, and increased sex drive are the features of Kluver Bucy syndrome. This occurs due to the damage to the amygdala.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which among the following are the yoke muscles of levodepression?
options: Right superior oblique (SO) and left inferior rectus (IR)
Right superior oblique (SO) and left inferior oblique (IO)
Right medial rectus (MR) and left medial rectus (MR)
Right medial rectus (MR) and right lateral rectus (LR)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Right superior oblique (SO) and left inferior rectus (IR)

Right superior oblique (SO) and left inferior rectus (IR) are the yoke muscle pair for levodepression.

The term "yoke muscles" refers to contralateral synergists.

* Includes a pair of muscles, one from each eye, which contract simultaneously during version movements.

* Examples are

* Right MR and Left LR for levoversion

* Right LR and Left MR for dextroversion

In an outward deviated eye, the elevation and depression is by recti. So here, one of the muscles is left inferior rectus.

Easy method to determine other muscle yoke muscle pairs:

Just take the opposite of each word:

Left  → Right

Inferior → Superior

Rectus → Oblique

So right superior rectus is the pair.

Similarly, the following are yoke muscle pairs:

* Right IO and Left SR - Levoelevation

* Right SR and Left IO - Dextroelevation

* Right IR and Left SO - Dextrodepression
questions.learning: Right superior oblique (SO) and left inferior rectus (IR) Right superior oblique (SO) and left inferior rectus (IR) are the yoke muscle pair for levodepression.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A preterm baby who was delivered at 28 weeks developed respiratory distress syndrome. Which of the following is true about surface tension and compliance in this baby?
options: Both surface tension and compliance decreased
Both surface tension and compliance increased
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Surface tension - increased; Compliance - decreased

Preterm infants lack adequate surfactant, leading to increased alveolar surface tension.

High surface tension causes alveolar collapse, resulting in decreased lung compliance and increased work of breathing.

This pathophysiology underlies neonatal respiratory distress syndrome.

Prematurity (Type II pneumocytes immature)

↑ Surface tension in alveoli

Alveolar collapse (atelectasis)

↓ Lung compliance (stiff lungs)

Respiratory distress

| Option | Surface Tension | Compliance | When it is Correct | Why NOT Correct Here | Exam Pearl

| ------ | --------------- | ---------- | ------------------ | -------------------- | ----------

| A | ↓ | ↑ | Surfactant excess | ❌ Opposite of RDS | Seen in therapy

| B ✅ | ↑ | ↓ | ✔ Surfactant deficiency | ✔ Correct | Classic NRDS

| C | ↓ | ↓ | Mixed pattern | ❌ Surface tension actually ↑ | Illogical combo

| D | ↑ | ↑ | Not physiologically valid | ❌ Compliance always ↓ with ↑ tension | Trap option

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: The greenish-black color of the first stool in the newborn is due to :
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Biliverdin

The greenish-black color of the first stool in the newborn is due to biliverdin.

Meconium is a dark, viscous material that is normally present in the intestine of the fetus and passed within 1st 48hour of life. Meconium appears after the 20th week and at term, it is uniformly distributed throughout the gut up to the rectum indicating the presence of intestinal peristalsis.

It is composed of various products of secretion, such as desquamated fetal cells, glycerophospholipids from the lungs, lanugo, scalp hair, vernix, and undigested products from swallowed amniotic fluid. The greenish-black color of meconium is due to the presence of bile pigments excreted by the biliary tract, especially biliverdin (pigment from the oxidation of bilirubin).

During intrauterine hypoxia, the relaxation of the anal sphincter due to vagal stimulation can lead to the passage of meconium into the amniotic fluid. Additionally, the release of arginine vasopressin (AVP) from the fetal pituitary gland due to intrauterine hypoxia can stimulate the colon muscles to contract, resulting in intraamniotic defecation. Meconium aspiration syndrome can occur when meconium is inhaled, as it is toxic to the lungs.

Other options:

Option A: Bilirubin is responsible for the yellow color of the stools.

Option D: Neonates do not harbor gut flora at birth.
questions.learning: Biliverdin — The greenish-black color of the first stool in the newborn is due to biliverdin. Meconium is a dark, viscous material that is normally present in the intestine of the fetus and passed within 1st 48hour of life.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: In a patient who sustains trauma leading to rupture of the bulbar urethra, in which anatomical space is urine most likely to collect?
questions.explanation: The bulbar urethra is the portion of the male urethra located within the superficial perineal pouch. A rupture of this structure, often caused by a "straddle injury" or a fall into a manhole, leads to the extravasation of urine and blood into the superficial perineal space. This space is bounded by Colles’ fascia, which is continuous with the Dartos fascia of the scrotum and Scarpa’s fascia of the abdominal wall. Consequently, urine tracks into the scrotum, penis, and anterior abdominal wall, but not into the thighs or the anal region. The deep perineal pouch (Option B) contains the membranous urethra; a rupture here would have a different extravasation pattern. Options C (Rectouterine pouch/Pouch of Douglas) and D (Uterovesical pouch) are intraperitoneal structures in females and are irrelevant to a male bulbar urethral injury. Clinical signs include a "butterfly-shaped" hematoma in the perineum and blood at the external urethral meatus, requiring retrograde urethrography for definitive diagnosis

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which of the following tests can be done for measuring long-term glucose control in patients with diabetes mellitus?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. HbA1c

In patients with diabetes mellitus, HbA1c is the best method to measure long-term glucose control.

Glycated haemoglobin, reported as HbA1c, has been used to monitor glycemic control in patients with diabetes for many years. HbA1c results from the attachment of glucose to the N-terminal valine of the hemoglobin β-chain.

The concentration of HbA1c depends on both the glucose concentration in the blood and the lifespan of the erythrocyte.

Since the half-life of an RBC is 120 days, the HbA1c test is primarily used to evaluate the average blood glucose levels over the past 3 months. Normal glucose tolerance is characterised by an HbA1c < 5.7%; any value of HbA1c equal to or exceeding 6.5 % is diagnostic of the patient being diabetic.

Other options:

Fasting blood sugar, random blood sugar, and urine sugar reflect the status of blood glucose level at the instantaneous moment.
questions.learning: HbA1c — In patients with diabetes mellitus, HbA1c is the best method to measure long-term glucose control. Glycated haemoglobin, reported as HbA1c, has been used to monitor glycemic control in patients with diabetes for many years.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: A patient has a blood glucose level of 200 mg/dL and GFR of 90 ml/min. What is the amount of glucose excreted if the transport maximum of the patient is as shown below?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 30 mg/min

The amount of glucose excreted in the above scenario is 30 mg/min.

Calculation:

Step 1: Calculate total filtered glucose:

In this question,

• GFR = 90 ml/min
• Plasma glucose concentration = 200 mg/dL= 2 mg/ml (1 dL=100 ml).
• Total filtered glucose = GFR X Plasma glucose concentration.

= 90 ml/min X 2 mg/ml
= 180 mg/min.

Step 2: Check transport maximum:

In the above question transport maximum is 150 mg/min.

Step 3: Calculate the excretion:

Excretion = Total filtered glucose - Total reabsorbed glucose (Transport Maximum)

= 180-150 mg/min
= 30 mg/min

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: When are the three doses of fIPV ideally given as per the National Immunization Schedule?
options: 3 doses at 6 weeks, 14 weeks, and 9 completed months
At 10 weeks, 14 weeks, and 9 completed months
At 6 weeks, 10 weeks, and 18 completed months
3 doses at 6 weeks, 14 weeks, and 18 completed months
questions.explanation: According to the updated National Immunization Schedule in India, Fractional Inactivated Poliovirus Vaccine (fIPV) is now administered in a three-dose schedule. The ideal timings for these intradermal doses are at 6 weeks, 14 weeks, and finally at 9 completed months (concurrently with the first dose of the Measles-Rubella vaccine). Options B, C, and D provide incorrect timing or dose counts for the standard schedule. The addition of the third dose at 9 months is a critical recent change to ensure robust and long-lasting immunity as part of the global effort to eradicate polio. fIPV uses a smaller volume (0.1 ml) than the full intramuscular IPV but provides comparable immunity. This schedule is integrated with other childhood vaccinations to ensure maximum coverage and protection. Ensuring every child receives all three doses is essential for preventing the re-emergence of wild or vaccine-derived polioviruses
questions.learning: According to the updated National Immunization Schedule in India, Fractional Inactivated Poliovirus Vaccine (fIPV) is now administered in a three-dose schedule.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A fracture of the cribriform plate has occurred. What symptom is the patient most likely to present with?
questions.explanation: The cribriform plate of the ethmoid bone is a thin, fragile, perforated structure that forms the roof of the nasal cavity and the floor of the anterior cranial fossa. It is in direct contact with the meninges and the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF). A fracture in this specific area often causes a dural tear, resulting in CSF rhinorrhea, where clear fluid leaks from the intracranial space into the nose. This is often accompanied by anosmia (loss of smell) due to damage to the olfactory nerve fibers. Hearing loss (Option A) is associated with temporal bone fractures. Visual loss (Option B) or diplopia (Option D) usually results from fractures involving the orbit or sphenoid bone. CSF rhinorrhea is a significant clinical finding because it creates a potential pathway for bacteria to cause meningitis. Management involves bed rest and precautions to avoid intracranial pressure spikes while the dural tear heals
questions.learning: The cribriform plate of the ethmoid bone is a thin, fragile, perforated structure that forms the roof of the nasal cavity and the floor of the anterior cranial fossa.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following best helps assess the quality of healthcare provided?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Ishikawa diagram/ Fish bone diagram

Ishikawa diagram or else better known as the fishbone diagram helps sketch out problems that affect healthcare in a community and thus uses those as pointers to better address them in the community.

The Ishikawa diagram, often known as the fishbone diagram, is employed by teams aiming to comprehend the numerous potential factors that contribute to a quality of care issue. This tool enables teams to concentrate their development endeavours on these identified causes. The utilization of this tool is applicable across several phases of the quality improvement framework, with its primary application commonly observed within the context of root cause analysis.

The fishbone graphic bears a resemblance to the skeletal structure of a fish. To depict the diagram about a quality of care issue, the problem (effect) is encapsulated within a box positioned on the extreme right of the diagram. A vertical line, referred to as the centre line or spine, is then positioned to the left of the box where the problem is documented. Subsequently, diagonal lines resembling fish bones are sketched emanating from the central line, also known as the spine. The diagonal lines depicted in the diagram signify distinct categorizations of the underlying factors contributing to the issue. Supplementary branches may also be delineated from the primary skeletal structure to symbolize underlying factors leading to the causes.

The groupings are typically structured into categories, commonly known as the five Ps (patients/clients, providers, policies, processes and procedures, and place/equipment), the six Ms (machine, method, materials, measurement, man, and Mother Nature), and the four Ss (surroundings, suppliers, systems, and skills). Nevertheless, the groupings need to be tailored to the organization and problem being investigated. The responsibility for ensuring this specificity lies with the quality improvement team. Once the categories have been delineated, the quality improvement team proceeds to partake in a brainstorming session to identify causes that are specific to each respective grouping. The aforementioned procedure persists until the team reaches a point where they are unable to ascertain any further underlying factors.

Other options:

Option A: Logistic regression may be used in some situations where we are not interested in a numerical outcome (like risk, etc) but we want a nominal or categorical one (like death/survival, developing a disease/not developing a disease). Here, the relationship between the variables will not be a linear one as the outcome from survival to death in relationship with the risk factor can change suddenly. Thus these outcomes are represented by 0 and 1.

Option B: A bar graph is a pictorial way of presenting a set of numbers, the magnitudes of which are proportional to the length of the bars in the graph. It can be simple, multiple, or component bar graphs and enable values to be compared visually. They are used to compare a single variable value between several groups.

Option C: A scatter plot is a statistical map used to study the correlation between two given variables. In scatter plots or scatter diagrams, the pattern made by plotted points along the two axes indicates the possible relationship. If the dots cluster along a straight line, then the relationship is linear. If there is no cluster, then there might be no relationship. Below is an example of a scatter diagram without a linear relation.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: The most potent natural estrogen is?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Estradiol

Estradiol (E₂) is the most potent natural estrogen with the highest receptor affinity. Estrone is predominant post-menopause, while estriol is weakest and rises in pregnancy.

| Estrogen Type | Source / Predominance | Potency | Key Feature

| ------------- | --------------------- | ------- | -----------

| Estradiol | Ovaries (reproductive years) | Most potent | Highest receptor affinity, main active estrogen

| Estrone | Postmenopausal women | Moderate | Main estrogen after menopause

| Estriol | Pregnancy | Weakest | Predominant during pregnancy

Estradiol is the main estrogen during reproductive years.

Source

• Granulosa cells of ovarian follicles
• Produced from androgens via aromatase enzyme

Major functions

| Function | Effect

| -------- | ------

| Endometrial proliferation | Prepares uterus for implantation

| Secondary sexual characters | Breast development

| Bone metabolism | Prevents osteoporosis

| Cervical mucus | Makes it thin and receptive

Estradiol dominates during the follicular phase of menstrual cycle.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: What is the drug of choice for scrub typhus?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Doxycycline

The drug of choice for scrub typhus is doxycycline.

To treat scrub typhus, oral doxycycline 100 mg is given twice daily for 7–15 days. In the case of pregnant women, oral azithromycin 500 mg for 3 days may be used as doxycycline is contraindicated in pregnancy.

Scrub typhus is a rickettsial infection caused by Orientia tsutsugamushi. The vector is a trombiculid mite. Humans are infected when they are bitten by the mite larvae known as chiggers. The incubation period is 1- 3 weeks. Patients develop a characteristic eschar at the site of the mite bite, along with regional lymphadenopathy and maculopapular rash. It can be associated with fever, headache, myalgia, meningoencephalitis, myocarditis, and pneumonia.

Serologic assays are used for diagnosis. Weil-Felix reaction is a heterophile agglutination reaction used for diagnosis, wherein the sera are tested for agglutinins to the O antigens of Proteus strains OX19, OX2, and OXK. OXK alone is agglutinated in scrub typhus.
questions.learning: Doxycycline — The drug of choice for scrub typhus is doxycycline. To treat scrub typhus, oral doxycycline 100 mg is given twice daily for 7–15 days.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: The enzyme deficient in Von Gierke's disease is ?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Glucose 6-phosphatase

Von Gierke disease is due to the deficiency of glucose 6-phosphatase.

Signs and symptoms of von Gierke disease are

* Seizures

* Doll-like facies (fat cheeks and relatively thin extremities)

* Hepatomegaly

* Growth retardation

* Hypoglycemia (blood glucose <60 mg/dL)

* Blood uric acid levels >5 mg/dL

* Lactic acidosis

* Elevated cholesterol and triglycerides

* Neutropenia (specific to Ib)

Treatment of von Gierke includes

* Maintenance of glucose levels by infusion of glucose or the use of uncooked cornstarch (as this is catabolized also by the debranching enzyme).

* Mild to moderate restriction of lactose, fructose, and sucrose.

* Ensure adequate intake of vitamins and minerals.

* Nicotinic acid, fibrates therapy should be started if triglyceride levels are >900 mg/dL, despite dietary therapy.

* Allopurinol (10 mg/kg/day) should be started for hyperuricemia if uncontrolled on dietary therapy.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: During a post-mortem examination, the hands are found to be clenched with no evidence of primary relaxation. What does this finding indicate?
questions.explanation: Cadaveric spasm (instantaneous rigor) is a rare post-mortem finding where the muscles that were in a state of high tension or voluntary contraction at the moment of death remain contracted, bypassing the usual stage of primary muscular relaxation. This is most characteristically observed as contracted hands tightly grasping an object (like a weapon or weeds in drowning). Rigor mortis (Option A) is the gradual stiffening of all muscles that develops 1–2 hours after a period of primary relaxation. Livor mortis (Option B) is the post-mortem settling of blood. Algor mortis (Option D) is the cooling of the body. Cadaveric spasm is of great medico-legal importance as it serves as definitive proof that the individual was actively performing a movement at the exact moment they died, which can help differentiate between suicide and homicide. It cannot be imitated post-mortem. Therefore, the immediate "frozen" state of contraction without prior relaxation is the defining feature of this rare phenomenon
questions.learning: Cadaveric spasm (instantaneous rigor) is a rare post-mortem finding where the muscles that were in a state of high tension or voluntary contraction at the moment of death remain contracted, bypassing the usual stage of primary muscular relaxation.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 45-year-old woman presents with acute pain and swelling of the great toe, and laboratory tests show hyperuricemia. To manage her condition, which enzyme should be inhibited by the chosen medication to lower uric acid levels?
questions.explanation: The patient is suffering from an acute attack of gout, caused by hyperuricemia. To long-term reduce uric acid levels and prevent further attacks, the standard pharmacological approach is to inhibit the enzyme Xanthine oxidase. This enzyme is responsible for the final steps of purine catabolism, converting hypoxanthine to xanthine and then xanthine to uric acid. Medications like Allopurinol and Febuxostat work by inhibiting this enzyme, thereby lowering the production of uric acid. Urease (Option A) is a bacterial enzyme not found in humans. Homogentisate oxidase (Option B) is the enzyme deficient in Alkaptonuria. Lysyl oxidase (Option C) is involved in collagen cross-linking. While acute gout is treated with NSAIDs or colchicine, xanthine oxidase inhibitors are the mainstay for chronic urate-lowering therapy. Understanding this biochemical pathway is essential for managing metabolic disorders related to purine metabolism and preventing the painful joint destruction and renal stones associated with chronic gout
questions.learning: The patient is suffering from an acute attack of gout, caused by hyperuricemia. To long-term reduce uric acid levels and prevent further attacks, the standard pharmacological approach is to inhibit the enzyme Xanthine oxidase.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text:
A 40-year-old man presents to the ER with severe abdominal pain. On examination, his HR is 110bpm, BP- 88/60mmHg. On per abdomen examination, guarding is present. The erect abdominal X-ray is shown below. Which of the following would you proceed with, for the management of this case?

1. USG abdomen
2. IV fluids
3. Exploratory laparotomy
4. Elective surgery
5. Conservative management
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 2 & 3

The given clinical scenario and erect X-ray abdomen showing gas under the diaphragm are suggestive of pneumoperitoneum, which is managed by initial resuscitation with IV fluids followed by exploratory laparotomy.

Pneumoperitoneum is the presence of air or gas in the peritoneal cavity. The most common cause of pneumoperitoneum is a perforation of a hollow viscus.  Other causes of pneumoperitoneum in adults include peritoneal dialysis, and mechanical ventilation, after procedures like colonoscopy and endoscopy. In children, it can be caused by necrotizing enterocolitis, hirschsprung's disease, meconium ileus and mechanical ventilation.

The patient presents with abdominal pain and distension, vomiting, fever, constipation, tachycardia, tachypnea, hypotension, and reduced urine output. Per-abdomen examination can show guarding and rigidity.

An erect X-ray abdomen is highly sensitive for the detection of free intraperitoneal gas. Some of the signs seen in the X-ray include:

• Cupola sign is the presence of air underneath the diaphragm, giving a dome-like appearance.
• Rigler's sign is where both bowel surfaces are seen together as a sharp margin.
• Falciform ligament sign is the outlining of the falciform ligament with free abdominal gas.
• Liver/gallbladder edge sign is where the sharp margins of the liver/gallbladder are visible due to the collection of air.

Management includes,

• Adequate preoperative resuscitation with intravenous fluids followed by correction of electrolyte imbalance, instituting broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics and
• Early surgical intervention/laparotomy to address the cause of pneumoperitoneum and prevent further contamination of the peritoneal cavity.
questions.learning: 2 & 3 The given clinical scenario and erect X-ray abdomen showing gas under the diaphragm are suggestive of pneumoperitoneum, which is managed by initial resuscitation with IV fluids followed by exploratory laparotomy.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 27-year-old woman presents with menstrual irregularities, acne, and excessive hair growth. What is the first-line approach to management?
questions.explanation: The patient's presentation of irregular cycles, acne, and hirsutism is highly suggestive of Polycystic Ovary Syndrome (PCOS). For all PCOS patients, the definitive first-line management is lifestyle modification, which includes weight loss, a healthy diet, and regular exercise. Even a modest 5% reduction in body weight can significantly improve hormonal balance, restore ovulation, and enhance insulin sensitivity. Oral Contraceptive Pills (Option C) are the first-line medical therapy specifically for regulating menstrual cycles and treating hirsutism, but they follow lifestyle changes. Metformin (Option A) is an insulin sensitizer used primarily for patients with metabolic issues or insulin resistance. Clomiphene citrate (Option D) is used for ovulation induction in patients seeking fertility but is not the general first-line management for the syndrome itself. Thus, non-pharmacological interventions are prioritized to address the underlying metabolic disturbances of PCOS

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: What is the most common clinical effect observed with cannabis use?
questions.explanation: Cannabis is a psychoactive substance derived from the hemp plant. Its most characteristic and predominant manifestation is the induction of a dream-like state or "high," marked by altered perception of time, heightened sensory awareness, and euphoria. Other common acute features include conjunctival injection ("red eyes") and a significant increase in appetite (the "munchies"), making Option D incorrect. While anxiety (Option A) can occur—especially in high doses or "bad trips"—it is not the typical primary desired effect. Depressed mood (Option B) is generally not the immediate effect of cannabis use. Long-term use is associated with an "amotivational syndrome" characterized by apathy and social withdrawal. In a psychiatric and forensic context, recognizing this dream-like state and the characteristic physical signs is essential for identifying cannabis intoxication. The primary active component, THC, acts on receptors in the brain to modulate neurotransmission and produce these classic psychological effects

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 35-year-old woman at 32 weeks of pregnancy is being evaluated for possible induction or augmentation of labor using oxytocin. Considering the potential risks associated with this drug, which of the following conditions represents a contraindication to the use of oxytocin?
options: Induction of labor in post-term pregnancy
Augmentation of labor in case of slow progress
Preterm labor with cervical dilation of 3 cm
questions.explanation: The condition where the placenta covers the internal os is known as Placenta Previa (specifically Type IV/Central). This is an absolute contraindication for both vaginal delivery and the use of oxytocin. Inducing contractions in a woman with placenta previa would lead to catastrophic maternal hemorrhage as the placenta is torn during cervical changes. Induction for post-term pregnancy (Option B) and augmentation for slow progress (Option C) are the primary, standard clinical indications for oxytocin use. Preterm labor (Option D) is managed with tocolytics to stop contractions, but the presence of cervical dilation doesn't necessarily make oxytocin a direct contraindication, though it would be counterproductive unless termination is intended. Other absolute contraindications for oxytocin include a previous classical cesarean scar and active genital herpes. Proper obstetric management requires identifying the placental position via ultrasound before any attempt at induction to avoid life-threatening bleeding during the initiation of labor

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A patient started on antihypertensive presented with the following picture. Which of the following drugs is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Lisinopril

The image shows edema over the lips and face and its occurrence following intake of an antihypertensive is suggestive of drug-induced angioedema. Lisinopril being an ACE inhibitor is most likely to be responsible for this condition.

Angioedema with ACE inhibitors:

In very few patients(0.1%-0.5%), ACE inhibitors cause rapid swelling in the nose, throat, mouth, glottis, larynx, lips, or tongue. Once the drug is stopped symptoms improve drastically over hours. Angioedema of the intestine can occur very rarely.

ACE inhibitor-associated angioedema is a class effect, and patients who develop this adverse event should not be prescribed any other drugs within the ACE inhibitor class.

Other adverse effects of ACE inhibitors:

Hypotension - A sudden fall in blood pressure can occur following the first dose of ACE inhibitors.

Cough - It can produce a bothersome dry cough due to the accumulation of bradykinin, substance P, or prostaglandins in the lungs. The cough usually disappears within 4 days of the stoppage of the drug.

Hyperkalemia due to K+ retention can occur.

Acute renal failure can occur with ACE inhibitors in patients with bilateral renal artery stenosis, stenosis of the artery to a single remaining kidney, heart failure, or volume depletion due to diarrhea or diuretics.

It should be discontinued in pregnant women as it can cause developmental defects.

It can also cause maculopapular skin rash in some cases.

Other options:

Option B: Nifedipine is a calcium channel blocker. Common adverse effects include headache, flushing, and dizziness. Peripheral edema may rarely occur.

Option C: Atenolol is a beta 1 selective antagonist. Bradycardia, fatigue, cold extremities are common adverse effects. CNS side effects like nightmares and depression are less frequent with atenolol than other beta-blockers.

Option D: Clonidine is an alpha-2 adrenergic agonist. The main adverse effects of clonidine are dry mouth and sedation. Bradycardia and sexual dysfunction are other effects.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient with peripheral edema has the following findings on clinical examination: • A soft systolic murmur at the lower left sternal border with raised JVP showing prominent C-V wave. • The murmur increases in intensity on deep inspiration. The most likely valvular abnormality is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Tricuspid regurgitation

Tricuspid regurgitation (TR) presents with a pansystolic murmur best heard at the lower left sternal border, prominent C-V waves in the JVP, and a murmur that increases with inspiration (Carvallo sign) due to increased venous return to the right heart. Peripheral edema and raised JVP are features of right-sided heart failure.

Why not the other options?

• A. Ventricular septal defect: Harsh pansystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border but no prominent C-V waves or inspiratory accentuation.
• B. Mitral regurgitation: Pansystolic murmur best heard at the apex, radiating to the axilla; does not increase with inspiration.
• D. Mitral valve prolapse: Characterized by a mid-systolic click followed by a late systolic murmur, best heard at the apex.
